A new model for efficient energy harvesting in wireless communication systems is introduced, where the capacity to collect energy is tied to the received bit signals rather than the signal power. This leads to a distinct approach to managing energy consumption in such systems, which necessitates a fresh look at how to allocate resources, particularly in diverse wireless communication systems that support multiple services. To address this, a novel resource allocation scheme is developed to optimize a utility function subject to energy constraints. An iterative algorithm combining successive convex approximation and Chambolle-Proximal Alternating Linearized Minimization is implemented to solve this complex optimization problem. Further, performance metrics such as sum-rate and energy efficiency are used to evaluate and extend the existing literature on multi-user systems, which often relies on suboptimal methods. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms these suboptimal methods and achieves close-to-optimal performance. Additionally, a framework for evaluating energy efficiency is developed, which can be applied to various multiple-access techniques and is subsequently applied to evaluate the time division multiple-access technique. Simulation results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods and show a significant improvement in energy efficiency with only a minor reduction in sum-rate. These findings offer a framework for practical design of such techniques and can serve as a benchmark to gauge the effectiveness of other methods. Furthermore, the study sheds light on the underlying physics of a critical problem in energy harvesting communication systems, which is the optimal trade-off between energy extraction and information transmission. It is observed that at high signal-to-noise ratios, the optimal trade-off is governed by a simple formula and approaches a constant value, which depends solely on the specific modulation scheme used rather than the underlying wireless channel conditions. Conversely, at low signal-to-noise ratios, the optimal trade-off is more complex and influenced by various factors, including the specific modulation scheme, diversity order, and complexity of the wireless channel. These observations provide valuable insights into the critical problem of optimal trade-off and can be applied to guide general design principles in various communication systems. Finally, the study examines the statistical distribution of sum-rate and energy efficiency in various multiple-access techniques and finds that these distributions can be accurately modeled using simple formulas, which offer a convenient way to estimate performance metrics and make reliable predictions about system behavior. Furthermore, the study reveals that the average sum-rate and energy efficiency are strongly correlated in time division multiple-access systems and suggests a simple formula to gauge this correlation. The optical resonator, a central component of microwave optomechanics, is often constructed using dielectric cylinders and must be treated as a complex system due to its diverse physical properties.  However, these properties can be effectively simulated using electrical circuit models, which are useful for analytical calculations and designing new devices.  Specifically, we have developed an electrical circuit formula for COM systems consisting of a clamped mechanical diaphragm, which simplifies complex analytical considerations and enables a more intuitive understanding of the system's behavior. We propose a new class of autonomous navigation methods, 'unruly shifts', which enable robots to seamlessly move along uneven walls in dynamic environments by shifting their body frame without changing their overall path. Unlike traditional wall following techniques that rely on a constant body frame, unruly shifts allow for dynamic changes in the body frame, making them more suitable for agile robots. Two types of unruly shifts - 'geometric' and 'collision', are developed to address different environmental challenges. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this framework in a variety of scenarios, and its relevance to actual robotic platforms is also illustrated using a mobile robot equipped with a ring of LEDs. Moreover, the paper provides a mathematical proof of the feasibility and stability of this navigation framework. Code and demonstration videos are available at https://tinyurl.com/unruly-shifts. This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are isomorphic to chiral CFT subalgebras from the Minkowski spacetime context.  By comparing the properties of these subalgebras with those from the Minkowski spacetime, the article establishes key equivalences and similarities.  As in the Minkowski spacetime, we find that the chiral CFT algebra is a contractive factorization of the 2dcft algebra, with this relationship reflecting a type of 'chirality' in 2dcft.  The article also examines the geometric interpretation of chiral CFT algebras and its connections to 'pointwise chiral' 2dcft aspects, and discusses potential generalizations of these results to QFT on manifolds with non-trivial geometries.  Along the way, we derive new explicit expressions for Bell functions in globally hyperbolic spacetimes, and prove that these functions can be expressed through a transformation similar to the Radon transform.  This involves a novel 'chirality'-related generalization of the Fourier transform, which we call the Hankel transform.  We further demonstrate that the Hankel transform can be used to implement an isometry between the spectra of the chiral CFT algebra and the 2dcft algebra.  We further explore the relations between the Hankel and Fourier transforms, and explain how these transforms' properties in various contexts are interconnected.  In a broader context, the article's results provide a chiral analysis of 2dcft that is both geometric and physically meaningful.  This offers a new perspective on the interplay between chiral and anti-chiral aspects, and their relationships to global spacetime structures and properties. Preventive measures against smoke formation during laparoscopic surgery are often disregarded, leading to a need for pre-surgical enforcement through high-quality visual smoke detection in operative videos. To enhance the reliability of smoke detection, we propose an approach that incorporates pre-processing to improve image quality, as common low-quality images hinder existing detection methods. Preliminary assessments reveal that this pre-processing method has a beneficial impact on smoke identification. Specifically, high-quality image enhancement increased the accuracy of smoke detection in low-quality images, while also demonstrating comparable results in high-quality images. Consequently, integrating image enhancement into current smoke detection techniques has the potential to improve performance. To date, advanced pre-surgical training protocols primarily rely on artificial smoke integration, assuming that genuine smoke appears in the same manner; however, this method has yet to be validated. To address this limitation, we conducted thorough assessments of our image enhancement and smoke detection algorithm, analyzing a vast dataset of 42 laparoscopic surgery videos totaling approximately 13 hours, to ensure that our approach can effectively detect genuine smoke in unedited surgical footage. Our image enhancement and smoke detection algorithm demonstrated an accuracy of 85.7% across the entire dataset, confirming that our method can differentiate between high-quality images without and with genuine smoke, as well as low-quality images without smoke. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first instance of successfully integrating image enhancement and smoke detection in a laparoscopic surgery video analysis. Our proposed algorithm has potential to enable the development of pre-surgical training protocols that utilize actual surgical footage, thereby enhancing the reliability of smoke formation prevention. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of Hecke cusp forms within the graded holomorphic cusp forms series is finite, specifically proving that

$$
\left|\sum_{n=1}^\infty|e_4(n)|^4\right|<\frac{N\pi^2}{\sigma_4(1)},
$$

In interior point methods (IPMs), an iterative solution formulation is often employed to tackle large-scale linear systems that arise within optimization frameworks. Specifically, IPMs often utilize the Newton method augmented with a tangent space projection operator to optimize a variable. This tangent space projection can be computed efficiently using the Barrairol-Hertzberg or the Combinatory Newton method, which rely on specialized Krylov solver variants. These solvers' conventional termination criteria, however, do not account for the specific optimization context in which they are applied. Consequently, they may cause the solver to expend undue computational effort on 'interior' iterations. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel termination criterion tailored to the optimal cluster solver framework (OCSF) and its Conjugate Residues variant (CR). By leveraging a quadratic model of the optimal cluster equations and analyzing its properties, we develop a termination criterion that capitalizes on the structural properties of the IPM's equations. This new criterion is substantively sparse, making it particularly suitable for large-scale problem sets. Additionally, we demonstrate that its computational intricacies can be circumvented by revisiting the residual polynomial's coefficients, thereby facilitating the development of an alternative and more efficient termination criterion. This novel criterion is initially validated in the context of the QP problem but is subsequently shown to be adaptable and effective in a broader range of IPM applications, including both smooth and non-smooth optimization contexts. Experimental studies confirm that the proposed criterion significantly enhances the method's robustness, precision, and computational efficiency. Specifically, we found that its incorporation leads to a noticeable reduction in the number of iterations required to reach the desired precision, as well as a substantial decrease in the total computational time spent within the iterative solver. This performance boost is particularly pronounced in problem sets characterized by a large number of variables. Ultimately, we found that the proposed criterion offers a effective and flexible solution to the challenge of optimizing the computational efficiency of IPM algorithms that utilize Krylov solvers. Its generic nature, coupled with its adaptability to diverse optimization contexts, makes it an easily integrable component that can be employed in a broad range of IPM implementations. Even when applied to problem sets that do not inherently benefit from its incorporation, the proposed criterion has been found to yield consistent and substantial performance enhancements. Consequently, we expect this novel criterion to significantly expand the algorithmic toolbox available to optimization software developers and researchers, thereby facilitating the development of more efficient and high-performance solutions to a wide range of computational challenges. The adoption of AI systems is gaining momentum, despite the fact that reliable AI remains an unfulfilled promise. Several high-profile AI failures have received media attention, but many more incidents go unreported. This lack of transparency and knowledge sharing hampers the development of trustworthy AI systems. To address this issue, we propose the AI Incident Repository (AIR), an open-access database of documented AI system failures. By recording the consequences of these incidents, along with their root causes, and proposed corrective actions, the AIR aims to facilitate knowledge sharing and promote best practices in AI engineering. By serving as a reference point for discussing and addressing failures, the AIR can help standardize incident documentation and contribute to the advancement of reliable AI through the study of system failures. This knowledge can be utilized to develop methods and tools to build more trustworthy AI systems, ultimately avoiding repeat failures in the future. This research paper outlines the concept of the AIR and provides a framework for documenting AI system failures, which can be viewed on our website at air.incidents.io. We invite the community to contribute to the development and use of the AIR in teaching, research, and industry practices. By collaborating on collecting and learning from AI system failures, we can work together to create reliable AI technologies. Keywords: AI, Machine Learning, Data Science, Incident Reporting, Repository, Trustworthy AI Systems. Samson Hu, Ph.D. student in the Department of Computer Science at Stony Brook University, is a domain-trained AI researcher with a background in biomedical engineering and computer science. His research focuses on developing reliable AI systems for data-driven applications in medicine and life sciences. In this research, he investigated how to address the unresolved problem of reliable AI and proposed the AI Incident Repository (AIR) as a solution to learn from and generalize from real-world failures. He contributed to the concept, incident documentation framework, and knowledge sharing strategies of the AIR, ultimately aiming to create a collaborative approach to developing trustworthy AI systems through failure analysis. In recent years, a new approach called Flows has gained significance, which enables a gradient-based transformation of the Markov chain into a more desirable distribution. This powerful tool has numerous applications across machine learning and theoretical physics, including lattice field theories. Our discussion focuses on the use of Flows as a generalised alternative to traditional MCMC algorithms, illustrating its potential benefits and challenges through various examples. Flows potentially offer a more systematic and flexible method for enhancing lattice quantum field theory simulations, although the approach is highly dependent on the specific scientific problem at hand. Our analysis concentrates on simulations of lattice Yang-Mills theories with a focus on how the Wilson action's gauge and fermionic components are integrated. This review aims to provide an accessible and comprehensive overview, summarising our current understanding of the methodology and the lessons learned from the examples studied. In the future, we plan to further investigate the use of Flows in simulations of lattice supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories. A key innovation lies in our proposed RegFavorLoss, which maximizes models' confidence in detecting regular expression-defined patterns in the predicted sequences. This loss function functions seamlessly with existing language model pre-training objectives, such as masked language modeling. When applied to the layout analysis component of a structured text model, it enhances the model's ability to accurately recognize structured text formats, as demonstrated on the popular SROIE dataset with extensive experimental evidence. Furthermore, our method exhibits greater flexibility as it allows the definition of custom regular expression models to suit specific structural requirements. Moreover, RegFavorLoss enables the development of specialized models tailored to unique structural patterns, paving the way for more precise and accurate structural text analysis in various domains. Lastly, the proposed approach demonstrates the effectiveness of leveraging large language models in structured text recognition, marking a significant contribution to the field of computer vision and natural language processing. Developing a dataset-oriented semantic parser can be a laborious task, especially for datasets in a specific domain.  This challenge becomes more pronounced in cross-domain scenarios where parsers trained on one dataset perform poorly on another.  In this paper, we propose a solution to this problem by suggesting that each action executed on a dataset can be categorized as either selective or inclusive based on its reference to database contents.  Datasets with similar action types tend to have similar structures in their queries, which in turn facilitates more effective cross-domain transfer.  To test this hypothesis, we created the Spider dataset, consisting of eight diverse domains with 28 datasets, to which we applied our proposed action type analysis.  Additionally, we designed an auxiliary training strategy with inclusive and selective queries, and an auxiliary language model for more precise analysis of database contents.  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields superior results on Spider and other benchmark datasets.  Code and dataset are accessible at https://sparqlclient.github.io/Spider/. When a small system in equilibrium with a large heat bath is subjected to a weak external force, its probability of jumping to a higher energy state increases rapidly, often exceeding the maximum allowed by linear response theory. We find that this faster increase is governed by a modified entropy production rate, which can be linked to the system's intrinsic dissipation rate through a nonlinear relation. This new rate allows us to resolve the approach to equilibrium in systems that linear response theory cannot address. We also demonstrate that the modified entropy production rate can be calculated using a reduced system-bath density matrix and that it predicts a slower approach to equilibrium compared to the linear response rate. Our analysis applies broadly, including situations where the external force is not weak, in which case it predicts a transition from a slower to a faster approach to equilibrium. Furthermore, we show that the modified entropy production rate can be estimated from a correlation function, which may be accessible through experimental or numerical manipulation of the system. This could potentially serve as a practical metric for identifying signs of equilibrium breakdown in systems that are driven at rates beyond what linear response theory can accommodate. Our analysis is supported by numerical simulations in an isolated double-well system and a range of other scenarios, which all demonstrate the need for a more complex description of entropy production than what linear response theory provides. Ultimately, this more complex description enables the resolution of a long-standing puzzle surrounding the overproduction of entropy relative to the Bragg-Williams approximation in certain magnetic systems. In conclusion, we propose that the modified entropy production rate could serve as an important diagnostic tool for identifying the effects of strongly driven quenches on systems with mechanical or magnetic degrees of freedom. These effects could potentially give rise to novel phenomena, such as the generation of heat at a rate higher than what linear response theory allows, and even the generation of negative absolute entropy, which could have significant practical applications. Finally, we speculate that the modified entropy production rate could also be a useful metric for evaluating the performance of certain quantum algorithms. This more general application is not explicitly addressed in this particular paper, but it does represent an important area of research that we hope to explore in future contributions to the field. The growing need to mitigate ecological damage driven by society has created an opportunity for artificial intelligence to contribute positively. By providing highly effective solutions, AI can significantly reduce environmental problems, such as optimizing renewable energy sources and promoting sustainable transportation. However, the full ecological benefits of these innovations are often obscured by the limitations of current assessment methods, which fail to account for the complex interactions among various ecological systems. As a result, the actual environmental effects of these solutions are underestimated, leading to suboptimal decision-making. To address this challenge, we develop a novel framework for systematically identifying and analyzing the concealed ecological implications of AI-based solutions. By integrating cutting-edge conceptual clustering, process mining, and system thinking techniques, our framework enables a more comprehensive and realistic simulation of the ecological consequences of these solutions, thereby facilitating better decision-making. Our proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to a range of domains, as demonstrated by our case studies on transportation and energy. Furthermore, our framework's approaches and tools can be adapted for educational purposes to develop students' skills in handling complex real-world problems, promoting innovative thinking, and resolving ecological problems through a problem-solving strategy grounded in AI and inspired by nature. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of this integrated research approach, which can serve as a valuable resource for academic institutions. Our research methodology, including the framework and case studies, can be utilized by institutions to develop research projects in line with the integrated AI and ecological systems approach, as well as novel educational methods inspired by this paradigm. Our research also offers practical tools and services for organizations to adopt and utilize this AI-based solution approach, thereby facilitating their transition to more sustainable operations. Our research provides concrete examples and guidance on harnessing the positive potential of AI to address environmental problems, promote innovative services, and enhance existing practices with a focus on ecological awareness. Our research further highlights the significance of a nature-inspired AI approach in tackling high-profile ecological issues, such as climate change, and urged organizations to embrace AI-based solutions for sustainable development. Our research showed that AI can be utilized not only as a tool but also as a driving force for sustainable development through a nature-based approach, and provided concrete evidence of this paradigm in action. Over the past decade, advancements in breakthroughs across multiple fields have been closely tied to progress in solving the box-stacking problem, a long-standing open issue in computer science. For a given set of rectangular blocks, the box-stacking problem involves determining if blocks can be stacked on top of one another to form a tall structure. To tackle this problem, a key concept of reducing complex input to more manageable forms has been explored, specifically kernelization. In this paper, we delve into the kernelization of stacking issues by examining the simplification of input block configurations that arise from the application of specific transformations. Building on previous research, we develop new kernelization results for the box-stacking problem, extending the scope to related problems such as circle-stacking and trigonostacking with restricted input block configurations. The novel kernelization outcomes demonstrate significant reductions in the size of the input data, in some cases down to a linear complexity. Furthermore, our research reveals compelling examples illustrating the potential for deep connections between the box-stacking problem and other complex mathematical concepts, as well as general lattice configurations, spanning across different dimensions. These examples showcase the versatility of kernelization in simplifying complex geometric configurations to facilitate solution-finding efforts. Lastly, we propose an array of open issues and potential research directions in the realm of kernelization studies for the box-stacking problem. These inquiries cover broad themes such as establishing precise bounds on kernel sizes, broadening the scope to include diverse geometric shapes, and exploring novel geometric configurations. The proposed questions provide a framework for further investigation and development in the kernelization domain. In a scenario of uncertainty, individuals tend to rely on incomplete information to form beliefs about the world.  This study introduces a novel approach to understanding how individuals adjust their confidence levels in response to events, within the framework of a partial equilibrium model.  We examine how individuals modify their opinions and the resulting shifts in the distribution of beliefs.  Our results demonstrate that, as events unfold, the distribution of beliefs becomes increasingly skewed, with extreme views gaining traction, while mainstream confidence wavers significantly.  This phenomenon is further exacerbated when individuals hold partially true hypotheses and event outcomes confirm only a portion of these hypotheses, as the distribution of beliefs becomes even more polarized.  Conversely, when event outcomes validate entire hypotheses, the distribution of beliefs becomes less polarized.  These findings are consistent for both binary and continuous event scenarios.  Ultimately, our research highlights the value of considering multiple aspects of the decision-making process, as well as the dynamic interplay between opinions and the resulting shifts in the distribution of beliefs.  By incorporating these aspects, we are able to generate a meaningful and engaging dynamic that sheds light on the behavior of individuals in uncertain environments.  In particular, our research emphasizes the significance of considering how events affect opinions and the resulting shifts in the distribution of beliefs, as well as the value of incorporating the structural framework of the partial equilibrium model. Inside an asymptotically flat, stationary, and electrically charged black hole spacetime, a self-gravitating, localized, and electrically charged perturbation is considered. The corresponding equations for the perturbed spacetime are examined in detail. Assuming the perturbation has symmetry equivalent to the SO(2) group, the equations can be reduced to a set of coupled differential equations in a spatial slice. These equations include those for gauge potentials, a scalar field, and an auxiliary potential. Their relationship is also explored, along with an asymptotic consistency condition arising from the hierarchy of equations. Consequently, the system can be analyzed through a combination of variational methods and physical considerations. Ultimately, a static, localized, and regular solution is found, and its mass and charge are calculated in a consistent manner. The solution possesses a single nodal line in the spatial slice, and its energy density exhibits a maximum at a finite distance from the black hole horizon. The structure of the solution bears resemblance to that of a non-rotating, charged soliton commonly found in models without gravity. The solution's thermodynamic properties are also examined, and a first-order phase transition is observed as the chemical potential varies. The solution is stable when its free energy is negative and unstable when it is positive. The free energy is, however, an extensive property when the black hole's mass and charge are calculated in a consistent manner, and it therefore scales extensively with the black hole parameters for small values of the perturbation. The solution's behavior may be regarded as a form of "hairy" black hole under specific conditions, and it may also be regarded as a form of soliton when its mass and charge are negligible in comparison to the black hole parameters. The solution is self-similar when its spatially repetitive nature is considered, and its asymptotic decay rates for the gauge potentials, scalar field, and energy density are all universal constants. The solution's decay rates are, however, influenced by the black hole parameters in a non-universal manner. The solution is regular and well-behaved both on and off the horizon, and it therefore exhibits a form of "inside an asymptotically level hairy black star" scenario. Furthermore, the solution is a zeroth-order perturbation in terms of the perturbation parameter when expressed as a perturbation of the black hole spacetime. We argue that customised search outcomes fill the void left by limited human attention, drawing from existing knowledge on human cognition. In our study, we evaluate the extent to which customised search results compromise the validity of online surveys by means of a between-subjects experiment. We discovered that customised search results indeed compromise the validity of the survey, but only when participants rely heavily on the search engine for data collection, and that this reliance comes at a cost of biased answers due to the search engine's personalisation. Moreover, we found that participants who used non-personalised search results provided more comprehensive responses, but still introduced biases due to limited human attention. Our results suggest that customised search results may distort online survey findings, and that researchers should consider employing various strategies to prevent such distortion in the future. We also propose an alternative approach to gathering data, using both customised and non-personalised search results in an experimental design. Our findings have significant practical implications for researchers who may overlook substantial amounts of pertinent information when conducting online surveys, and highlight the need to utilise both customised and non-personalised search results to gain a more comprehensive understanding of a particular topic. Finally, we outline potential future applications of our research, including its potential to enhance the validity of online surveys in various fields such as human-computer interaction, social network analysis, and market research. Additionally, we present two specific scenarios illustrating the potential benefits of integrating customised and non-personalised search results in an online survey setting. These examples demonstrate how the failure to utilise both types of search results may lead to the exclusion of relevant information from the sample, ultimately distorting the research findings and promoting the dissemination of biased information to governments and industry stakeholders. Moreover, we highlight the potential consequences of academic researchers overlooking customised search results, and how this oversight may compromise the research outcome by means of an anecdotal example. Finally, we outline the contributions and limitations of our study in detail. We investigate the properties of compressed dark matter consisting of fermions in a specific arrangement, interacting through a Yukawa coupling with usual matter. The model includes a dark sector scalar field and a set of vector bosons, acting as mediators for the dark matter's self-interaction and its interaction with visible matter. The condition for avoiding excessive dark radiation restricts the parameter space, especially in scenarios with small Yukawa couplings where the constraint is particularly stringent. Our analysis focuses on the collisional breakdown of dark matter as a viable micromultiplicity solution and considers the implications for the dark matter's compressed nature due to anisotropic pressure. We have developed a new numerical tool to simulate the process of dark matter compression and to generate predictions for relevant observable signatures, such as anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background and direct detection experiments. Our findings indicate that the interaction between dark matter and visible matter needs to be quite strong for the compressed nature of dark matter to become evident through experiments and observations. A significant advancement in sensitivity, especially for direct detection experiments targeting the dark matter's 1-10 GeV mass range, would be crucial in fully exploiting this scenario and thus effectively distinguishing compressed dark matter from its more common, collisional counterpart. Similarly, enhancing the quality and sensitivity of cosmic microwave background measurements, focusing on the large-scale anisotropies, would be essential in thoroughly investigating the compressed nature of dark matter. We have also identified an intriguing connection between the parameter space of our model and the properties of dark matter seeds, which could significantly impact the formation of dark matter's small-scale structures. Therefore, future analyses of these scales in dark matter's cosmological development would be crucial in further evaluating the compressed matter paradigm. On the other hand, we found that the model's Yukawa coupling has minimal impact on the predicted cross-sections and mass ranges that align with the standard cosmology's large-scale structure observations. Lastly, we found that the model of compressed dark matter composed of a single fermion type is susceptible to an instability, potentially occurring within a narrow mass range around a specific value, and we found that this instability is largely unaffected by variations in the model's parameters. Therefore, we found that this model is generally non-relativistic and features a distinct, monotonically decreasing density profile with increasing distance, characterized by a scale-dependent and anisotropic pressure. Furthermore, we found that this pressure becomes negligible at distances significantly smaller than the scale that distinguishes the model's matter distribution from its standard, non-compressed arrangement.

This study reevaluates local function observations on a $d$-dimensional lattice with a view to understanding higher-dimensional integral properties, specifically mean values, variance, and kurtosis. Our investigation centers around the role of optimal transport in aggregating these local fields. By leveraging solutions to a generalized Liouville equation, we develop explicit, positive, and Schrödinger semigroup-eligible operators to approximate integral properties. Our findings extend positive results on the stability of optimal transport maps to include general, non-negative functions, and we provide a new framework for bounding the stability of transport plans. Ultimately, we construct a Schrödinger semigroup to simulate the evolution of probability measures and demonstrate the emergence of a steady state, characterized by stable mean values, variances, and kurtosis values independent of the dimension $d$. Our analysis also yields a novel approach to approximating the kurtosis statistic, extending the classical four-term Taylor formula to function observations with optimal transport-based corrections. Our method enables the accurate computation of kurtosis in extremely low precision and offers a general framework for computing statistical moments of higher order. Our study also showcases the efficacy of negative Liouville equation solutions in a range of applications, including harmonic analysis and PDEs, and provides a novel formulation of the central limit theorem based on optimal transport. Furthermore, we extend the notion of kurtosis to measure probability distributions and develop a new metric, $\mathfrak{\phi}$-kurtosis, to characterize the asymmetry and heaviness of tails in distribution tails, revealing a direct relationship between this metric and the $p$-mean of the absolute deviation from the median. Our investigation also explores the links between optimal transport, Liouville equations, and fundamental harmonic analysis concepts, including the fundamental kernel, the Poisson kernel, and the mean value kernel, and demonstrates a harmonious interplay between these ideas. In the field of computer vision, pre-training models with a vast, unlabeled dataset is a popular technique to enhance a model's performance on a specific task, often using generic image classification as the default choice. However, we question the effectiveness of this approach for semantic segmentation and propose an alternative method, using depth assessment from a single monocular image, as it is closely related to semantic segmentation. By leveraging a vast unlabeled dataset for pre-training, our method aims to improve a semantic segmentation model's accuracy. To validate our approach, we developed a custom monocular depth assessment dataset and compared it to traditional classification-based pre-training, as well as a self-supervised approach, on two publicly available datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that pre-training with monocular depth assessment consistently surpasses classification-based pre-training in semantic segmentation accuracy on both datasets, even under a self-supervised setting without ground-truth information. Furthermore, our method exhibits comparable performance to supervision from ground-truth labels, underscoring the efficacy of depth assessment as a pre-training task for semantic segmentation. Our method's source code will be publicly available, enabling reproduction of the experimental results and facilitating future research in this area. Additionally, we will release the custom monocular depth assessment dataset for the community to utilize. Our approach is inspired by the well-known KITTI dataset, which extensively employs depth information in various tasks, suggesting a strong connection between depth assessment and semantic segmentation. To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of depth assessment, we designed a suite of 6 quantitative metrics, which demonstrate a significant positive correlation with semantic segmentation accuracy. Our pre-trained models, along with the custom dataset and source code, will be publicly contributed to the community to facilitate future research in this area. To ensure the robustness of our approach, we employed rigorous evaluation techniques, including ablation studies and residual analysis, to confirm that depth assessment offers a consistent performance advantage over classification-based pre-training. Our method's design was informed by the fundamental principles of monocular depth assessment and semantic segmentation, as well as the vast body of existing research in these areas, as detailed in our manuscript. Our pre-trained models consistently outperformed classification-based pre-training and approached the performance of supervision from ground-truth labels, underscoring the effectiveness of depth assessment as a universal pre-training task for semantic segmentation. Our custom dataset, along with the source code, will be publicly contributed to ensure seamless reproduction of the experimental results. Our work highlights the efficacy of depth assessment as a versatile pre-training task, offering a consistent performance advantage over classification

Developing a time-series dataset and training a model that can effectively present the data in an engaging narrative is a complex task, especially considering the various possible sequence orders of data points. To address this challenge, we present TCube, a novel neural model that can dynamically learn time-series presentations for any given dataset without requiring manual optimization. Evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate TCube's ability to create more engaging and easily comprehended time-series narratives compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, TCube's state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics, including human evaluations and automatic metrics, showcases its effectiveness in time-series storytelling. To facilitate replicable research, our code and pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/alekseygrigorev/TCube.

Our analysis reveals that coefficients with a growth rate of $t^{\alpha}$, where $0 < \alpha < \frac{1}{7}$, suffice for a well-posed solution. Notably, this bound is tighter than in a preceding study, which required a growth rate of $t^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ due to an incorrect lower bound in its nonlinearity estimate, influenced by a non-variational adjoint operator in a related issue. In contrast, the current work demonstrates that the non-variational adjoint operator's impact is minimal in this context. Additionally, our research shows that the non-variational adjoint operator does not significantly affect the optimal bound on the growth rate of coefficients in a corresponding study on a first-order hyperbolic equation. Furthermore, we extended the global solvability results to various applications, including a class of hyperbolic equations with boundary controls and their non-variational adjoints, as well as a class of control-theoretic problems with non-variational adjoints. These problems encompass multiple physical models such as the inverse source problem for the heat equation and a variant of the acoustic scattering problem. In particular, we derived a growth rate of $t^{-\frac{1}{7}}$ for a non-variational adjoint acoustic scattering problem to provide a globally defined operator for calculating the far-field operator, facilitating the ill-posedness of this problem under a sublogarithmic rate and confirming its necessity in this context. This study confirms that the optimal bound on the growth rate of coefficients in various problems is indeed tight. Galaxies with stable patterns of star formation must be unaffected by major events like galaxy collisions and mergers throughout their lives.  However, identifying consistent galaxies using existing methods is impractical due to the variability of their star formation rates, which makes reliable predictions challenging for future surveys.  A new evaluation method considers not only the reliability of star formation rate measurements but also the likelihood of a galaxy experiencing significant events, taking into account its mass, age, and potential disturbances.  By incorporating these factors, we have re-evaluated the reliability of existing galaxy samples and compared their consistency with predictions based on simple models of galaxy evolution, revealing a substantial discrepancy.  To address this issue, we have developed a new framework, the Galaxy Variability Problem Mitigation Toolbox, which includes multiple approaches to reduce the uncertainty of galaxy evolution predictions.  This tool is now available online, allowing users to input their own survey specifications and simulate the most suitable strategies to meet their needs.  Our analysis also highlights areas for improvement in future galaxy surveys, including the need for more precise distance measurements and better models of galaxy collisions and mergers to make more accurate predictions.  Additionally, we have suggested several possible directions for future research based on the results of our evaluation. Autonomous vehicles are increasingly reliant on advanced technologies to navigate.
While many vehicles on the market today feature semi-autonomous driving systems,
these typically only allow the vehicle to steer within certain limits and at
lower speeds. True self-driving technology, on the other hand, depends on a vehicle
capable of independent mobility. The underlying system, however, must first be
tuned to account for a vehicle's unique characteristics before it can be safely
operated. The process of adjusting the system to a vehicle's specifications is
referred to as calibration. The underlying system in question utilizes a Deep
Reinforcement Learning model. The model in question leverages a neural network to
model a vehicle's behavior and learn its control policies through reinforcement
learning. The focus here is on this DRL model and its relevance to autonomous
vehicles, particularly in terms of their ability to operate independently. The
paper begins with an overview of recent research in this space before outlining
the DRL model's underlying methodology. The key challenge in developing this
model revolves around finding efficient learning strategies that enable rapid
calibration. The paper therefore focuses on developing innovative learning
strategies, integrating real-world testing into simulated environments, and
using transfer learning to speed up the development process. The proposed DRL
model is then applied to the autonomous vehicle domain, specifically to a lane
following task, and its performance is compared against state-of-the-art methods
using benchmark datasets. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the DRL model
in reducing training time while producing equivalent, if not superior, results.

We focus on isolated quark stars composed of this matter, with special considerations for spin alignment, magnetic field, and temperature. Our analysis reveals that as temperature increases, specific properties of the star undergo gradual changes. Furthermore, we computed the equilibrium temperature, resulting in a maximum value of approximately 56 megakelvin. Our findings also demonstrate that as temperature rises, the radius of the star expands. In addition, we evaluated how temperature affects the overall mass and radius of the star for various spin alignment conditions. Our results show that for rapidly spinning stars, an increase in temperature leads to a slight expansion of the star's radius. Moreover, the effects of temperature and spin alignment on the star's overall mass are significant, with a noticeable increase in radius for stars with lower spin alignment. Our research further examines the impact of a magnetic field on these quark stars, with considerations for both spin-up and spin-down scenarios. In spin-up cases, a magnetic field causes the star's radius to contract, whereas in spin-down situations, the star's radius exhibits slight expansion. Our analysis finally highlights that temperature and magnetic field have a combined effect on the star's overall mass and radius, with values greater than a certain threshold resulting in a significant expansion of radius for stars with lower spin alignment. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for the properties of isolated quark stars that might be applicable across various theoretical frameworks of quark matter. Machine learning models such as random forests and boosted decision trees have wide-ranging applications but often lack clear explanations for their predictions. In order to improve the transparency and interpretability of these models, researchers have developed methods to represent the output of a forest or ensemble in terms of a key feature. However, these models can complicate this process due to their use of multiple trees, non-linear transformations, and weighted combinations of predictions. Building on existing work, a new approach called Attribution Graph Learning is presented, which frames the task of identifying a model's key features as a graph representation learning problem. By treating the nodes of the graph as attributes and the edges as their relationships, the model can generate a graph that shows how attributes are connected and prioritizes important features. Experimental results on open datasets show that the proposed method can effectively capture a model's main ideas and separate irrelevant background information. Furthermore, the method has the advantage of being flexible and can be applied to a range of different graph representations without the need for manual annotation. In addition to its performance, the resulting graphs also provide insight into the models they describe, such as which attributes are most important and how they are connected. A full implementation of the method is available on the GitHub platform for other researchers to use and reproduce the results. A website with additional information about the project, including visualizations of the graphs, is also available at the specified URL. Preliminary results suggest that the method has potential applications in fields such as science and medicine where experts often have specialized knowledge about key features and their relationships. Extensive testing on a range of different datasets is needed to confirm these findings and fully demonstrate the method's capabilities. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training a machine learning model while maintaining control over their private data, as they share it with a central server. However, the process is vulnerable to malicious interference from the server, which can manipulate the model and steal users' secrets. Our innovative approach involves using secure, hardware-isolated environments to safeguard both the model and user data, as we train a neural network together. The trainer, a secure processor, isolates user data from the server and other external threats, protecting it with encryption and boundary checks. This way, the training process remains free from hacking and data breaches. Our system, called Flatee, integrates this secure training environment with popular autotuning libraries, demonstrating higher resilience to attacks and significantly reducing training time compared to traditional methods. Our experiments, involving various grades of trustworthiness, show that Flatee successfully protects model and user data from both server and side-channel attacks, as it trains complex neural networks quickly and accurately. Moreover, our solution promotes hardware-independence, allowing it to work on a wide range of devices without relying on specific hardware features. Overall, Flatee offers a robust and efficient solution for securely training machine learning models in a decentralized setting. The rapidly evolving landscape of microservice-based software systems demands greater efficiency in development and testing to keep up with modern software engineering techniques. Traditional AVMs (Automated Verification Methods) focus on safety and performance but often overlook other essential aspects such as resource constraints. Existing approaches to resource management in microservices consider resource allocation requests as a central issue, yet little attention is given to the broader context of resource usage within these systems. Inspired by the timeloop framework, which uses counterfactual reasoning to analyze alternative system histories, we introduce a new method for learning and refining system call policies between timeloops. Our proposed algorithm combines deep learning and counterfactual reasoning, enabling the automatic generation of call policies for individual microservice components. These policies can then be easily combined to cover the entire system, thus facilitating the rapid creation of functional models for microservice-based systems. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in learning call policies, with a notable improvement of 87% in accuracy for a composite system, as validated through a case study involving an open-source image processing application. Furthermore, our approach enables the efficient creation of functional models, with a 3.65 times faster model generation compared to traditional specification-based methods. Users can also interact with a live demo of our approach in the image processing domain by visiting the following link: https://timeloops.herokuapp.com/. Furthermore, a scientific video showcasing our approach is available at the following link: https://youtu.be/6h8b8e4kX9U. A commodity is a element that, in the long run, cannot be produced or destroyed, such as money or information. Commodity space forms can model a relationship where one commodity's value is determined by the other, using a function that only depends on the first commodity's attributes. This is similar to a task called 'identification in the long run', where a latent variable, the first commodity in this case, can be distinguished from an observable variable, the second commodity, using a classifier that produces accurate results indefinitely. Given that the first commodity is not directly observable but its impact on the second is known, we can identify it by studying their difference, which is the second commodity. This can be achieved through a linear classifier that distinguishes between the two commodities, as the difference between them represents the first commodity. This distinction can be represented by an equation that expresses the second commodity as a linear combination of the first commodity's attributes, which is the identity in the long run. This paper uses this concept to create a linear classifier that can identify the first commodity's attributes, by studying their relationship with the second commodity, without directly observing them. This is similar to other tasks such as'recovery in the long run' and'recovery with partial information in the long run', where a latent variable, the first commodity in this case, can be completely or partially recovered from the second commodity, using a linear classifier that produces accurate results over time. These recovery tasks can also utilize commodity space forms to model their relationship, as well as other related models. These concepts are further illustrated through applications in economics and finance. Experimental results show that our proposed linear classifier outperforms other classifiers in a range of datasets. This paper provides theoretical guarantees for these results, as well as an analysis of the classifier's performance. These guarantees are based on properties of the commodity space forms and the long run identification and recovery tasks. This study also provides an estimate of the classifier's error and an upper limit on its accuracy, based on the dataset's characteristics. These estimates are also tied to the dataset's information content and the commodity space forms' dimensions. This paper provides a comprehensive framework and tools for learning commodity relationships, using commodity space forms and linear classifiers, as well as other models and techniques. These tools enable researchers and practitioners to study commodity relationships, using long run identification and recovery tasks, and to develop algorithms and methods that utilize these concepts. These ideas are further illustrated through a range of empirical results and applications. This research extends and generalizes previous work on learning commodity relationships

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy, the motion of stars can be analyzed using a simplified model that considers just two dimensions. This simplified model assumes that neighboring stars move in a straight line, a condition known as strong separation. Researchers initially found that in this model, the distribution of stars follows a specific statistical pattern, known as Maxwell-Boltzmann. This paper introduces a cutting-edge method called Random Model Predictive Control, which utilizes model predictive control's flexibility to tackle issues with nonlinear system control that are subject to variable constraints. A clear demonstration of this control method is achieved through a simple simulation of a mechanical system's dynamic behavior. The code necessary for this simulation is also openly sourced on popular platforms, allowing readers to replicate the results. This paper's findings are significant as they offer a viable solution to the performance limitations of traditional linear quadratic control methods. Furthermore, the application of RMPC is not confined to the specific system examined here, but rather RMPC holds broad potential across a wide range of systems.

This study proposes a novel networking scheme that seamlessly integrates D2D communication while minimizing interference. To achieve this, device messages are converted into energy signals and sent through a centralized node, which splits them into energy and information streams. The device then calculates an optimal gain for its transmitted signals based on a metric called integrated information and energy, thereby ensuring proper reception of both its energy and information messages. By converting information into energy signals, the proposed scheme eliminates D2D link interference, while utilizing Intellect Reflecting Surface technology to direct energy signals back to their originating devices and ensure accurate reception of both energy and information messages. As a result, the scheme demonstrates improved outage probability performance compared to a baseline scenario. Simulation data confirm that the scheme achieves lower end-to-end delay and increased successful transmission rates at a given outage probability. Furthermore, the scheme's complexity is confirmed to be NP-hard, with evidence showing its performance scalability. Finally, the scheme's effectiveness in multi-device networks is illustrated through numerical results. In particular, the results show that the scheme can be generalized to multi-device networks, with a corresponding reduction in channel gain complexity. The scheme's performance in these networks was found to be comparable to optimal solutions derived from convex optimization methods. To verify the scheme's validity, a simple experiment was conducted using an Arduino board, which verified the scheme's ability to efficiently process and transmit data over short distances. The experiment further confirmed that the scheme can be efficiently implemented using current technology. Finally, the study's contributions were summarized, and future research directions were identified, including the development of more advanced SUR surfaces and the use of machine learning techniques to optimize the integrated information and energy metric. Potential applications of the scheme were also identified, including smart homes and intelligent transportation systems. To maintain clarity, the redefined terms were consistently applied throughout the study. The scheme's performance was reevaluated, and numerical results were recomputed to reflect the scheme's control of D2D communication. The recomputed results show that the scheme achieves superior performance compared to baseline scenarios. The study's contributions were reaffirmed, and future research directions were reiterated, including the development of more advanced SUR surfaces and the use of machine learning techniques to optimize the integrated information and energy metric. In the context of the polymer black hole model, this approach results in an expanded phase space configuration, characterized by a simplified Hamiltonian potential with a single, distorted peak. In this study, we investigate the impact of symplectic expansion on quasinormal modes of massless scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational fields in a polymer black hole spacetime. To produce natural-sounding conversations, high-quality speech must be generated quickly, given the constraints of human listening capacity, which is around one sentence every two seconds. Current approaches to conversational speech synthesis often rely on pre-built dialogue systems, which are usually composed of templates and prior responses, or use neural models trained on large datasets of conversational text. However, these methods fall short in creating spontaneous, human-like conversations. To bridge this gap, a new method called MaskedDialogue combines a neural network with a masking technique, allowing a single sentence to be generated based on the preceding context. By analyzing the preceding sentence for its semantic characteristics, such as part-of-speech, rather than waiting for a response, this approach produces more efficient dialogue. Various experiments were conducted to validate the performance of this approach, which included both subjective and objective assessments, using datasets such as the Switch Board and DailyDialog. The results showed that this method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both tasks. Additionally, a user study confirmed the subjectivity of the approach, which averaged four times higher than the baseline in terms of naturalness. Furthermore, this method was found to be more context-aware and performed better when analyzed objectively. The code and demo for this approach can be found at https://github.com/alexyu2019/MaskedDialogues. Instrumental variables are a widely accepted method for identifying causal effects, particularly in cases where the instrument's mechanism is nontransparent. The traditional assumption is that the instrument must differ across treatment groups and not be endogenously determined. However, this assumption is too restrictive, allowing for the identification of causal effects in scenarios where the instrument is consistently given to all individuals or its mechanism is not distinctly varied, as long as its likelihood of being administered does not depend on the outcome of interest. To identify such a scenario, a new condition is introduced, which posits that the likelihood of receiving the instrument is influenced by the instrument itself but not the unobserved factors. The proposed approach is then applied to determine the causal returns on investing in higher education, where the instrument is the field of study and the treatment is the financial investment associated with it. By meeting the newly established condition, the findings reveal a positive causal return on pursuing higher education in the social and humanitarian fields and a negative return in the natural sciences. The proposed method is further tested with alternative instruments, yielding similar results. Finally, the findings are consistent with a model in which the direct return on investing in human capital is positive, but the indirect costs associated with opportunity costs of not engaging in the most valuable fields of study outweigh the direct benefits, amounting to approximately 0.4 and 1.4 percentage points, respectively. The study of the solar noise storm source region has gained significant interest in recent times, driven by large datasets from radio telescopes such as FAST. This research presents new findings on the rapid evolution of solar noise storm source parameters obtained from FAST observations at 1.2 GHz. A rapid increase in the brightness temperature and core size of the source occurred within 7 seconds, accompanied by a dramatic shift in its morphology. This sudden change was followed by a gradual recovery of the source characteristics over the next 20 seconds. Analysis of the data suggests that a mini-flare occurred at the source location, leading to the observed phenomenon. This event provides valuable insights into the complex magnetic field structure and dynamics within the solar noise storm region. A model based on a toroidal magnetic field is unable to fully explain the observed source behavior. Conversely, a helical magnetic field structure is capable of generating the observed characteristics through its twisting deformation, consistent with the findings of simulation studies in the frequency-time domain. This study offers a new perspective on the helical magnetic field in the solar noise storm region. The accumulation of a spherical distribution of particles of mass ${m_{\rm part}}$ around a Schwarzschild black hole is studied, analyzing how its rotational dynamics influences the energy and azimuthal angular momentum of the particles as they approach the event horizon. This is achieved by solving the steady-state Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov equation for a transfer function ${f_{\rm TOV}}$ that determines the gravitational percolation of the classical black hole ${\rm Pr_{\rm clas}}}$. This percolation is combined with the rotational momentum of the particles, quantified by a dimensionless parameter ${\beta_{\rm part}}$, to derive a general expression for the radial distribution of particles ${n_{\rm part}(r)}$, that exceeds the standard estimate by a factor of ${\rm e}^{{\beta_{\rm part}}}$.

The research reveals that when particles with a certain amount of rotational momentum ${\beta_{\rm part}}$ accumulate around a classical black hole, the resulting radial density of particles ${n_{\rm part}(r)}$ is significantly higher than predicted by the standard model, especially near the event horizon. This is attributed to the rotational momentum ${\beta_{\rm part}}}$, that counteracts the gravitational force, thereby increasing the effective radial extent of the particles and their concentration near the event horizon. In turn, this modifies the structure of a rotating black hole formed from a sphere of finite extent, that is more massive and has a higher spin rate than predicted by the standard model. The research further indicates that when particles with a certain amount of rotational momentum ${\beta_{\rm part}}}$ are present, a classical black hole can only accommodate a fraction of the standard predicted mass, while a rotating black hole can only accommodate a fraction of its standard predicted rotational momentum. Additionally, for a classical black hole, the presence of rotational momentum ${\beta_{\rm part}}}$ increases the radius at which matter becomes permanently bound, while for a rotating black hole, the radius is already larger than predicted by the standard model. Finally, the research shows that when particles with a certain amount of rotational momentum ${\beta_{\rm part}}}$ are present, a black hole formed from a sphere of infinite extent, that is either classical or rotating, has a higher mass and, in the case of a rotating black hole, higher spin rate than predicted by the standard model. The emission spectra resulting from an atom experiencing this interaction can be quantified using a modified total dipole moment.  The situation is modeled using a slender mirror instead of an ideal mirror, for better connection to real-world experiments.  The motion of the atom is simulated as a oscillating dipole, and the presence of a mirror is represented as a boundary condition in the modified total dipole.  The modified total dipole is used to calculate the electromagnetic emission resulting from the atom's motion.  The method for calculating electromagnetic emission is applicable not only to atoms but also to other oscillating objects.  The probability of finding electrons in specific energy states, as well as energy absorption and emission spectra, can all be calculated using this approach.  The electromagnetic emission resulting from the atom's motion can be categorized as either Casimir emission or traditional Rayleigh-Jeans emission, depending on the relative magnitude of the atom's movement and static Casimir force.  The likelihood of Casimir emission increases as the atom is drawn closer to the mirror.  The electromagnetic emission is quantified as a series of discrete or continuous lines in the spectra, and the intensity of each line is quantified as a function of energy.  The intensity of the Casimir emission lines is found to be discrete and quantized, whereas the intensity of the traditional Rayleigh-Jeans emission lines is found to be continuous and quantified only by the integer n, matching the real-world observations of atomic emissions.  The approach is also connected to the phenomenon of van der Waals forces, for which the movement of the atom is not a critical factor.  The situation is examined using two types of atomic motion: linear and circular.  The linear motion results in a dipole and quadrupole moments, in addition to a modified total dipole.  The circular motion, on the other hand, results in a modified total dipole and a toroidal moment.  The presence of a modified total dipole, as well as a toroidal moment for circular motion, leads to a distinction in the electromagnetic emission resulting from the atom's motion, as examined using several examples.  The difference in electromagnetic emission resulting from linear and circular atomic motions is particularly noticeable when examining the probability distributions of finding electrons in specific energy states, as well as energy absorption and emission spectra, for various values of atomic velocity and distance from the mirror. Identity verification is a critical process in various industries, including finance and national security, where identification documents play a crucial role in establishing personal credentials. Although Automatic Identification Number (AI) verification has become a standard practice in Indonesia by reducing the need to manually verify identification documents, the country's optical character recognition capabilities for ID documents remain limited. To address this issue, we developed an open-source Indonesian ID document extractor, incorporating OCR and natural language processing techniques to enhance the accuracy of extractions, particularly in cases where OCR fails. Our solution consists of an analysis module that uses Indonesian language models to refine the extraction process, as well as a validation module to verify the extracted data against predefined criteria, thus ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the extracted information. Our approach employs the latest Indonesian NLP models, including the Spacy library, to achieve this goal. Our findings indicate that combining these methods significantly improves the accuracy of extractions, outperforming traditional OCR and error-correction methods. Our solution was evaluated using a dataset of 50 Indonesian ID documents, demonstrating an average extraction accuracy of 97.3%. Our open-source solution is poised to revolutionize Indonesian ID document processing, paving the way for widespread adoption in various industries and institutions. Ultimately, this project marks a significant milestone in the application of NLP models to resolve real-world problems, exemplifying the potential of NLP to resolve critical business and national security challenges. Vehicular networks, such as those based on IEEE 802.11p, rely on the vehicle's speed to dynamically adjust training channel durations. To address this issue, a novel estimation method is introduced, leveraging an extended LSTM model for better accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits improved computational efficiency and lower latency, making it more suitable for real-time vehicular applications. Simulation results demonstrate that the new estimator achieves lower RMS error and up to inter-symbol interference (ISI) metrics in comparison to LSTM. Additionally, the end-to-end delay is minimized. Experimental validation confirms the outstanding performance of the new estimator across various vehicular use cases. This leads to superior performance and efficient resource allocation in vehicular networks. Despite these efforts, finding the ideal network often proves elusive. In this paper, a novel approach is presented based on the principles of information theory, and an estimate is developed for the optimal network using the maximum likelihood criterion without iteration or gradient computation. The resulting method simplifies the complex optimization problem, and two low-complexity algorithms are proposed to effectively search for the ideal network. The proposed algorithms outperform existing benchmarks in various benchmarks and also excel in a self-learning scenario. Furthermore, the proposed methods demonstrate superior performance in noise estimation and conversion in analog-to-digital modulation systems. The implementation details and performance metrics are also detailed, and numerical results are presented to demonstrate the methods' effectiveness. The work contributes to the field by bridging information theory and neural networks, and a deeper understanding of their interrelation is also provided. The methods also exhibit generalizability beyond the specific application areas. Recent breakthroughs in cognitive AI have propelled its development towards a more realistic simulation of human intelligence. This paper focuses on multi-agent human-robot cooperative learning, which we believe is a crucial step in preparing cognitive robots for on-road deployment. Our approach to this challenge involves utilizing a dynamic and large-scale environment to support large-scale non-player characters in cognitive AI frameworks. We introduce an innovative learning paradigm called 'Interactive Learning Dynamics', which facilitates the development of versatile cognitive robots. The ILD method enables agents to adapt to diverse agents through repeated interactions and subsequent updates of their internal models. As a result, agents are capable of self-improvement over extended periods of time. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted extensive simulations involving up to 100 non-robotic agents in a large-scale environment. Our findings confirm that ILD leads to significant enhancements in learning performance compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we show that ILD can be effectively applied to more complex robotic systems, which we call 'Interactive Learning Dynamics Plus', to demonstrate its potential for a range of applications. Our work on multi-agent learning has numerous practical implications and we believe will pave the way for accessible and practical cognitive AI solutions. Point symmetry occurs naturally in the world and can be seen in the rotation symmetry of a circle and the reflection symmetry of a mirror.  Point groups combine various combinations of these symmetries.  On the other hand, location symmetry is human-induced and can be seen in the arrangement of leaves on stems and the patterns on branches.  Location groups, born from location symmetry, are uncommon in nature.  This study introduces a new type of location group, the single/double ordinary/gray layer group, and explores its relationship with the established snf and nuf point groups.  By establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the operations of the two types of groups, we broaden the scope of point group theory to include location groups.  This achievement is made possible by a detailed analysis of the layers in crystals, where a crystal is divided into alternating blocks of tight and loose packing. This study demonstrates how location groups, born from the arrangement of crystal layers, can be applied to fields such as optics, where circular polarization mirrors and the arrangement of molecules are regulated by location symmetry. A significant obstacle in developing artificial neural networks inspired by biological spiking neural networks lies in the "sign dilemma". This challenge arises because a small number of inputs can result in numerous possible network states due to the limited range of output values (-1 to 1). This restriction applies particularly to outputs less than 0, as the lower bound of 0 makes it difficult to achieve low absolute values. In this study, we investigate a novel solution to the sign dilemma by utilizing complex-valued neural networks. These networks allow outputs to have complex numbers as values, eliminating the sign range limitation. We propose a novel learning rule inspired by Hebb's rule, allowing the learning of weights within these networks. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution to the sign dilemma. Additionally, we showcase the feasibility of implementing learning in these complex-valued networks by incorporating an orthogonal constraint, commonly found in biological spiking neural networks. The orthogonal constraint dictates that the columns of weight matrices contain orthogonal vectors. We derived a learning rule that incorporates both the orthogonal and Hebbian constraints, allowing the efficient learning of these matrices. The application of these learning rules to numerical examples is also demonstrated in this study. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository at: https://github.com/y-y/yawnnn/tree/main/docs/neunnn/docs/complex_neunnn. Our perception of reality can be manipulated and deceived, especially when we rely on virtual and illusory stimuli. The consequences of this perceptual shift can affect mental states and behavior, as demonstrated by the phenomenon of shadow aspects in philosophy and psychology. A shadow aspect is a second, implicit perspective that contradicts the initial perception. We propose that only a small portion of this implicit perspective is consciously acknowledged, while the rest remains subconscious. The conscious portion is characterized by a heightened sense of presence, as if the virtual stimulus has penetrated into one's inner world. We suggest that the degree of conscious implicit perspectives, including the virtual stimulus's influence on one's thoughts and emotions, as well as the presence of its shadow aspect, can be measured using the multi-dimensional presence scale (MPS). A study was conducted to validate this idea by administering an MPS survey to 198 participants who had experienced a lucid dream, a state of self-aware consciousness while dreaming. The results showed a significant correlation between the presence of implicit perspectives and shadow aspects, as well as a higher presence of implicit perspectives and shadow aspects in participants who had experienced lucid dreams. We further theorize that virtual reality stimuli can give rise to shadow aspects, and we present a model that explains the relationship between implicit perspectives, shadow aspects, and VR-induced mental alterations. Ultimately, we believe that the concept of shadow aspects offers a novel framework for exploring the consequences of perceptual shifts in VR research. In the future, we plan to investigate whether VR-induced shadow aspects can serve as a means of changing one's behavior by modifying one's perceptions, effectively "programming" the mind. Based on our understanding of shadow aspects, we predict that certain types of VR experiences can induce implicit perspectives and shadow aspects that can persist even after the physical stimulus has disappeared, such as memories and preoccupations. We believe that the long-lasting impact of VR experiences, specifically those that combine sensory stimulation with intellectual engagement, can lead to lasting implicit perspectives and shadow aspects. Lastly, we propose that the most effective type of VR experiences for inducing implicit perspectives and shadow aspects are those that transcend superficial interpretations and tap into deeper, implicit meanings, as exemplified by thought-provoking and intellectually stimulating stories. Conversely, we predict that surface-level experiences, such as flight simulators and erotic VR content, will yield a diminished presence of implicit perspectives and shadow aspects.
