Our solution to this challenge lies in a revolutionary model called the Multilingual Model (MM). This model, supported by a large pre-trained dataset, can learn and process text in up to 260 languages, learning an underlying grid of similar words in various languages through self-supervised learning. Our analysis reveals that while the model excels in identifying similar words in known languages, it underperforms in unseen languages, also known as zero-shot learning. To improve upon this limitation, we developed an innovative method called the Adaptor Adapters approach (A2). This approach modifies the model's grid of similar words in two ways, first by identifying and removing duplicate data from the training set and second by refining the model's understanding of words through additional, more precise information. Our results show that the A2 model significantly enhances the model's accuracy in zero-shot learning. Recent studies have analyzed the reliability of machine learning models when attacked by malicious parties, yet developing robust models remains an open problem. particularly in high-stakes applications. One crucial gap in current research is that proposed models are not grounded in statistical inferences. To address this, we develop a method for building robust models that is based on Bayesian statistics, where the model's reliability is quantified as the likelihood of withstanding attacks. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, this likelihood converges to 1 as the number of training examples increases, thus meeting the standards of classical robust statistical inference. Furthermore, our method has the advantage of being immediately applicable in practice, as the traditional assumptions remain the same, whereas the reliability of modern deep learning models erodes as the number of adversarial attacks increases. Through thorough testing, we show that our method outperforms existing approaches in handling diverse types of attacks without requiring additional modifications. One key benefit is that the newly proposed models can be seamlessly integrated into standard Bayesian analysis techniques, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, thus facilitating easy adoption. Experimental findings confirm that these models remain reliable in the presence of unknown types of attacks. In early 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic led to a surge in rumors circulated online in China, with the government mobilizing efforts to counter these false narratives. This research aims to fill a gap in existing literature by examining how misinformation spreads online and its impact is measured in China. A study was conducted to identify the common dissemination mechanisms of rumors through analysis of news articles and user comments collected from Baidu Tieba. The results show that the primary methods of rumor dissemination online are via discussion threads centered on the affected area, user comments which often originate from anonymous accounts spreading Stokesian information, and online maps used as visual aids for reference. The findings also reveal that the majority of Chinese netizens trust official channels of information and criticize the anonymity of online discussions, which facilitates the spread of misinformation. The study provides data for evaluating the effectiveness of the government's efforts to combat rumors and offers suggestions for improving online debate through the adoption of verified accounts. Additionally, the research outcomes may be useful in informing strategies for combating misinformation in other countries experiencing outbreaks of rumors. Beyond achieving high accuracy, the choice of classification outcome representation becomes crucial as models increasingly make decisions that impact people's lives. In this study, we investigate how altering the loss function to mitigate the unfair effects of biased class probability distributions affects model performance. Experimental outcomes using synthetic and real-world data reveal that, contrary to expectations, modifying the loss function to address bias often results in reduced overall accuracy, with a significant decline in underrepresented class accuracy in imbalanced datasets. Consequently, models trained with such modifications are less reliable and more prone to errors in cases where the underrepresented class is involved. To put this into practice, we introduce a new evaluation metric, the relative class error rate (RCER), which quantifies the accuracy loss for each class relative to a fair model. Our analysis also identifies potential drawbacks of existing bias metrics and introduces a new framework for evaluating biased models that takes data distribution into account. This study's findings are significant because they highlight the dangers of non-neutral classification outcomes and prompt a reevaluation of the costs associated with them. Additionally, our research provides insights into the underlying relationships between loss functions, class costs, and model performance, offering guidance on the practical application of loss function manipulation to create more transparent and user-friendly neural classifiers. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexkts/biasmetric. Additionally, the trained models and processed data can be found on MIST https://mist.uqcloud.uq.edu.au/d/1144/. The developed analytics framework can be applied to other domains, such as customer service, to improve communication and resolve issues more effectively. When a finite number of Cooper couples within the material are in a triplet state, the material's response to an external magnetic field, particularly at low temperatures, can be described in terms of a magnetization that increases at a rate proportional to the square of the applied field. This phenomenon is characterized by the same underlying physical processes responsible for the material's non-linear transport properties at low temperatures and is independent of the specific details of the triplet Cooper couples' spin configurations. Notably, the material's response to an external magnetic field is paramagnetic in nature, despite the absence of unpaired electrons. Furthermore, the material's superconducting properties persist as long as the external magnetic field remains below a critical threshold. We propose a new research direction in machine learning, namely Minimax Engaged Learning, whose initial instantiation we study in depth. A key concept in this approach is the introduction of a competitive strategy operator, denoted as $\mathcal{S}$, which systematizes the maximin design of games for learning. This framework allows us to define and examine the minimaxity of a learning method, $\mathcal{M}$, in the context of game theory. By engaging in a minimax strategy with $\mathcal{S}$, the learner can achieve superior performance, thereby prompting us to investigate the fundamental limits of this approach. To this end, we develop a theoretical framework that provides essential properties for $\mathcal{S}$ and analyzes the asymptotic performance of minimax engaged learning. Through experimentation, we further demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach, which outperforms traditional non-competitive methods, particularly in challenging real-world scenarios involving inductive learning and online settings. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenZheng1/MinimaxEngagedLearning. A technical report detailing our work is available at https://arxiv.org/doi/2105.07097.html. (The full text of this paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07097.)

To study the underlying characteristics of musical data across different eras, we calculated the spectral density of acoustic instrumentations in eight periods of Western music, spanning from the Baroque to the present day. We discovered that previous studies accurately described the evolution of musical instrumentation. We then explored the notion that the complexity of musical data could be measured by the variety of instruments used in a composition. We estimated the data complexity of each musical period by analyzing the characteristics of instrument distributions in notable works from the corresponding style. Our findings reveal a significant increase in musical data complexity over time, with each period exhibiting greater variability than the last. We also determined that the complexity of instrumental combinations in major works is distinct from that of the overall instrumental repertoire of each style. Our research suggests that the complexity of musical data has been on an upward trajectory since the Classical period, with a particularly notable surge in the Modern period. We observed interesting patterns in the frequent combinations of instruments in modern music, with vocalists increasingly accompanied by electronic elements. Our analysis indicates that the complexity of musical data is not solely the result of instrumental variety, but also of the ever-changing relationships between instruments. We believe that our research contributes valuable insights to the ongoing discussion of how musical data complexity evolved over time. Additionally, our work demonstrates the practical applications of spectral analysis and complexity theory in the analysis of Western music. We hope that our findings will stimulate further research in this field. We also made available the code and data used for our research at github.com/music-informatics/mid-benchmark. We invite the community to reproduce our results and conduct further analysis using our code. We propose a set of tasks, defined by the mid-benchmark framework, that researchers can tackle to advance the field of musical data complexity. We envision that a collaborative effort, involving scholars from both theoretical and applied musicology, along with machine learning experts, can lead to novel applications and fresh perspectives on the evolution of musical data complexity. We believe that a shared understanding of the subject, derived from the analysis of Western music, can foster new insights across the entire spectrum of music informatics. We see this research as a starting point for an inclusive initiative, aiming to disseminate knowledge and promote educational activities, such as data challenges, workshops, and conferences, that explore the complexity of musical data. We aim for the mid-benchmark framework to become a widely recognized standard, enabling researchers to present their work in a unified manner and showcase their contributions to the field. In our investigation, we uncovered an unexpected phenomenon where multiple entries into a test statistic within a sequential analysis procedure significantly decrease the likelihood of type I errors, yet simultaneously increase the severity of its coverage, leading to underestimations of confidence intervals in the context of time series data and heavy-tailed distributions. To address this limitation, we developed a new method for constructing asymptotic confidence intervals and testing hypotheses without relying on traditional asymptotic distributions. Instead, we employed a distinct approach, leveraging the behavior of finite-block distributions. Specifically, for the case of multiple entries into a test statistic in a sequential analysis procedure, we found that the block mean of the test statistic converges to a mixture distribution, ultimately leading to the characterization of the finite-block distribution through a mixed normal. By analyzing this mixed normal, we determined the critical values for our proposed method and demonstrated its ability to provide accurate coverage and test statistics in hypothesis testing. Furthermore, we showcased the practical utility of our approach in a real-world application involving financial risk assessment. Although our method addresses a specialized case, the underlying techniques and strategies hold promise for generalization and future innovation. We show that the Smyth powerdomain of a directed-complete domain has core-compact covers if and only if the original domain possesses core-compact covers. Consequently, this implies that core-compactness of the Chalmers upper powerdomain also retains the original domain's core-compact covers. Furthermore, this leads to the conclusion that the Smyth and Chalmers powerdomains preserve core-compact covers in a variety of domains, including upper continuous lattices, continuous lattices, and domains with Scott open covers. Additionally, in a similar manner, we prove that the core compactification of a domain constructs core-compact covers by taking the Smyth powerdomain. Finally, this core-compactification process is closed over a broad class of functors that construct upper powerdomains, Smyth powerdomains, and Chalmers powerdomains. This functor is defined as taking a domain with Scott open covers on its subids. It is shown to be equivalent to the core-compactification functor, thereby establishing a categorical equivalence between domains with Scott open covers and core-compact domains, where the former is mapped to the latter through the Smyth powerdomain. This equivalence is also extended to upper continuous lattices, continuous lattices, and domains with Scott open covers, and is shown to be equivalent to the core-compactification functor for upper powerdomains, Chalmers powerdomains, and Smyth powerdomains respectively. In a related vein, we prove a similar result but for the Scott compactification and Scott open compactification functors, demonstrating a categorical equivalence between domains with Scott open covers and Scott compact domains, where the former is mapped to the latter through the Scott compactification functor for upper powerdomains, Smyth powerdomains, and Chalmers powerdomains respectively. This equivalence is also extended to domains with Scott open covers, and is shown to be equivalent to the Scott compactification and Scott open compactification functors for upper powerdomains, Chalmers powerdomains, and Smyth powerdomains respectively. In a separate line of reasoning, we establish a natural transformation from the Scott compactification to the core-compactification followed by the Smyth powerdomain functors, and show that it factors through a natural transformation to the core-compactification followed by the Smyth powerdomain functor. This is further shown to imply a similar result for the Scott open compactification functor. We establish a similar result for the Chalmers upper powerdomain. Vortex rings in an ideal 2D liquid with a finite circulation will always dissipate due to radiation, but the rate of dissipation can become negligible if the circulation is sufficiently large. In the limiting case, the rings' energy loss approaches zero in both ideal and real scenarios, albeit at a faster rate for ideal scenarios. The minimum circulation required to halt energy loss in ideal scenarios is proportional to the strength of the surrounding radiation, whereas in real scenarios it is proportional to the viscosity. This critical value marks the transition from dissipative to conserved energy states for vortex rings and provides a new definition for solitonic behavior, encompassing not only steady-state configurations but also those with extremely long lifetimes. In addition to vortex rings, this definition can also be applied to other solitonic structures such as anticyclonic vortices and straight waves. All conserved energy states for ideal scenarios exhibit steady positional movements and retain their shape over extended periods of time. Conversely, in real scenarios with sufficient circulation, these structures not only remain intact but also transfer from one form to another, where the most prevalent transformation involves a transition between a vortex ring and a plane wave. This latter transfer is highly efficient in real scenarios, converting the initial ideal energy into heat with an efficiency rate approaching 14%, a rate that in real scenarios approaches 100% due to the emergence of a highly damped plane wave that eventually loses its energy to dissipation. This highly efficient transfer has significant practical implications and highlights the relative importance of ideal models when approximating real-world vortex dynamics with high accuracy. All conserved energy states for ideal scenarios, including those with moderate and high circulation, can be accurately modeled using Gaussian potentials with low-order polynomial corrections, thereby providing a highly versatile and easily applicable framework for solving both ideal and real 2D vortex dynamics problems. In the limit of very low viscosity, the ideal Gaussian solutions can also accurately model corresponding 3D liquid scenarios with negligible error. Finally, despite the significant impact of viscosity on ring stability in real scenarios with low circulation, the overall positional distribution remains approximately log-normal, thereby retaining a resemblance to their ideal counterparts. Conversely, in real scenarios with high circulation, this overall positional distribution transforms into a near-normal Gaussian shape, thereby exhibiting a smooth transition from log-normal to normal positional distributions. This study provides a comprehensive and in-depth analysis of vortex rings in both ideal and real 2D liquids, encompassing all critical parameters and scenarios. A cutting-edge method for addressing missing values in time series data is the Enhanced Inverse Probability Weighting (EIPW). This approach uses a predictive model to fill in gaps in data, and then weights and adjusts the data points based on their predicted error. However, the traditional EIPW method has several limitations: it only allows for linear interpolation, and can only handle a single type of prediction model. In contrast, the recent Standardized EIPW (SEIPW) algorithm has made several key advancements over the original EIPW method: it uses a more sophisticated interpolation technique, and can incorporate a variety of prediction models in an efficient and streamlined way. Our research builds on the SEIPW algorithm by incorporating the predictions of multiple models, and using a neural network to refine the weight and adjustment calculations. This novel approach, which we call the Neural SEIPW (NEIPW) method, uses a neural network to predict the optimal interpolation weights and adjustments for a given time series, and has been shown to outperform a range of established methods in both synthetic and real-world data sets. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the NEIPW method is highly adaptable and can be applied to a wide range of data sets without requiring any prior knowledge or parameters. In particular, our results in climate modeling demonstrate that the NEIPW method is capable of accurately reconstructing long-term climate time series from sparse observational data, and can be extended to analyze the probabilistic uncertainties in such predictions. This research has significant practical applications and could be applied to a variety of fields including climate science, epidemiology, and finance. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/alexeygurev/neipw. In addition to the NEIPW method, our work also explores a range of other algorithms that can be used to address challenges in time series data, including imputation, prediction, and modeling of discrete and continuous data. These methods include Neural EIPW, Model Ensemble, Model Averaging, and the Random Forest algorithm. A comprehensive evaluation of these methods, known as the Time Series Pharaoh, has been developed to efficiently and fairly compare their performance across a wide range of data sets and scenarios. This research has applications in bioinformatics and can be used to make accurate predictions in fields such as human health and finance based on irregularly sampled data. A laboratory study was conducted to examine the formation and evolution of baroclinic waves in a rotating, differentially heated annulus using water as the working fluid. The results obtained from this experiment were compared with numerical simulations performed within the scope of the European Thresholds of Change program. The findings show that baroclinic wave instability occurred in both the experimental and numerical studies when the sign of the temperature error was opposite to that of the Coriolis force. The wave patterns and frequencies observed in both experiments were similar. The frequencies obtained from the numerical simulations matched the experimental values with an average error of less than 2%. The amplitude of the baroclinic waves in both experiments increased over time, but at different rates due to non-linear interactions, leading to the development of multiple wave components in the amplitude spectra. The frequency spacing between these components increased linearly, consistent with theoretical expectations. The general characteristics of the baroclinic waves in both experiments aligned with the classic 'bubble' regime theory. The research found that the baroclinic wave instability in this setup was highly resistant to changes in the flow regime and heat transfer system. The rotation axis was also found to be located near a plane of symmetry for the baroclinic waves, with very slight deviations. The research suggests that the baroclinic wave instability in this system is largely two-dimensional in nature. The research also found similarities between the baroclinic waves observed in both experiments and those observed in a study conducted by Green using air as the working fluid, despite differences in aspect ratio and rotation rates. A comprehensive analysis of the baroclinic waves was conducted using various diagnostic tools and metrics to characterize and compare the waves in both experiments and simulations. The study concluded by highlighting the success of the experiment in replicating complex baroclinic wave patterns in a controlled laboratory setting, paving the way for future research using this setup to study other geophysical and astrophysical flows. Additionally, the study found that the baroclinic wave instability in this system could serve as a valuable test bed for validating numerical models and simulating complex flows in geophysical and astrophysical contexts. A standard approach in extreme value statistics involves analyzing rare and extreme events. They are typically modeled as non-homogeneous Poisson processes with parameters linked to distribution types such as the Weibull or generalized Pareto distributions. However, working with these parameters can be challenging, as changes in their values lead to complex and hard to interpret variations in the extreme event rates. In this study, we explore a simplified method based on the mean and a quantile of the extreme events where the parameters are easier to understand and vary. They represent the average number of events above a certain threshold and the rate at which extreme events exceed that threshold. This new method has a straightforward connection to the original parameters and allows for a clear interpretation of the results in Bayesian analyses. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using real data and the performance of the estimator under different scenarios. Furthermore, this method has been implemented in the R package PEEST. Offline reinforcement learning has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its implications in creating Robust AI systems, particularly in critical industries such as transportation and aerospace, where fraudulent data can pose a significant threat to the training process. The primary challenge in handling counterfeit data lies in its potential to mislead the training algorithm, thereby increasing the likelihood of developing policies that could compromise safety. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of fraud-resilient offline reinforcement learning, whose ultimate goal is to develop robust policies despite being trained on fraudulent data. Theoretical insights reveal that, under certain conditions, the optimal fraud-resilient policy achieved through value function optimization can withstand data corruption. Furthermore, we outline a practical approach to approximating this ideal solution and evaluate its effectiveness in a simulated environment. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach remains resilient to data corruption and consistently outperforms traditional methods in offline RL. The code used in this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robotics-ai/fraud-rl. Additionally, the generated datasets can be found at https://github.com/robotics-ai/robust-rl-datasets. Detailed documentation of the methods is available at https://robotics.ai/docs. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability, which leads to impulsive controllability of the one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions. We define a controllability criterion for systems with fast-changing controls and derive a H\"older estimate for the left boundary null controllability in the case of rapid controls. This leads to the implication that coherent piecewise-constant controls can be used to achieve null controllability in a short time frame. Furthermore, we derive a finite-dimensional characterization of the control cost and establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal solution to the L^2 minimal time null-controllability problem with piecewise-constant controls. Finally, we prove that the optimal coherent piecewise-constant control achieves almost optimal costs in the large time framework. Our results generalize the known properties of the finite-dimensional characterizations, H\"older estimates, and optimal costs of the standard heat equation to the corresponding problems under dynamic boundary conditions. The proof of our main findings relies on the construction of a non-extendable, critically convex variant of the Fourier variable's action and the derivation of a non-extendable, critically convex variant of the boundary operator's action in the space of functions that are harmonic with respect to the interior of the domain in question. The criticality of these actions allows us to utilize the concepts of optimality of non-abnormal geodesics, which we adapted from the theory of non-abnormal geodesics in contact sub-Riemannian geometry, to prove our results. In particular, we demonstrate a logarithmic convexity of the Fourier variable's action and the boundary operator's action in the space of functions that are harmonic with respect to the interior of the domain in question, which we call the \emph{convexity of minimal times}. This new concept allows us to generalize the known properties of the finite-dimensional characterizations, H\"older estimates, and optimal costs of the standard heat equation to the corresponding problems under dynamic boundary conditions. In particular, we prove a new estimate for the cost of coherent piecewise-constant controls in terms of the time it is controlled for in the relevant problem under dynamic boundary conditions, which we call the \emph{estimate of costs in the large time framework}. This new estimate generalizes the known estimate for costs in the large time framework in the case of rapid controls to the corresponding problem under dynamic boundary conditions. This research targets the out-of-domain detection challenge, aiming to classify unseen text into four categories: online posts, product descriptions, and two distinct types of informal text, including personal stories and humorous content. To achieve this, we propose a new dataset, called FourTag, consisting of 9,772 annotated texts, which serves as a benchmark for comprehensive evaluation. By decomposing the out-of-domain dataset into sub-categories and analyzing the characteristics of each, we design optimized datasets for out-of-domain detection, yielding improved results with current leading models. Additionally, we present a novel approach that integrates a unified model to process both product descriptions and online posts, reducing reliance on individual fine-tuned models and demonstrating greater computational efficiency, while also facilitating easier data labeling and a more cohesive training process. This model surpasses the performance of independent models, successfully identifying domains in 92.1% of cases. Furthermore, we present a unified strategy to handle informal texts, integrating the models for personal stories and humorous content, achieving high accuracy rates of 0.918 and 0.944 respectively. By consolidating the models for distinct types of out-of-domain text, we have developed a unified out-of-domain detection model, capable of accurately classifying texts across all categories with an overall accuracy of 0.913. This research provides a benchmark, benchmark datasets, and novel approaches for out-of-domain detection, offering potential solutions and insights in this domain. The dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/4urth/FourTag. Experimental findings can be reproduced using the provided code, with our models demonstrating consistent performance in domain classification through repeated experiments. This research sets a new standard in out-of-domain detection, serving as a point of reference for future research in this area. From a practical perspective, this work enables the development of advanced chatbots capable of accurately assessing the coherence of user input, facilitating more natural and realistic human-chatty interactions with the system. From a theoretical perspective, this research contributes to the advancement of research in out-of-domain detection, specifically in the area of multi-category out-of-domain detection, with a novel dataset and novel approaches for efficient domain classification. Additionally, this research offers practical solutions to tackle the out-of-domain detection challenge. With continuous learning and adaptation, our models will become increasingly proficient in identifying domains, ultimately leading to more sophisticated and natural human-like conversations. This research enables the development of more advanced and human-like chatbots by effectively assessing user input, ensuring the system can recognize when a conversation is becoming too abstract or illogical

Utilizing quantum-thermal fluctuations, molecular motors can generate mechanical work at the atomic level. One theory suggests that work is produced by utilizing local electric potential variations to attract and repel molecular components, much like an electric motor. However, investigating this theory's validity requires highly realistic simulations of electric currents interacting with molecules. The DFA model consists of multiple stages with bidders making a limited number of bids, each carrying a cost and aiming to maximize their profit by assigning assets to the highest priced auctions with the lowest costs. A major area of focus in robotics research is efficient learning, which involves developing methods for quick and cost-effective skill acquisition. Current efficient learning approaches often rely on prior knowledge, but the source of this information remains unknown. This study aims to determine if robots benefit from past experiences by analyzing the end results of previous tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this direction-based learning algorithm is universally applicable across a range of learning tasks and outperforms traditional learning methods in challenging real-world scenarios. In multi-view datasets, a network's capacity to navigate in an unseen, real-world environment is tested by remembering previously seen images and making predictions based on recalled information.  The effectiveness of this approach is limited by the network's ability to select relevant past observations and adapt them to the current situation.  Although networks can learn to select memorable moments, their recall abilities are generally unresponsive to changing situations.  To address this, we present MemoNav, a multi-view navigation framework that trains a memory selection module and a moment transformation module using multi-view datasets.  The memory selection module chooses informative recollections and the moment transformation module transforms them to match the current observation.  By combining these memories, networks can better navigate and make predictions in novel situations.  We tested MemoNav on the MatterPort and NYU-VS datasets and found it outperformed existing multi-view navigation models.  By analyzing the network's memory selection behavior, we found that it effectively chose memorable moments and this ability drove navigation performance.  As a result, MemoNav has great potential as a general navigation method for a wide range of multi-view datasets.  The code for this project is available at https://github.com/pcyin/MemoNav.  W. Y. Furthermore, the use of complex numbers in quantum physics extends to applications such as atomic and particle physics, as well as in the rapidly developing fields of quantum information science and quantum-inspired machine learning. We strongly make the case that complex numbers are an essential requirement for quantum physics and provide a clear, simple explanation for their necessity. We also address common misconceptions surrounding the use of complex numbers in quantum physics, particularly the misconception that real numbers alone can suffice if 'imagination' or 'interpretation' is involved. We contend that this perspective is misguided and contradicts the core understanding of quantum mechanics, thereby undermining the entire framework of quantum physics and rendering it inconsistent with experimental evidence. Finally, we highlight that the quantum-inspired approaches to machine learning, which rely on complex numbers, have shown significant advantages in various benchmark tests. Consequently, the decision to utilize or refrain from utilizing complex numbers in quantum mechanics does not apply to machine learning; rather, the use of complex numbers is essential for both quantum physics and quantum-inspired approaches to learning. We advocate that future research in quantum physics and quantum-inspired theories should consistently employ complex numbers to ensure that results are reliable, consistent, and truly harness the power of quantum mechanics. We hope that this perspective will help to clarify misconceptions and promote a deeper understanding of the essential role that complex numbers play in shaping our understanding of reality. We also highlight that our perspective is consistent with the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and the underlying physics, as demonstrated by a diverse range of experiments and studies in atomic, particle, and condensed matter physics, as well as in quantum information science and learning. We look forward to seeing how the use of complex numbers will continue to revolutionize our understanding of the world, from the behavior of tiny atoms to the intricate mechanisms of quantum algorithms. We hope that this note will help to inspire novel ideas and innovations in quantum physics and quantum-inspired theories, as well as in related fields such as artificial intelligence and physics. Deep learning has predominantly focused on problems that have a single optimal solution, but many real-world issues, such as legal cases, medical diagnosis, and decision-making, often involve navigating uncertain and potentially conflicting information. This paper introduces a novel task called quantified ambiguity, which refers to the need to make definitive choices in the face of multiple possible outcomes. To address this challenge, we develop a new class of models, called Indecision Forests, which learn to reason about arguments both quantitatively and qualitatively. These models are versatile and can be applied to a range of problems, including argumentation, decision-making, and preference learning. To showcase their effectiveness, we also propose new datasets that highlight the subtleties of quantified ambiguity in practical scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that Indecision Forests outperform existing models on these tasks. Ultimately, these models provide a framework for addressing complex decision-making problems that require consideration of qualified outcomes. A popular approach in time series similarity search involves using DTW pruned search (DPSS), which aims to accelerate query processing by dismissing time series that are clearly dissimilar early on in the search process. However, this method's time complexity is not guaranteed to improve with larger datasets. In response, we introduce a new technique, eliminating DPSS (EDPSS), which integrates DPSS with an optimized alignment strategy. Our approach effectively discards unsimilar time series sooner during the comparison process, yielding improved linear complexity in the number of series. Moreover, EDPSS retains DPSS's original results, thus offering enhanced precision. By combining EDPSS with efficient query algorithms, unsimilar time series can be swiftly identified, and similar ones can be thoroughly compared, ultimately maximizing the overall search efficiency and effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that EDPSS significantly reduces processing time with minimal trade-off in precision, compared to using DPSS or existing top-performing methods. Furthermore, EDPSS outperforms state-of-the-art methods in an extensive test, achieving a 97\% reduction in processing time with a negligible decline in precision. The proposed method's code is openly available on GitHub at the link provided. In summary, the proposed EDPSS technique effectively addresses the long-standing issue of efficiently dismissing unsimilar time series, thus overcoming a significant limitation of DPSS-based methods. Conceptual coverage evaluation, a lesser-known approach in software testing education, focuses on assessing whether a test suite covers a program's significant aspects, as perceived by a stakeholder, to indirectly indicate the program's overall correctness. In contrast, traditional evaluation methods in software testing emphasize achieving high statement or function coverage. This empirical study examines the effect of instructing students to prioritize inquiry-based conceptual coverage over detailed evaluation of their test suites during a practical assignment. The findings reveal that prioritizing conceptual coverage leads to better task completion rates, improved program correctness, and reduced maintenance effort, as evidenced by the students' performance. A survey also revealed a positive impact on the students' understanding. The study's benefits are discussed, along with potential variations of the inquiry-based approach, which could be applicable to other areas of software testing education. The research also suggests its potential extension to other fields within software testing. The study's findings were subject to two rigorous evaluation methods: statistical analysis and readers' interpretation through a focused group study. The within-subject design employed was motivated by educational goals, specifically to gauge the effect of the testing approach on students' performance when the task requirements are clear, as opposed to the state of the students' understanding. The tested software tool, SITTool, was used for the practical assignment to ensure uniformity in evaluating the students' work. The study's methods and design align with guidelines for educational research and provide a tangible example of applying software testing concepts to assess program correctness, as well as the stakeholders' expectations, as part of software education. The research offers a fresh perspective, as well as reusable teaching tools, that can be utilized in software testing education to achieve its educational objectives. The study's results are a real-world demonstration of the application of software testing's inquiry-based approach. Two potential research avenues are identified, as well as the existing challenges associated with this line of inquiry within software testing education. Our method, called CAMEO, integrates three key components: pinpointing crucial features via concept analysis within an optimization framework, generating human-friendly attribute descriptions through integer programming, and utilizing these explanations to facilitate understanding between humans and machines. By doing so, CAMEO offers a novel, highly customizable technique with the capacity to provide detailed, feature-driven explanations for DNNs, even when human experts are unavailable to provide input. Additionally, the explanations produced by CAMEO promote cross-domain understanding between humans and machines, as evidenced by the outcomes of human evaluations. Deep learning methods have gained significant popularity for handling high-dimensional data, particularly those linked to graph structures. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a leading choice for graph-based machine learning tasks. Notably, GCNs have effectively resolved problems in social network analysis, drug recommendation, and citation network understanding, among others. Despite their success, we contend that GCNs have inherent limitations, primarily affecting their ability to capture detailed patterns. Consequently, their performance may decline when confronted with complex graphs requiring precise feature extraction. In response, a novel neural framework, the Multi-Head Self-Connecting Network (MHSCN), is introduced to enhance feature representation. THMSCN's key innovation involves a novel multi-head self-connecting operation that allows for more precise control over information propagation. By comparing MHSCN to GCN, we evaluate their relative effectiveness on six benchmark datasets, showcasing MHSCN's superior performance across all benchmarks. Additionally, we provide a thorough analysis of the theoretical underpinnings of MHSCN's design. Our work presents a well-suited solution to the 'over-blurring' effect often associated with GCNs, offering a valuable contribution to the ongoing development of neural graph models. We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$-dependent distributions in terms of Wess-Zumino terms, which are relevant in hard processes involving heavy particles. These functions, dependent on the relative transverse momentum of partons, help in understanding interactions between partons and hadrons in the transverse plane. They also play a crucial role in quantifying effects of internal momentum configurations in the transverse plane, characteristic of hadrons, but absent in particles like photons. To quantify this, we define 'quasi' distribution functions for charged pions, by comparing the transverse momentum spectra of pions and electrons in e+e- collisions. By calculating the Wess-Zumino term for this process, we extract information about the 'quasi' distribution function. Furthermore, we generalize this approach to $k_\perp$-dependent distribution functions, relevant in deep inelastic scattering and semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering. Our analysis highlights the distinct contributions of quarks and gluons to these functions and their relationship with conventional parton distribution functions. It also raises questions about the quark and gluon distribution functions being adequate descriptions, although they neglect transverse momentum configurations of partons. To address this concern, we propose an alternative distribution, tied to the Wess-Zumino term and characterized by a non-zero transverse momentum of partons, as observed in hadron physics. This, however, requires transverse momentum configurations to be shared equally by quarks and gluons, a requirement not met in processes like deep inelastic scattering and semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering. To resolve this paradox, we suggest that distribution functions solely based on momentum configurations, forgetting transverse momentum effects, are adequate descriptions in processes not involving hadrons in the final state. Our work opens up new avenues to study transverse momentum configurations of partons and their implications for understanding processes like deep inelastic scattering, semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, and heavy quark production. It also indicates that transverse momentum configurations of partons, as measured in hadron physics, are not relevant in processes like deep inelastic scattering, semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, and heavy quark production. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of processes like deep inelastic scattering, semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, and heavy quark production. They also indicate that transverse momentum configurations of partons, as measured in hadron physics, are not transferable to processes involving parton distribution functions and parton fragmentation

Research into remote epitaxy has gained significant momentum as a controlling method for growing crystals, offering the ability to manufacture large-area wafers with high quality crystals without being limited by substrate constraints.  However, achieving complete control over the epitaxy process remains a significant challenge, particularly in reducing the influence of substrate epitaxy.  This study presents findings on the epitaxy mechanism of La$_{0.65}$Sn$_{0.35}$Te (LST) films grown using a graphene-covered sapphire substrate.  Through the analysis of crystallographic, structural, and optical properties, it has been determined that a thin graphene layer cannot completely prevent substrate epitaxy, which is due to the remote epitaxy mechanism facilitated by van der Waals adhesion.  However, it has been discovered that a high Sn content of 35% in the LST films is pivotal in enhancing the quality of films grown using the remote epitaxy mechanism, resulting in the production of high-quality crystals with near-ideal structures even when grown at relatively low temperatures of 450^\circC.  This research provides valuable insights into regulating the equilibrium between different epitaxy mechanisms, offering valuable information for scaling up remote epitaxy technology.  Additionally, it has been found that La$_{0.50}$Sn$_{0.50}$Te films grown using this method exhibit exceptional properties, with a 14% higher carrier concentration compared to those grown without graphene, while films with higher Sn content content exhibited even better performance, with a significantly enhanced carrier mobility of up to 100 S/cm in comparison to those grown without graphene, which displays a significantly reduced carrier mobility of only 10 S/cm.  As a result, this study yields thin films with high Sn content and exceptional electrical properties, along with high structural quality, making them highly suitable for a variety of technical applications.  Consequently, these research findings significantly advance our understanding of regulating the equilibrium between different epitaxy mechanisms, thereby expanding the possibilities for remote epitaxy technology.  This has led to groundbreaking discoveries regarding the growth conditions of LST films, which could have far-reaching implications for the production of high-quality semiconductors.  This research further enables the production of high-quality semiconductors with robust electrical properties and exceptional structural quality using innovative, scalable processes.  This has significant potential to revolutionize the field by removing traditional substrate constraints, thereby expanding the possibilities for scalable remote epitaxy technology.  This could lead to significant breakthroughs in energy-efficient technology, enabling the development of highly efficient devices

Researchers have developed the HSMM model, a non-parametric statistical model, to analyze multivariate time series data that exhibit excessive variability. The original model was adapted from hidden Markov models, but its initial inference methods became impractically complex when dealing with large datasets, requiring approximations such as limiting the model's complexity and imposing a Gaussian distribution on errors to ensure inferable parameters can be estimated reliably, especially in large datasets. However, this led to suboptimal performance as the errors do not follow a normal distribution in real-world data. Neural networks are currently the most effective text-to-image generators available, outperforming previous art generation tools in various evaluation benchmarks. However, the artistic quality of their output images is often subjective and difficult to quantify. In this research, we introduce a novel method to directly evaluate image aesthetics using human assessors, providing clear instructions and guidelines to ensure reliable and uncontested ratings. Our study compares the generated images produced by GANs, CVAEs, and SVAEs in terms of their overall aesthetic appeal rather than purely measuring their similarity to real images as in previous studies. Our analysis of the aesthetic ratings reveals that neural network-based generators primarily reproduce previously existing images while struggling to capture the underlying artistic skills required to create unique and visually appealing images. On the other hand, programs that incorporate explicit artistic templates, such as DALL-E, demonstrate better aesthetic results due to their access to pre-trained visual features. Interestingly, the best ratings were awarded to images produced by GANs over other neural network-based methods, highlighting the significance of discriminative training in generating more aesthetically pleasing images. Our study's findings and image datasets are openly available for other researchers to reproduce and build upon. Additionally, we have released open-source code for the image generation tasks and aesthetic evaluation framework, allowing for the reproduction of our study's results. Our study's code and image datasets can be accessed via https://github.com/jbarnessp/The-Delight-of-Neural-Artistry. In our analysis, a nonstandard finite difference scheme is proposed and evaluated for an epidemic SISI model, where the model's behavior is analyzed under two time-step scenarios. A boundary value problem is derived from the continuous model, specifically for a particular time-step case, and its solution is shown to replicate the behavior of the original differential equation with a specified level of error. This numerical method is then shown to preserve the positivity of solutions, providing valuable insights into epidemic modeling. Furthermore, we examine the influence of discrete noise on the model's solutions, as well as the impact of changing time steps on the epidemic model's trajectory, particularly in relation to the epidemic model's fundamental parameters. A central finding is that distinct-time updates can result in a second outbreak occurring later, even if not observed with standard time steps, and that the epidemic model's behavior may persist indefinitely, particularly in small populations where the disease prevalence never reaches zero. Conversely, the epidemic model may resolve itself, particularly in larger populations where the disease prevalence reaches 100% under certain time-step conditions. A series of numerical examples are provided to illustrate and verify the analytical findings obtained from the epidemic SISI model. Based on these results, it is suggested that distinct-time updates can lead to differing qualitative outcomes compared to the continuous epidemic model, with implications for policy interventions aimed at mitigating the spread of diseases. Consequently, it is recommended that updates to disease prevalence should be made using small time steps to ensure accurate tracking of the epidemic model's trajectory, particularly when making policy decisions based on the epidemic model's qualitative behavior. Finally, a discussion is presented on the distinct-time epidemic model, along with recommendations for future research in this area. This study reveals that even in the absence of direct heating sources, an AC-driven toggling mechanism can produce substantial heat being either directed to a particular point or efficiently rejected. Notably, the interference caused by different tunneling paths at specific points can significantly influence the thermoelectric effects, thereby resulting in the conversion of electrical signals into heat at specific points or multiple heat sources being utilized efficiently. Our research provides a framework for quantifying thermoelectric effects within complex quantum systems and offers insights into the interplay between different electronic properties and heat transfer. DNA data storage, a cutting-edge technology, allows for the conversion of digital data into DNA sequences that can be stored at extremely low costs. The DNA sequence is initially compressed using a prefix-sum data structure, which helps with data retrieval and sequence recovery. However, the highly compressed data leads to complications in the DNA sequence, particularly with data retrieval, due to the need to decompress data. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a hierarchical retrieval system, allowing for multiple levels of data access without requiring the entire DNA sequence to be scanned. This leads to a significant reduction in the number of DNA sequence reads, and consequently, in the time and energy required for data retrieval. The hierarchical system comprises multiple levels of data access, with each level utilizing a distinct DNA sequence, and is achieved through the use of index sequences, which enable rapid data location, thus obviating the need for sequence scanning. The hierarchical system also addresses another major issue in DNA data storage, namely data refreshes, which involve updating stored data over time. The system allows for simultaneous sequence reads and writes during data refreshes, and efficiently manages the handling of complex data, particularly during refreshes of deeply nested data components. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, revealing that it leads to a substantial reduction in read time, as well as in read and write energy during data refreshes, thus enhancing overall system performance and efficiency. The paper explores key issues surrounding wave equations in quantum theory, presenting arguments for and against these equations. Although they have significant advantages, we argue against using wave equations to represent quantum states, as they are not uniquely defined without a well-defined phase function. This problem is typically addressed by introducing Laplace-Belanger conditions, which can lead to misinterpretation of the quantum theory. Another approach is to adopt a double-role for wave functions, utilizing both Schrödinger and Helmholtz equations in quantum context. However, this duality raises concerns about loss of physical information. Furthermore, even if wave equations excel at describing physical phenomena, they do not necessarily offer a superior mathematical framework for quantum theory. Our analysis also touches on the dual role of wave functions in quantum theory and the absence of determinate waves in the vacuum state. Finally, we examine how the dual roles of wave functions and the absence of determinate waves in the vacuum state relate to the concept of non-physical waves, which may be observable only through their physical derivatives. Lastly, we speculate on how the dual roles of wave functions and the absence of determinate waves in the vacuum state could lead to a deeper understanding of the measurement problem and the nature of physical reality in the quantum theory. In particular, we explore how the non-physical waves, which may be derivable only from the physical waves via the Schrödinger equation, could be responsible for inducing measurements, thus providing a possible resolution to the induction problem in the quantum theory. In addition to these topics, we discuss other debates for the wave equations in quantum theory, such as their role in determining physical reality, their connection to the Born rule, and their relevance to the double-role of wave functions in the quantum theory. Built on top of PyTROCR, a robust reinforcement learning library, L2E encompasses a comprehensive suite of 123 diverse reward functions, which can be combined to create 1,228 distinct learning objectives. This extensive collection of rewards, which are tied to dynamic systems with adjustable dynamics and dimensionality, allows for the exploration of a vast multidimensional space. As a result, L2E offers a range of features that support the evaluation of lifelong reinforcement learning methods, including a search tool and a comprehensive dataset of 180,000 simulated scenarios. A key challenge in intent detection lies in how a model can effectively discover and learn unknown intent categories when confronted with unfamiliar data. Current research often relies on reinforcement learning (RL) to tackle this issue, however, it tends to result in a 'over-cautious' model that excessively focuses on preventing misclassification. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that combines pre-training and a novel contrastive loss function. The pre-trained model is crafted to prioritize exploration of unknown intents by assessing data points that are hard to categorize into familiar ones. Meanwhile, a new loss function enhances the model's ability to distinguish between different intent categories by crossing it with an auxiliary classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves better accuracy in identifying unknown intent categories compared to existing models. Additionally, it reduces the influence of over-cautious behavior and improves the model's overall performance on intent detection tasks. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/Chen-543/NEIL.git.

This research introduces the Virtual Protected Framework, a hybrid, five-stage cycle cycle-accurate processor over the TFHE protocol, designed to support multi-level hierarchical secret data sharing. The VPFW framework encompasses both VPU and DCU components, with its VPU segment complemented by a custom Instruction Set Architecture. The study involves an in-depth evaluation of the VPFW's performance, where numerical values are substituted for program variables in both native and protected mode executions, with key performance metrics obtained through cycle-accurate simulation. Cycle counting and throughput were the performance indicators used. To mitigate the impact of garbled circuits on performance, garbled circuits were partially optimized in this work, resulting in a cycle-accurate VPFW model with optimized garbled circuits, facilitating faster cycle counting in simulations. A comparative analysis of the VPFW model with and without secret data sharing in hardware implementations is also presented. Recent advances in pre-trained language models have shown remarkable performance in a variety of tasks, however their effectiveness in analysis tasks, particularly those that need to understand a single sentence or phrase, remains unclear. We have conducted comprehensive experiments to examine the analysis capabilities of these models, comparing their performance to models specifically designed for analysis. Our results show that pre-trained models excel in both unsupervised and few-shot analysis tasks, outperforming specialist models in many cases. Additionally, we found that the pre-trained models can develop their own semantic analysis framework without any guidance, in addition to leveraging existing semantic information. Our findings afford insights into how language models develop semantic understanding and open up new possibilities for using these models in a range of analysis tasks. To address this, a new approach uses hyperspectral images, which capture each pixel's spectral properties, to enhance image representation and performance. Experimental results confirmed that the proposed method surpassed state-of-the-art approaches, validating the benefits of using hyperspectral images in semantic segmentation tasks. To facilitate effective session-based suggestion, users' historical preferences should be taken into consideration. However, existing recommendation models either ignore the session-level structure or overlook the user's past behavior. In this study, we combine session-based suggestion with user preference exploration by developing a self-supervised graph co-training framework. It integrates a recommendation model with a session-aware encoder to leverage both current and past session data. This innovative approach uniquely combines two objectives - enhancing both suggestion relevance and inter-session connectivity - using self-supervised learning. As a result, the entire system is trained end-to-end without requiring manual labeling. Experimental evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over cutting-edge recommendation models in both relevant domains. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of exploring historical user activity for session-based suggestion. This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard framework. By applying a previous code transformation, it is demonstrated that an LCD code can be mapped to a subcode of a linear code within a group ring, and vice versa. Under specific conditions, it is proven that the resulting subcode maintains the LCD property, and optimal LCD codes are subsequently identified in specific settings, such as binary and ternary group rings. Additionally, a method is proposed to create group LCD codes through the selection of non-singular matrices, and a comprehensive database of optimal binary group LCD codes is developed. Furthermore, it is shown that LCD codes can also be formulated using group rings with elements not consisting solely of linear components, and a method for achieving zero weight in group LCD codes is developed. Examples illustrating the achieved advancements are also presented in this study. Consequently, it is possible to access a wider variety of LCD codes compared to the conventional approach using elementary abelian groups, and a systematic way of developing optimal binary group LCD codes is established. Consequently, the proposed methods demonstrate the superiority of the group ring approach over conventional techniques. We introduce an innovative technique, two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method, for studying three-dimensional charge transport in wide bandgap semiconductors. We apply this approach to single-crystalline diamond and demonstrate its utility by mapping the three-dimensional path of a photo-generated charge packet in a scanned area. Utilizing a femtosecond laser source with 800 nm wavelength, we explore charge transport across the entire diameter of diamond substrates, either in a round-trip mode or by shifting the boundary point to explore different paths. We show that the charge transport speed and efficiency can be evaluated and compared across the entire diameter of the sample. This novel technique enables us to gain a deeper understanding of single-crystalline diamond quality and to optimize growth conditions to achieve high-quality materials for advanced quantum sensing applications. Additionally, this method can be adapted for use in a wide range of semiconductor materials. We successfully demonstrated a 0.5 mm long travel in a single scan, however we anticipate this approach could achieve even longer distances with the aid of a linear scanner system or by employing a higher average power laser source. Ultimately, this technique enables us to thoroughly examine the properties of semiconductors over significant distances, exceeding the limitations of the injection-luminescence method. In order to achieve the same level of understanding, the injection-luminescence method requires a corresponding increase in sample size, resulting in a significant loss of injection efficiency due to increased carrier recombination in the transparent substrate. We have developed a mathematical model which predicts a minimal loss of 16.4% for 1 mm long samples, significantly decreasing as the sample size increases and the injection efficiency approaches its maximum value at a very large size. Nonetheless, this inefficiency would not be a concern for 1 mm long samples as the injection-luminescence method does not become inefficient until reaching such large sizes. Conversely, we have also discovered that a wide range of semiconductor materials could benefit from this novel approach due to their wide bandgaps and high carrier mobility values. These wide bandgap materials include diamond Raman, zinc oxide, gallium nitride and silicon carbide. In conclusion, we thoroughly examined the properties of single-crystalline diamond and determined a wide range of wide bandgap semiconductor materials could greatly benefit from the novel three-dimensional charge transport mapping capabilities offered by the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method. This innovative technique allows us to thoroughly examine wide bandgap materials, efficiently testing their properties over long distances and providing valuable insights into their behavior.

We establish a formalization of the Scott framework for PCF within univalent type theory, incorporating a fundamental definition of continuity and proving its equivalence with a type-theoretic interpretation of PCF. Our work is based on an previous study (Brent Norris's thesis) and is formulated within the univalent framework of the Coq-unicap library. This decision yields novel proofs, such as a demonstration that the continuity principle underlying PCF is inherent to univalent type theory. As an adjunct to this research, we also develop a type-theoretic formulation of the inverse-limit construction for universal domains, a key concept in the theory of domains. This entire development has been formalized and verified within the Coq-unicap library. 

Note that the original paper had to adhere to strict pagination constraints, resulting in an abbreviated discussion. For a more complete exploration of the underlying ideas, refer to Norris's thesis. 

In this formalization, we drew upon the following sources:

- Allen Blanchard's work on domain theory in univalent type theory
- Guillaume Dubois's research on continuous functions in univalent type theory
- Mike Shulman's discussion of continuity in univalent type theory
- Eric Sherman's investigation of PCF in univalent type theory

In particular, we updated the following files within the Coq-unicap library: Continuity, DomainTheory, and PCF.

The escalating climate crisis and associated economic disruptions necessitate a swift global response.  This paper examines how diverse societal norms surrounding carbon pricing are currently represented and proposes two new standards that can serve as viable alternatives, both of which can facilitate carbon trading.  A stylized game-theoretic model is developed to analyze the dynamic behavior of price paths generated by these different norms.  Our study reveals that the widespread adoption of one particular trading system is likely, yet also that the different standards can coexist and influence one another.  A carbon tax becomes the preferred global policy in the long run, yet the current mix of policies, particularly the lack of one, contributes to climate-related damages.  Our findings demonstrate that the various societal norms are distinct and influential, and that their interplay has significant implications for climate policy.  In particular, the persistent reliance on non-market-based standards like capping and the recent emergence of the tax standard as a global phenomenon, born out of economic considerations, can simultaneously coexist and impact carbon pricing.  A sudden shift towards the tax standard would result in an immediate and significant increase in carbon pricing.  Conversely, a corresponding rise in the price of carbon can serve as an early warning sign for a potential shift towards the tax standard.  Furthermore, our study also explores the impact of the pandemic-driven economic changes on carbon pricing.  In this regard, we find that a permanent economic effect of the pandemic, as reflected in the shift towards remote work and decreased energy consumption, would result in a long-lasting and significant increase in carbon pricing.  Conversely, a temporary economic effect would result in a short-lived and less substantial increase in carbon pricing.  Our study contributes to the body of research on carbon pricing and highlights the various societal norms surrounding this concept and their implications for climate policy.  Furthermore, it also examines the behavior of carbon pricing in the presence of different norms and their interplay, as well as the impact of global economic changes and the pandemic.  Finally, it also provides a new and innovative perspective on the analysis of dynamic systems with multiple equilibria, particularly in the context of carbon pricing. While NLP is not as authentic as spoken language, written text can be considered authentic in various contexts. In this study, we provide an overview of the levels of authenticity in written text and how reinforcement learning can be applied to enhance text authenticity, particularly for reinforcement learning models that utilize written text as states or actions. We examine existing reinforcement learning models that aim to produce authentic language samples, focusing on two levels: phrase-level and sentence-level. At the same time, we aim to promote the development of more sophisticated written text generation through the incorporation of self-supervised learning methods, such as language pre-training. These methods can serve as valuable tools for reinforcing text authenticity and fostering more natural written descriptions. Our understanding of the conditions in the intergalactic medium (IGM) is derived from observations of high-redshift quasars. Their radiative output is obstructed by the IGM, resulting in absorption signals visible in their spectra, which originate from neutral atomic species at various redshifts. By implementing a machine learning approach, we can reverse the inverse hierarchy of data generation and obtain the IGM's energy density distribution. This is achieved by reversing the forward hierarchy with a deep learning network trained on simulated data, thereby yielding the IGM's energy density distribution. Our findings indicate that the resulting energy density distributions exhibit periodic fluctuations in the IGM's density at $z \sim 4-5$. Additionally, we find that these models can accurately quantify the IGM's incoherent scattering power and estimate the associated uncertainty. Our analysis further suggests that the redshift of the peak IGM density fluctuation lies around $z \sim 4.5$. This transformation poses a significant challenge to established model training methods, which often require significant fine-tuning to achieve desirable results. A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication is being developed to mitigate the issues of increasing data rates and emerging new services on existing wireless networks. We envision a future network where a "negotiator" and "verifier" communicate over a "signaling channel" to establish a semantic understanding between them. The negotiator represents a data source that specifies a set of target receivers and a data generation mechanism, while the verifier represents the communication channel, which tests the validity of data received from the negotiator. During a "signaling game" initiated by the verifier to request data, the negotiator responds with "semantic labels" that include statistical information about the generated data. We model this interaction as a mixed strategy game where the verifier dynamically selects its exploration and exploitation probabilities based on the received labels and past validation outcomes, and the negotiator responds with a probability distribution of valid data conditioned on the labels. Through this exchange, the verifier learns to separate actual data from artificial data generated by the negotiator, which in turn adapts its labeling strategy. We train these strategies using deep neural networks known as neuro-symbolic networks, which combine graph neural networks for data representation with a reinforcement learning module that emerges during training. Our results show that the trained neuro-symbolic networks perform well in a variety of signaling games, even when we simulate a communication channel with random errors. Furthermore, the negotiator labels the data correctly without any noise, while the verifier successfully validates the data without any exploration, which confirms the effectiveness of our approach. Our research provides a framework for the emergent semantic communication system known as the signaling game, as well as the neuro-symbolic architectures that learn to operate within this framework. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to the development of reliable and efficient wireless data exchange mechanisms. Additionally, this study validated the hybrid approach's generalizability on other datasets, including Yelp and IMDB, showcasing its versatility and practical applications. Lastly, the proposed hybrid approach has substantial practical implications and can be scaled up for use in industry and academic research, as demonstrated by the successful deployment of Latent Knowledge in the clinical question answering dataset ClinQA. To safeguard AI systems from hostile attacks, we examine the security of an unfamiliar decision-based Black-Box model in a real-world setting. Our investigation reveals that the original decision-based approach has a critical flaw: it can be easily deceived in advanced adversarial scenarios. To resolve this issue, we develop a reliable method for evaluating the confidence of Black-Box models, which is subsequently utilized to create a robust metric for measuring their performance. With this new metric, we can compare and surpass existing grading methods in various challenging scenarios. Furthermore, our improved evaluation method enables the development of a reliable performance metric that can effectively transfer knowledge from trained models to untrained ones without prior knowledge. Notably, our method exhibits superior performance in practical, real-world applications, outperforming previous methods in these scenarios. A new approach is proposed for determining the extent of treatment interference in a specific network using the k-neighborhood framework. Under this framework, the effect of a treatment on a unit is influenced solely by its k nearest neighbors who have not received the treatment. While this model offers simplicity in understanding the spread of a treatment, its ability to accurately represent the spread of a treatment in a graph is proven to be equivalent to solving a maximum independent set problem in that graph. As a result, identifying the proper value of k becomes equivalent to solving a combinatorial optimization problem, although both issues become computationally complex when the graph becomes increasingly dense. However, a method is developed to approximate both problems using a local improvement strategy that provides a constant ratio of efficiency to the optimal solution. Furthermore, a way to statistically evaluate and identify the proper value of k is developed by incorporating the use of permutation-based p-values in this analysis. In this work, a novel method utilizing voltage reduction in SRAMs for genuine random number generation is proposed. By temporarily lowering the SRAM's supply voltage below what's safe for normal data access, the device can enter a volatile state. We allow the SRAM to retain these low voltages for a statistically significant time, harvesting the resulting bit flips that occur. These unstable bits are fed into a hash function, generating high-quality random numbers. The extracted randomness has been extensively evaluated using standard statistical tests and has demonstrated robustness in various scenarios, including those involving temperature changes and process variations. Furthermore, our approach exhibits advantages in terms of real-time randomness generation, scalability, and hardware implementation ease. The proposed scheme has been successfully integrated into a real SRAM process, showcasing its feasibility as a reliable and efficient solution for securing random data in practical applications. The developed prototype, TuRaN, has been fabricated using 40nm technology and has outperformed leading commercial PRNGs in terms of randomness quality, while also offering faster generation times and lower overheads compared to alternative hardware random number generators. The performance figures highlight up to 30% higher throughput and significantly reduced latency, as well as a 5x smaller area, all while maintaining exceptional randomness quality. The detailed design files for TuRaN are available online at bitbucket.org, allowing for easy customization and integration into user-designed ASICs. During training, neural networks often develop simplified features, even though this can lead to inaccurate predictions. The source of this phenomenon has been debated, with theories ranging from the network's ability to detect patterns to its reliance on random variations. Our research reveals that the underlying cause lies in the numerous built-in regulators of complexitiy within the geometric structure of neural networks. We demonstrate that the inherent relationships within the network's connectivity graph lead to the discovery of feature simplifications. In particular, we show that the Bass value of a neural network acts as an effective complexity regulator, limiting the complexity of the network's solutions. Our findings apply to a broad range of neural network architectures and the Bass value's properties enable it to be computed efficiently. Moreover, we have developed an online algorithm that allows for the automatic detection and elimination of unnecessary complexity during training. Our experiments using MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets show significant performance enhancements when simplifying complex neural networks.
