A new approach is proposed for determining the four Wilson coefficients contributing to rare $b\to s$ processes by analyzing $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays without intermediate assumptions about hadronic parameters.  This method, primarily sensitive to $q^2$ dependencies in two-dimensional Wilson coefficients, can provide accurate fit results for Wilson coefficients with better statistical precision than standard analyses using one-dimensional representations.  Consequently, this approach should enable more stringent limits on new physics contributions beyond the Standard Model and more precise tests of its presence in $b\to s$ processes.  We further demonstrate that this method remains effective even in the presence of theoretical uncertainties in hadronic parameters, thereby facilitating ongoing Wilson coefficient determination.  To validate our approach, we performed a fit using the available $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ data and obtained the coefficients $|c_7/w_7|$, $|c_9/w_9|$, $|c_{10}|$, and $\text{Arg}(C_9)$ with better statistical precision than standard analyses.  We have made the relevant software available for public use.  We have evaluated our approach's sensitivity to systematic uncertainties in LHCb and Belle II experiment environments and found that it remains effective, albeit slightly limited, in those settings.  We have proposed and evaluated a simple statistical strategy to enhance the sensitivity of this approach to new physics contributions.  Finally, we have investigated its potential to inform $b\to s$ processes at Belle II and LHCb experiments in the near future.  We have explored the theoretical uncertainties in hadronic parameters that affect this approach and found that it could be refined by incorporating relevant chiral perturbation theory results. A ground-truth data set of 409,909 New York City taxi trips from March 1 to March 31, 2011, is utilized to create an agent-based model (ABM) of taxi travel. The detailed taxi trip information in the data set, however, cannot be directly incorporated into the ABM due to its large size and disordered structure. Consequently, researchers often rely on simplified representations of taxi behavior, disregarding the rich information in the data. This study proposes a novel statistical technique that enables large data sets to be incorporated into computational models. This method, called data-informed modeling, integrates a computational model with a data set through statistical analysis, informing model parameters and behaviors. Specifically, a negative binomial regression is employed to synthesize the data set and generate taxi trip counts for each hour of the simulation day, while an average-based method is used to distribute these trips into trips per hour. These methods transform the large data set into a set of manageable parameters, eliminating the need for data resampling or model dismissal. When incorporated into the ABM, these methods yield notable improvements in simulation outcomes, as evidenced by enhanced statistical fit and more accurate predictive capabilities. Furthermore, the integrated approach contributes valuable insights to taxi management, facilitating the identification of optimal taxi stand locations and helping to assess the feasibility of introducing mini-cab hailing. Ultimately, this research outlines a data-informed modeling paradigm that can facilitate a more responsive and data-driven decision-making process. A practical implementation of this method, known as collaborative data-informed modeling, is demonstrated in which multiple agents, including human experts and computational models, contribute to a shared understanding of the system, as exemplified by the shared parameters and behaviors of the taxi agents. This collaborative approach is versatile and can be applied in diverse domains to address various challenges. This study presents a novel research on density parity-check codes constructed using degree-degree relationships, which provide clear criteria for designing and assessing these codes. We thoroughly examine various parameters, including cycle structure, error correcting capabilities, and density parity-check code performance, specifically in a binary erasure channel. Our research reveals that the distribution of cycle lengths in our proposed codes is more uniform than in standard density parity-check codes, resulting in superior performance and increased error correcting capabilities. However, our methods also have inherent limitations, particularly a maximum allowed variable node degree, which can negatively impact density parity-check code performance as the erasure probability increases. We find that our degree-degree related density parity-check codes outperform standard density parity-check codes in most cases but struggle with extremely high erasure probabilities. To address this limitation, we develop a hybrid approach combining density parity-check and low-density parity-check codes, which inherits the excellent cycle structure properties from density parity-check codes while also capturing the error correcting capabilities of low-density parity-check codes. The resulting codes display superior performance, specifically in extremely high erasure probabilities, while still maintaining comparable or better performance in lower erasure probabilities. The potential applications of these codes are vast and diverse, encompassing areas like satellite communication, interplanetary communication, and short-range terrestrial communication. The associated source code for generating these codes is included. Experiments demonstrating the superiority of these codes in satellite communication and short-range terrestrial communication scenarios are also conducted and showcased. Furthermore, we provide clear design guidelines for implementing these codes in practical scenarios and offer suggestions for further enhancing their performance. The concepts presented in this study can be extended to other areas, such as quantum computing, and we provide a potential direction for integrating our degree-degree related density parity-check codes into quantum error correction protocols. The integration of these codes in quantum systems could lead to significant performance enhancements in future quantum computers. The minimum error correcting capabilities of these degree-degree related density parity-check codes can be compared to Reed-Solomon codes, specifically the maximum distance profile, which can be utilized for designing and assessing density parity-check codes. The techniques employed in this study can be applied to other coding schemes, such as low-density parity-check codes, and we provide a potential approach for improving the efficiency of LDPCs using degree-degree relationships. Conversely, research into the influence of the size and composition of the training dataset on the performance in-context learning has been scarce. In this research, we examine the effect of training dataset size and content on the achievement of in-context learning with large-scale language models. Our analysis indicates that models trained on larger datasets tend to exhibit superior performance in a variety of tasks, and that these models are particularly adept at handling more complex tasks. When dealing with the Cauchy distribution, parameter estimation presents significant challenges, primarily due to its lack of convergence in the mean. Nonetheless, researchers have developed methods to create reliable intervals for estimating its parameters, albeit these intervals do not satisfy the usual properties of confidence intervals. Notably, the intervals are finitely bounded, making them absolutely accurate, which is an uncommon feature in this context. Building on this idea, this paper proposes a novel approach to defining intervals for the Cauchy distribution's parameters, using a different framework. Specifically, we will use the variance or squared deviation as a measure of dispersion, as this quantity is finite and well-behaved. Under this alternative framework, we design intervals that not only provide precise estimates but also satisfy increasingly tight bounds as the sample size increases. These intervals are comparable to those obtained by maximum likelihood estimation and outperform them in several respects. Moreover, we examine the proposed intervals' behavior in cases of small or finite sample sizes, demonstrating that they converge rapidly and uniformly. The methods developed in this paper can also be extended to estimate the parameters of related distributions, as well as those of the within-cluster distribution in cluster-sigma models. Lastly, we illustrate the effectiveness of these proposals using numerical examples and Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have made the relevant R code publicly available at https://github.com/congdonstats/Cauchy_estimation/tree/main. This code can also be used to estimate the parameters of skew-Cauchy distributions, which generalize the Cauchy distribution and whose parameters' estimation shares similar characteristics with our proposals. Specifically, the 'cauchyRL' package at https://github.com/congdonstats/cauchyRL/tree/main contains the necessary R code. Alternatively, the 'clusterCCE' package at https://github.com/congdonstats/clusterCCE/tree/main also contains relevant R code for estimating the parameters of cluster-sigma models, as described in our paper's simulation examples. Furthermore, the'scauchyRL' package at https://github.com/congdonstats/scauchyRL/tree/main contains the necessary R code for estimating the parameters of skew-Cauchy distributions. In a related work, we have developed new methods for estimating the parameters of skew-Cauchy distributions using a general approach, as described in 'A General Framework for Estimating Skew-Cauchy Distributions' (arXiv:2208.05191, 2022). In basket trials where diseases are studied based on genetic markers rather than location, researchers investigate various subsets of patients with specific marker profiles. Our proposed method addresses the challenge of determining suitable sample sizes for each subset of patients, taking into account the costs involved, under a Bayesian framework. To optimize results, we implement a simulation-based approach, in addition to offering a theoretical probe. The Bayesian framework allows us to share information across different subsets, effectively and efficiently. The proposed method is compared to traditional fixed sample size designs and a prior version of our approach, through simulations involving two scenarios, one with known associations between markers and patient outcomes, and another with unknown associations. Our results show that the Bayesian approach produces more accurate estimates of treatment effects, with reduced variability, when there's little initial knowledge, and meets predetermined statistical criteria more frequently, especially in cases with known associations. Furthermore, the Bayesian method outperforms other designs in identifying significant results, particularly in scenarios with known associations. A numerical example is included to demonstrate the proposed method's capabilities, using data from a basket trial involving three subsets of patients, where the method successfully determines appropriate sample sizes and identifies significant results. Finally, we discuss the limitations and potential future applications of our method. It could be applied in various clinical trials, such as trials comparing a new treatment with a standard treatment, and in trials involving multiple treatments with varying dosages. In addition, it has potential applications in trials involving different species, as seen in toxicology studies. To achieve high motion system accuracy, it's crucial to regulate the position with high precision, which necessitates a priori knowledge of system parameters and slight variations in the environment to predict and adjust for dynamic changes. However, extreme changes in these parameters render traditional static design approaches ineffective, prompting the need to incorporate real-time estimation of varying system parameters. Although linear parameter-varying (LPV) models can accommodate parameter fluctuations, real-time LPV state feedback controllers face significant challenges, primarily due to the large number of possible parameter values, which typically range from 10 to 200. This paper presents an innovative LPV sequential loop shutting (LSLS) strategy that integrates an LPV state feedback controller with an online parameter estimation module, which actively identifies and transmits relevant system parameter data to the controller. By focusing on a specific set of critical parameter values that significantly affect system performance and limiting controller interaction with non-critical parameters, this LPV LSLS approach optimizes real-time computation, thereby facilitating real-world application. The proposed methodology is evaluated using both simulation and hardware tests of a motion system testbed and demonstrated to provide superior performance with online tuning of critical parameter bounds, achieving a 30-fold reduction in non-optimal parameter-related error and outperforming conventional techniques by approximately 50%. Furthermore, this LPV LSLS approach exhibits robustness and can be adapted for use in other sophisticated motion systems and advanced aircraft flight control systems. Experimental data from the testbed also validate the theoretical findings of this paper, which provide a solid foundation for the development of future advanced control technologies. In particular, this research contributes to the ongoing work on LPV technology and offers an innovative solution to the long-standing problem of tuning parameter bounds in LPV systems, thereby facilitating real-world application and showcasing the potential benefits of this technology. To facilitate replication of these results, the associated code has been openly shared on relevant platforms, including GitHub, which hosts the testbed data and code used in this research, and DOI, which indexes the paper. By sharing these resources, the authors aim to stimulate discussion and collaboration within the control engineering community, ultimately advancing the state-of-the-art in LPV technology. In particular, this research addresses an open question in the LPV community by developing an innovative LPV state feedback controller with sequential loop shutting (LSLS) strategy that actively estimates and transmits relevant system parameter data to the controller, which is subsequently used to tune critical parameter bounds. We introduce a novel framework called PRNet, a fully automatic, image-based method for partial registration. Building on the success of deep learning in whole-to-whole registration, we leverage its benefits for partial-to-partial cases. The PRNet approach relies on a self-supervised learning technique that enables a single network to perform alignment without the need for a specific dataset or model. The framework's key component is a loop-connected auto-encoder, designing an image-to-image translation model that learns from itself. The network's output is a mapped image, which serves as a reference for performing a direct comparison. We derive a suitable loss function by combining cycle consistency and identity, along with spatial regularization to refine the results. The effectiveness of PRNet is demonstrated through experiments on public datasets, specifically the NTU-RDTS dataset and the Multi-Dataset challenge benchmark, where it demonstrates superior performance over existing approaches, significantly outshining them in terms of execution speed. The source code for PRNet is available at https://github.com/zhangzhangzhangzhang/PRNet. The registered results generated by PRNet are publicly available at https://zhangzhangzhangzhang.github.io/PRNet/demos.html. The datasets used in this research can be accessed via https://www.robustai.org/nturdt/ and https://robustai.github.io/MDPC/. MDPC stands for Multi-Dataset PC (partial-cortex) challenge, an open dataset containing various brain scans. The dataset's leaderboard can be found at https://robustai.github.io/MDPC/leaderboard.html, where PRNet consistently ranks first or near the top in nearly all categories. The PRNet approach can be applied to a wide range of applications beyond brain imaging, such as registering partial body scans in outdoor environments. The method's generalizability has been demonstrated through additional experiments on the Oxford RobotCar dataset, where PRNet was used to perform partial-to-partial place recognition while being exposed to varying environmental conditions. Despite the low surface temperature, spectra obtained in the near ultraviolet reveal the presence of numerous metal lines, suggesting that the majority of these emissions originate from heated chromospheric plasma.  Analysis of the line intensities yields a pressure of approximately 10^3 dyn/cm^2 and a temperature of about 10^4 K.  Observations taken shortly after the eruption also show increased emission from Balmer lines, indicating a significant expansion of the star's outer layers. In modern high-performance computing, administrators must efficiently manage memory to achieve optimal system performance. A common technique for this is memory reduction by dividing the system into smaller units and evenly distributing workload across them. For a general-purpose computer architecture, a standard method is the cartridge allocation where each process or thread is isolated in its own memory segment. However, this can lead to underutilized system resources, particularly when dealing with smaller-scale applications. An alternative approach, flat partitioning, involves allocating contiguous memory segments to processes or threads, allowing for more flexible and efficient memory management. However, it is primarily used in specific applications such as network processors. Despite its potential, flat partitioning is largely unexploited in the context of general-purpose computer architecture. Our research introduces a novel run-allocating algorithm that maximizes system performance by utilizing previously underexplored flat partitioning method. This MaxFlatP algorithm can efficiently distribute workload across multiple, independently managed memory regions, even in the presence of memory fragmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that MaxFlatP outperforms traditional cartridge allocation while offering a more adaptable solution. Furthermore, MaxFlatP rapidly finds optimal or near-optimal solutions even for complex-scale applications. In particular, it outperforms other algorithms by up to 5.46 times in finding optimal or near-optimal solutions and by up to 3.06 times in overall efficiency for a comprehensive set of benchmarks. MaxFlatP is comprised of two key components, the MaxFlatP Heuristic and Optimal Construction (HOC) algorithms and the FlatP Library (FPL). The MaxFlatP Heuristic and Optimal Construction algorithm employs a heuristic based on flat partitioning to efficiently construct and improve potential cartridge allocations. On the other hand, the FlatP Library provides a set of precomputed, high-quality flat partitioning configurations that can be easily integrated into existing operating systems to enhance their memory management capabilities. Both components facilitate efficient, high-performance system management. Our research validates the performance of MaxFlatP through extensive empirical evaluations using a custom simulator. Specifically, we analyzed the algorithm's efficiency in memory management for various applications including network processing, direct memory access, and multiple memory allocation scenarios. Our results demonstrate that MaxFlatP significantly outperforms traditional cartridge allocation in these practical tests. Furthermore, we analyzed the algorithm's parameters to identify key factors that influence its performance. Our findings suggest that cartridge size, flat partition configuration, and run allocation all contribute to the algorithm's efficiency. Our research contributes to the area by extensively evaluating the performance of MaxFlatP

By analyzing line-of-sight power spectra, this technique aims to study the large-scale structure of the universe. To achieve this, cross-correlations between HI intensity maps and other cosmic fields are going to be used to derive the neutrino density, while linear distortions will be investigated through the Rees-Penrose tensor in matrix disturbance theory. Predictions for power spectra are created using a semi-analytical approach to compare theoretical models with future experiments like HIINTENSITY out to a redshift of 4.5. Specifically, this research demonstrates how to calculate the 1D line-of-sight power spectra using a Fourier $k$-space approach with angular Wigner functions and matrix disturbance theory, then applies these methods to simulate HI intensity maps in $k$-space with Poissonian uncertainty. To remove foreground signals, this research employs a machine learning-based approach called WiDenesep that's compared with other popular methods like MODE-SUB and SPECIMEN. The results show that WiDenesep significantly reduces the impact of foreground signals more effectively than MODE-SUB and SPECIMEN, ultimately yielding better agreement between theoretical and observed power spectra on large scales. The large-scale structure of the neutrino power spectrum is successfully probed with HI intensity maps, while linear distortions are predicted to be negligible at $10^{-4}$ or smaller. Recommender Systems, particularly hybrid ones, have become essential in assisting users in navigating the overwhelming data environment. From a holistic perspective, we address the limitations of existing hybrid recommender systems, which predominantly focus on integrating context-aware and non-context-aware methods. We recognize that (1) existing hybrid approaches primarily concentrate on single-user profiling, ignoring group dynamics, and (2) lack sufficient contextual consideration in recommending documents. To address these research gaps, we present a new hybrid framework that integrates document context and behavior-oriented recommender systems. We enhance the context-awareness of document-based approaches and incorporate group profiles into the recommendation process. Experimental results from two real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in surpassing the performance of traditional hybrid systems and maintaining comparable performance to standalone contextual and non-contextual methods. Furthermore, we have made the code available on GitHub for the research community to access. Our findings offer novel insights into hybrid recommender systems, specifically addressing issues related to document context, user groups, and the integration of different recommender techniques. We believe that our proposed framework will be useful in practical applications, such as research paper selection, movie recommendation, and news article suggestion. Ultimately, our work contributes to the ongoing efforts in developing more comprehensive and accurate recommender systems. To address this gap, we develop an adaptive graph convolutional network framework to capture long-term dependencies and relationships in multidimensional time series. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with efficient computation, knowledge distillation from a group of pre-trained models, known as multi-teacher distillation, has been adopted in industrial settings. However, existing methods focusing on labeled distillation have limitations in handling diverse distributions of data labels generated by multiple teachers. To address this challenge, we present a new method called PILE that combines multiple teachers' prediction distributions and leverage their confidence in data labels to gradually gather label information. PILE achieves this through an iterative process that initially aggregates each teacher's logit for a single sample, followed by iterative rounds that gather label information and propagate it to all teachers. As labels become more accurate, they are learned by all teachers, leading to enhanced learning representations. We applied PILE to the commercial product search ranking task and observed substantial improvements of 5.0% and 10.0% in terms of relative absolute metrics when compared to individual pre-trained models and a basic multi-teacher distillation method, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/mayu-lyu/PILE. Experimental results confirm that PILE efficiently learns unified label information and achieves consistent improvements across a wide range of datasets. Furthermore, PILE outperforms strong baselines, including complex multi-task distillation methods, by a substantial margin. PILE's code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/mayu-lyu/PILE. The method was implemented using PyTorch and the source code, including pre-trained models used in the experiments, can be accessed via the provided link. By implementing non-ideal spatial configurations and programming the magnetic field sequences accordingly, the bosonic dark matter field's small-amplitude and long-duration responses can be amplified, leading to a resonant frequency shift that is directly proportional to the dark matter field's local gradient and square of the magnetic field strength. Numerical simulations demonstrate that even small improvements in spatial configuration or magnetic field modulation can significantly increase the bosonic dark matter signal. Notably, by optimizing the coil design and magnetic field protocol, the dark matter signal in the sensor output power spectrum can be increased by multiple orders of magnitude over traditional techniques, thereby lowering the detectable mass, with potential applications in particle physics, gravitational physics, and astrophysics. Furthermore, strength interferometry offers versatile avenues for signal enhancement and extends beyond solely optimizing coil design, encompassing various excitation protocols and geometries, such as loops, grids, and multiple-coil configurations, as well as localizing the dark matter source in space. We examine the basis pursuit problem in infinite-dimensional spaces under a slightly modified condition, considering the availability of continuous and convex measurements. A specific problem is studied: determining whether a unique solution exists for Minimizing $\|y\|$ subject to $Ax \leq y$ in any convex, closed subset of $R^n$. The condition is satisfied by various continuous measurement functions. However, unique solutions do not exist for certain other measurement functions, such as the absolute value, even in the case of strictly positive data. Consequently, we develop a method for efficiently calculating a solution with minimal norm for a basis pursuit problem with a continuous measurement function. This method can be applied to solve other related problems, such as finding a Chebyshev center in a closed, convex set and a minimal-norm solution for a linear equation with a positive definite matrix in infinite-dimensional space. Furthermore, we extend the method of alternating projections to demonstrate the convergence of a sequence of approximations for a general minimization problem with a continuous measurement function. The properties of infinite-dimensional matrices are also explored in relation to a mapping that assigns a minimizer with minimal norm to each bounded, convex subset of $R^n$. The properties include continuity, convexity, and a specific form of continuity that we call 'weakly-continuous'. This form of continuity is equivalent to a previously defined 'weak-projectivity' in the context of Chebyshev centers. The properties of weakly-projective matrices are then applied to efficiently calculate a Chebyshev center in a closed, convex subset of $R^n$ and a minimal-norm solution for a linear equation with a weakly-projective matrix in infinite-dimensional space. Finally, we demonstrate that a weakly-projective matrix has a specific property: its inverse has a non-negative diagonal. As a result, we show that a Chebyshev center in a closed, convex subset of $R^n$ with a weakly-projective matrix can be calculated efficiently using a method of alternating projections. Moreover, this algorithm converges to a unique point as the dimension of the space increases to its infinite limit. The properties of weakly-projective matrices can also be applied to efficiently calculate a minimal-norm solution for a basis pursuit problem with a continuous measurement function, as previously mentioned. Consequently, we show that a method of alternating projections converges to a unique solution for a basis pursuit problem with a continuous measurement function as the dimension of the space increases to its infinite limit. The result is valid for various forms of continuous measurement functions

The P416 compiler is a proven and reliable system for creating configuration files for network equipment, allowing programmers to define custom packet processing applications. Due to the growing demand for programmable hardware in networking, developing a reliable compiler is crucial for commercial network devices to execute user-submitted programs securely. In this research, we demonstrate the development of an open-source P416 compiler for reconfigurable match-action table switches and showcase its accuracy by comparing compiled configurations to those generated by commercial network devices. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of our compiler in terms of scalability, flexibility in hardware utilization, and transparency in output configurations. By utilizing our compiler, developers can create and customize applications for programmable network devices, enhancing security and reliability. To improve accuracy, post-processing techniques are developed, combining weak error estimation and a perturbation method. The implementation involves computationally efficient methods, including one based on additional linear solver iterations and another requiring only matrix-vector multiplications. Both strategies can be applied without increasing the computational cost. The proposed approaches are demonstrated to be effective in various numerical experiments. Furthermore, the proposed post-processing strategy does not rely on specific complex finite element implementations, as exemplified by numerical test cases using both Firedrake and MOAB software. To validate the accuracy of the modified numerical solution, a weak error estimator is developed, influenced by the stochastic discretisation of the vector transport equation. This paper delves into the intersection of fairness and privacy in federated learning. Building on existing research, we expand the framework to include statistical sensitivity and investigate trade-offs between fairness and differential privacy in FL. Our analysis focuses on the relationship between the privacy-cost curve and the fairness-cost curve under various loss functions, revealing key properties and generating new inequalities. Specifically, we demonstrate that the trade-off between privacy and fairness is more restrictive under radial losses, such as squared loss, compared to non-radial losses, and that this trade-off is more challenging to analyze in heterogeneous datasets. Our findings provide essential design considerations for developers of fairness-enhancing and private federated learning algorithms. Furthermore, we apply our framework to examine the fairness-privacy trade-off in two real-world applications: image classification on the CIFAR-10 dataset and medical diagnosis in the MedCare dataset. Our empirical evaluations aim to answer previously unaddressed questions in the ML fairness and privacy communities. In particular, we investigate whether there is an inherent balance between fairness and privacy, and whether this balance varies based on the dataset and loss function utilized. Our analysis also explores the impact of the dataset heterogeneity on the privacy-fairness trade-off and provides a empirical examination of the interplay between privacy and fairness under radial and non-radial losses. Our results offer novel insights and contribute meaningfully to the ML fairness and privacy communities, ultimately shedding light on the design principles of machine learning models in the federated learning context. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexandryan/fedlearn_equity_privacy. This material is the result of a collaborative effort between the authors and the ML fairness and privacy communities, and we look forward to continuing this dialogue. In the past few years, using multiple GPUs to train neural networks has become a standard practice.  There have been significant advancements in distributed deep learning training, including data parallelism, model parallelism, and the hybrid approach that combines both.  This research focuses on model parallelism where different layers of the neural network are trained on separate GPUs.  There are only a few studies that utilize multiple GPUs for deep learning tasks, primarily due to the limitations of previous architectures such as wide and deep networks.  This research introduces the regional reviewer technique (RRT) that enables training of wide and deep neural networks on multiple GPUs by dividing and combining them into blocks.  The experimental results show that the regional reviewer technique can achieve better accuracy and faster training times compared to existing model parallelism approaches.  Additionally, we demonstrate that the regional reviewer technique can be effectively applied to a wide range of neural network architectures and can even be used to explain the results of the model's output.  This research further develops an automatic block division module (ABD) that enables rapid training of neural networks on GPUs without the need for manual division.  The experimental results show that the automatic block division module can produce better results compared to traditional model parallelism approaches.  Finally, we showcase an open-source implementation of the regional reviewer technique using the PyTorch framework, which can be freely accessed on GitHub and used as a foundation for future research and development.  The experimental results show that this implementation produces comparable results to existing model parallelism approaches and can be effectively applied to a range of neural network architectures and learning tasks.  The experimental results also highlight the potential of the regional reviewer technique as a new model parallelism approach that can outperform existing techniques.  The validation of the approach is demonstrated through a series of comprehensive experiments that compare the performance of the regional reviewer technique with other state-of-the-art model parallelism approaches.  The code for these experiments can also be accessed on GitHub for replication and verification purposes.  The experimental results show that the regional reviewer technique can achieve faster training times, better accuracy, and more robust results compared to existing model parallelism approaches.  The comparison of the regional reviewer technique with other state-of-the-art model parallelism approaches is comprehensive and highlights the versatility of the approach.  The experimental results also show that the regional reviewer technique can be effectively applied to a range of architectures, including ResNet, MobileNet, and DenseNet, which further demonstrates the potential of the technique.  The validation of the approach in real-world scenarios is also demonstrated

The stable orbits within these islands exponentially decay as the hull's thickness further increases, however the rates of this decay and the rates of island formation are dissimilar due to the influence of nonlocal effects, thereby causing the islands to accumulate and form a labyrinthine structure in the phase space.  The rates at which the islands merge and the rates at which new islands emerge balance each other, resulting in a self-similar pattern of Wada basins, the persistence of which relies on the nonlocal properties of the microresonator.  The topological characteristics of the Wada basins are resistant to variations in the resonator's working conditions, thereby indicating potential applications in nonlinear photonics.  The Wada basins can be utilized to store and manipulate photons within the resonator.  The use of Wada basins could provide a foundation for the development of a nonlinear photonics system capable of supporting complex, interconnected qubit networks.  The unique properties of the Wada basins could also serve as an ideal test case for the study of complex, interconnected systems.  The findings of this research could also be applied to other systems with similar characteristics, such as Josephson junction arrays. In the realm of computer vision, the task of identifying specific actions within videos has been a long-standing challenge. The key to overcoming this challenge lies in developing models capable of accurately recognizing diverse actions, some of which are highly generic while others are very specific. To meet this requirement, we introduce the Hierarchical Focus Network (HFN), a novel model designed to capture the core aspects of actions in a hierarchical manner. By doing so, the HFN model bridges the gap between general, umbrella-like actions and their precise, target-focused variants. Through extensive testing on established action recognition datasets, including UCF101, JHMDB, and Charades, our model consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, our model's hierarchical architecture enables seamless adaptation to more intricate, multi-stage tasks, such as action detection and segmentation, thereby demonstrating its versatility in real-world applications. The proposed HFN model is made available on GitHub for public access. Additionally, the model's pre-trained weights can be obtained by contacting the authors. Theoretical frameworks suggest three primary mechanisms through which gas clouds collapse and form new stars.  These mechanisms, all involving the transfer of energy from nearby stars, either directly, or through the medium's own motion, either by generating magnetic fields or heating up dust particles, leads to a steady loss of mass by the cloud and ultimately, to the formation of new stars.  Observations of young stars and starless clouds offer a unique perspective to comprehend this complex process.  By analyzing data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, scientists identified numerous young stars and starless clouds, ultimately paving the way for a study on the emergence of new stars.  Using a machine learning algorithm to correct for background noise and confusion, researchers were able to spot young stars and starless clouds in the Milky Way without relying on other star-forming regions' templates.  By comparing the masses, sizes, densities, and surface temperatures of these clouds to theoretical frameworks, researchers were able to gain valuable insights into how stars are born.  Further analysis revealed a direct proportionality between cloud density and temperature, confirming earlier studies' findings.  Using a simplified model, scientists estimated the timespan between a cloud's visual emergence and its starlight-powered heating, suggesting a relatively short time frame of around 0.5 million years.  By combining data on cloud sizes and densities, scientists were able to estimate masses and predict a cloud's survival based on its mass-to-surface density ratio.  These predictions, confirmed by earlier studies, left only one mechanism unconfirmed: the magnetohydrodynamic collapse, which might be visible as extended, starlight-powered clouds.  By comparing the observed cloud populations to two distinct models, researchers found the observed ratio of dense to extended clouds to be higher than the magnetohydrodynamic collapse model, suggesting a relatively high efficiency of star formation in the Milky Way.  By combining data from the observed cloud populations and theoretical star-forming regions, researchers were able to estimate a relatively high efficiency of star formation in the Milky Way, ranging between 0.3 if the magnetohydrodynamic collapse is included, and 0.6 if it's excluded. A powerful computational tool, nested sampling, enables the estimation of integral quantities including entropy in complex systems, especially those dominated by rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations. This method involves constraining one's interest region to a series of spherical volumes with increasing masses, updating parameters on each to achieve this transformation efficiently. As a result, nested sampling can provide accurate estimates of entropy, a highly valuable property in characterizing statistical physics phenomena. This discussion will explore how nested sampling calculates entropy, highlighting its benefits and drawbacks in various applications. Additionally, we will examine the relationship between nested sampling and maximum entropy frameworks, revealing a natural connection between these concepts. Ultimately, we will consider several example systems, including stellar mass distribution and a simplified model of galactic rotation, to demonstrate the versatility of nested sampling in estimating entropy in diverse contexts. This method has the potential to broaden the scope of entropy estimation Significantly. This research introduces NBcoded, a lightweight network assault detection system tailored for resource-constrained IoT devices. NBcoded combines an autoencoder and a naive Bayesian classifier to pinpoint unusual network traffic patterns. Since high-dimensional network data poses identification challenges for Bayesian classifiers, a binary encoding step is incorporated into NBcoded. This system addresses a critical gap in security for low-power devices, offering a cost-effective solution. Our experiments, conducted using the Dataset of network traffic from universities, demonstrate that NBcoded achieves an accuracy of 91.6% in classifying normal and DoS attacks. Additionally, NBcoded showcases its versatility by detecting DoS assaults on an IoT device connected to a Wi-Fi network, showcasing its practical applicability. Our study highlights the effectiveness of NBcoded compared to a traditional Bayesian classifier, underscoring the significance of binary encoding in enhancing accuracy. Crucially, NBcoded's accuracy surpasses alternative intrusion detection systems designed for low-power devices, solidifying its potential as a practical solution for a critical security concern. The code for this research is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/abdullahalowais/NBcoded.git. It has been successfully deployed on a Raspberry Pi 3 for real-world testing. In insect vision, biological movements are defined as disparities between the retinal images captured by an moving fly as it changes direction. This concept has been explored in the Insect Motion Parallax hypothesis, which proposes that flies use this information to create a three-dimensional spatial map of their surroundings. This theory has been the basis for an automated method to detect biological movement in video footage. This method was successfully tested and validated using video recordings of artificial objects in motion, as well as microscopic recordings of flies' retinal images while they performed figure-eight maneuvers. The method was then used to process these recordings and identify the resulting optical flow patterns, which were subsequently analyzed to determine their prevalence in real-world recordings. The results of these experiments support the Invariant Scale Hypothesis, which states that the size of the moving objects is relatively constant. Furthermore, the optical flow patterns obtained from real recordings exhibited a wide range of orientations, which is consistent with random expectations. All of these findings provide strong evidence for the Insect Motion Parallax theory in vertebrates, which is also known as the Kinesphere model. Additionally, the Invariant Depth Extent hypothesis was found to be less certain but still worthy of further investigation. The developed method can now be employed in various applications, such as image stabilization, object depth perception, and navigation, which are essential skills that insects and other animals, including humans, use every day to interact with their three-dimensional surroundings. The search for fundamental physical laws is a key goal of theoretical physics. Currently, the standard model and its extensions serve as the primary framework for physics. However, this approach may not be the most effective way to develop a complete theory. An alternative method involves an data-driven or inductive approach, where the form of laws is unknown and they are derived solely from experimental data. In this paper, a universal data analysis method is proposed that can recover both consistent and inconsistent global principles from data in a model-independent manner. A novel, nonparametric algorithm is developed to systematically generate and evaluate physics laws, where their certainty and significance are quantitatively assessed. An in-depth case study is conducted with simulated data to examine the proposed method's performance. This study, which simulates infinite precision, confirms that our approach can accurately discover both the standard model and its quantum corrections solely from data, regardless of initial conditions. Furthermore, our method identifies several unforeseen global principles that govern the evolution of scale, confirming previous findings and revealing their universal, wide-ranging applicability. Additionally, our approach discloses several discrepancies between the quantum theory of electroweak interactions and the simulated data at very high energies. These discrepancies are found to be in agreement with real data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), where similar inconsistencies were discovered using the same analytical method. This demonstrates the potential for the proposed method to reveal novel, nonstandard physical principles and even challenges established theories, such as the standard model and its extensions. An important implication of these findings is that the inductive approach to physics may hold the key to developing a complete and self-consistent quantum theory of the universe. Finally, an important connection is established between the proposed inductive approach and the fundamental concept of determinism in classical philosophy, highlighting the deep underlying roots of this methodology. An overview of the historical development of inductive philosophy is provided in the supplementary materials. Additionally, the publicly available UPATool can be used to derive physics laws from data, where users can explore the model-independent, nonparametric universe and discover novel principles, laws, and their own research questions. This tool can also facilitate collaborative research and help resolve inconsistencies between different paradigms in physics, where the inductive approach can provide valuable insights and clarity. An important area for future development is the integration of the proposed inductive approach with other machine learning techniques, such as generative models and transfer learning, to further enhance and diversify the model-independent, nonparametric universe. We conducted in-depth experiments using neutron scattering to examine the material with the highest boson ratio, which is a key component in the study of superconductors. Our experiments involved measuring the momentum-dependent dynamic structure factor of this material, and our findings were later compared with theoretical simulations. Our data reveal a significant short-range order that persists up to high temperatures, and our results also demonstrate the existence of a peculiar state near the boson ratio. Furthermore, our study has shed light on the mystery of the missing density of states near the boson ratio, and it has also identified a unique wave-like behavior in the material's quasiparticles. Our study has further refined the material's phase diagram, particularly near the boson ratio, and it has also provided a deeper understanding of the electronic interactions within the material. Ultimately, our study has provided a comprehensive framework for studying complex electronic phenomena in related materials. We propose a new evaluation method for multi-particle processes that incorporates the concept of effective theories at the one-loop level, enabling the precise calculation of sub-processes while disregarding less relevant terms. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by calculating the inclusive top-quark pair production cross-section at next-to-leading order, achieving an accurate prediction with a 0.5% uncertainty, which is compatible with the anticipated precision required in the forthcoming high-luminosity collider era. We also discuss potential applications and extensions of this evaluation method to incorporate two-loop corrections and additional uncertainties associated with hadronization and parton distribution functions. We find that a substantial contribution to the overall precision comes from the top-quark pole mass, followed by non-pole-scale dependencies and the effects of parton distribution functions, which highlights the significance of incorporating different scales in the calculation. Furthermore, we show that the top-quark pole mass contribution can be accurately extracted from the differential cross-section as a function of the hadronic top-quark mass, while the scale dependence outside this region dominates the overall scale uncertainty. These findings enable the precise extraction of scale dependencies and facilitate the matching of short-distance physics with the underlying parton distribution functions, which is crucial for the understanding of particle physics in the Standard Model and beyond. A key factor in the effectiveness of many optimization algorithms is their ability to generate a diverse and varied set of solutions. In this study, variations in the solution space of multiple optimization algorithms are analyzed through the lens of information complexity. Different approaches are used to analyze and compare the diversity of solutions produced by algorithms such as multi-objective optimization, quality diversity optimization, and independent component analysis. Our findings highlight the connection between diversity analysis and the underlying characteristics of these optimization problems, and demonstrate how varying complexity affects the distribution of solutions in different dimensions. Ultimately, our results show that higher solution dimensions can lead to previously unseen solutions that better match the problem's optimal characteristics. The implications of our findings are two-fold: first, multi-objective optimization and quality diversity optimization produce more varied solutions than expected, and can exploit the inherent complexities of these problems; second, the success of these algorithms can be attributed to their ability to capture and utilize the inherent diversity present in the solution space. Finally, our results suggest that solution dimensionality can be leveraged to acquire additional information and improve solution quality. The study provides guidance on the design of future optimization algorithms based on the information complexity of solution spaces. The authors also make available a suite of tools for evaluating diversity in solution spaces and experimental data, known as the Information Complexity Diversity Analysis library. This resource can be used by researchers to analyze and visualize the diversity of solutions produced by a range of optimization algorithms. The IDCAL library encompasses multiple algorithms and can be extended to accommodate custom implementations. The authors make available a range of codes, including PyNEWS for multi-objective optimization and QDO for quality diversity optimization, all of which can be accessed through the repository at https://github.com/limaoin44/Idcal\.lib. The authors also distribute the PyNEWS code at https://github.com/limaoin44/PyNEWS. The PyNEWS algorithm was originally developed by Limao et al. and is described in detail in the manuscript 'Information Complexity in Multi-Observable Optimization', published in NeurIPS 2020, under a separate name, and is also available at the above repository. Similarly, the authors distribute the QDO code at https://github.com/limaoin44/Idcal\.lib. The authors also make available the independent component analysis library, known as PyIA, at the repository https://github.com/limaoin44/Idcal\.lib. The authors also distribute the ICA code at https://github.com/limaoin44/Idcal\.

In a situation where resources are limited, individuals make the most of what is available by assigning values to different possible allocations. When individuals have unique and indivisible resources, the allocation process becomes a matter of priority, where some may receive greater benefits than others. Building on existing concepts, we develop a model to tackle this type of allocation, where the value assigned to an item can be split among multiple people. Through mathematical analysis, we investigate the existence and features of a stable equilibrium, ensuring that the allocated amounts remain additively divisible. Additionally, we find that a specific instance of this problem does not adhere to the fundamentals of fair distribution, even in situations where resources are evenly distributed. Interestingly, we find that a general stable equilibrium may not exist for all situations, but does so in cases where resources are evenly distributed. Lastly, we propose a constructive method to achieve a stable equilibrium, ensuring a smooth and progressive allocation of resources. This novel approach provides a framework for a singular allocation, where every person receives a clear and direct allocation amount. This work expands upon existing research in fair, progressive, and interceptive allocations. Conversely, we also demonstrate a scenario in which even a small disturbance to a stable state results in an irreversible and never-ending distribution imbalance. This finding highlights an inherent challenge in resource allocation, where a stable state may not exist. This paper presents an innovative, 3D steady roommates problem with a unique value system, where the allocated amounts remain additively divisible. As a result, the proposed fair, progressive, and interceptive allocations may not adhere to the fundamentals of a stable state. A critical issue in machine learning is the challenge of creating models that balance optimal performance and generalization capabilities.  In the field of supervised learning, models often achieve exceptional outcomes on in-domain datasets but struggle with generalization when applied to out-of-domain data.  This paper examines the problem through a comprehensive analysis, highlighting the obstacles and proposing a new approach.  The primary notion of this approach is to vastly increase the size of the feature set by incorporating all key characteristics from the training dataset.  This is accomplished by utilizing an optional set of features for each data sample, where a sample's optional features are those that are not used in the current iteration of the model's training.  By incorporating a vast number of features that are not currently in use, the model is compelled to incorporate additional characteristics from the available data, thereby enhancing its generalization capabilities.  Through this mechanism, the model is able to break free from local optima in the performance-generalization curve, ultimately resulting in improved outcomes.  The proposed framework is demonstrated to yield superior results in 12 benchmark datasets for supervised learning, outperforming a range of innovative techniques in optimal feature selection.  Additionally, the paper investigates the issue through the lens of a biologically realistic neural network and provides an implementation in Jupyter Notebook.

A new technique known as the Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera (RASCAM) utilizes the coherent propagation of light to identify and track turbulent patterns in the atmosphere. This method uses a small, low-cost sensor to monitor the light field from a target object, allowing it to maintain high frame rates and evade the impact of speckles. We have successfully applied RASCAM in a laboratory setting using 10 and 40 laser beams, and obtained promising results, which match well with computer simulations. This technique has the potential to be used in space-based telescopes and other applications where high-quality imaging is crucial despite the limitations of atmospheric distortion. Our test results show that RASCAM can effectively remove the effects of speckles and maintain high image quality up to 150 Hz, even with a 10-fold increase in the complexity of the atmosphere. This achievement has surpassed our initial expectations and indicates that RASCAM holds great promise for real-world applications. Although some residual speckles persist due to the finite size of our sensor, we have successfully developed an algorithm to simulate the behavior of larger sensors and "pull up" the remaining speckles to improve image quality. This advancement has enabled us to achieve 0.5 arcseconds of resolution on a 10-meter telescope, which is on par with conventional adaptive optics systems. Our research has removed a major barrier to the widespread adoption of RASCAM, and we are now confident in its potential to serve as a low-cost, high-performance alternative to conventional adaptive optics systems. Moving forward, we aim to refine RASCAM further and demonstrate its effectiveness in a flight-test-grade telescope, as well as explore its applications in remote sensing and other areas. Additionally, we have discovered an unexpected benefit of RASCAM in enhancing the sensitivity of astronomical telescopes by up to 30 times, effectively transforming a small telescope into a large one under specific conditions. This breakthrough has significant implications for the design of future space-based telescopes, and we have proposed a concept for a 10-meter RASCAM telescope that is capable of reaching a diameter of 10 meters, thereby achieving a signal enhancement of three orders of magnitude. This innovative design leverages the coherent properties of light to "transform" the light from a small telescope into that of a larger one, and could serve as a vital component in the development of future large-aperture telescopes. Consequently, the proposed 10-meter RASCAM telescope would maintain a signal-to-noise ratio comparable to that of a conventional 10-meter adaptive optics telescope

Currently available simulation methods either conduct detailed particle-level analysis or comprehensive fluid flow simulations but a comprehensive method either directly modeling collision between particles or utilizing a collision detection system does not exist. This study develops a novel integration technique that incorporates a variable time step method to accurately simulate collisions between particles over extended periods of time. By utilizing a particle contact algorithm with a collision duration threshold, this method prevents overestimation of collision duration. Subsequent numerical analysis verified the integration technique's effectiveness in capturing collision behavior. Additionally, this method was applied to simulate fluidized particles to demonstrate its practicality and accuracy in complex systems. Results show that this method successfully models collision behavior and produces realistic fluidized patterns consistent with experimentally observed results. This method enables more accurate simulation of matters where collisions play a crucial role. Furthermore, this method potentially standardizes collision detection algorithms, enabling greater coupling between particle-level and fluid-level simulations in the future. This could lead to high-resolution simulations of fluid dynamics directly informed by particle-level analysis. Finally, this method enables more realistic incorporation of collision mechanisms into molecular dynamics simulations, potentially altering our understanding of material properties and behaviors. This study focuses on developing an advanced approach to measuring medication interactions using a combination of relational deep learning and attention-based mechanisms. Our approach addresses two key limitations of existing methods: its ability to accurately assess low-frequency and high-risk interactions and its capacity to learn nuanced, context-specific insights into interactions between specific drugs. We introduce a novel, cohesively designed neural network model that integrates attention, memory-based mechanisms, and a flexible embedding technique to capture complex interdependencies between drugs. Our findings and the evaluation of our model's efficacy are presented in detailed case studies. Imitation learning seeks to bypass extensive gaming data with human annotations, instead using observations of human actions to create a trainable policy. However, current approaches rely on domain-specific assumptions and pre-trained models, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. We introduce a new framework that enables policies to be transferred and imitated across different areas using only unmarked gaming footage. This is achieved by separating the agent's action mechanisms from domain-specific components through modular representation. We then employ self-supervised learning to identify correlations between the two without any labels. We also demonstrate that our framework can synthesize plausible human actions in domains that the trainer has never seen before. This study investigates how court-ordered community service for non-severe crimes affects the mental health of individuals who have not been diagnosed with a mental disorder, in contrast to those who have been diagnosed with such a disorder. This research introduces an innovative approach to identifying anomalies in industrial settings by analyzing the behavior of Hidden Markov Models. Typically used in probabilistic predictions, these models evaluate the likelihood of underlying states based on observed data. However, in many industrial applications, real-time feedback is limited to binary or qualitative measurements, which can be approximated as Gaussian-distributed. Building upon existing ANOM metrics, this study proposes a new evaluation method, called GaPE, that estimates anomaly likelihood by merging Gaussian probability and Hidden Markov Model measures. To validate this method, simulated case studies were conducted, and the findings demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting anomalies. Moreover, the study highlights the advantages of GaPE over traditional anomaly detection methods in the presence of noisy data. Although the study's results are specific to the context of industrial electrical drives, this methodology can be applied to a broad range of industrial applications involving qualitative feedback and Hidden Markov Models. Finally, the study outlines potential future research avenues in this domain. Achieving complete data confidentiality while allowing valuable query analysis is a significant challenge. The one-sided differential privacy framework addresses this issue by ensuring that sensitive data remains private, without revealing nearby databases. However, the limited research in this area focuses on the confidentiality of individual data points, ignoring dependencies between characteristics. This study aims to address a critical problem by determining the confidentiality breach probability when a data set's characteristics are dependent. Specifically, we examine how the probability of breach is affected when a data set's features are linked, as opposed to being independent. Furthermore, we provide a bounding value for the breach probability and investigate how it changes with increasing data dimensionality. Our results demonstrate that dependent characteristics significantly impact the breach probability, exceeding the expected bound by a factor of at least four when data dimensions are cubic in number (e.g., images) and exponentially in number (e.g., text). To address this issue, we propose a method for reducing breach probability by utilizing symmetric random matrices in the covariance generator. Our research demonstrates that the breach probability can be substantially reduced, with a minimum fourfold improvement when data dimensions are cubic in number and exponential in number. Our study also shows that the optimal covariance generator is based on the Laplacian of an Erdős-Rényi graph, which is a random matrix with edges connecting adjacent data characteristics. Our findings offer a novel approach to addressing confidentiality breach problems in dependent data characteristics, marking a significant contribution to the one-sided differential privacy field. The complexity of this problem is NP-hard, but we approximate the breach probability within a small error margin (plus/minus a factor of O(Δ) ≈ 0.16) by developing a simplified formula. Our innovative method involves utilizing the spectral properties of the covariance generator's matrix, which enables efficient computation without resorting to the matrix's inverse. This approach enables a practical evaluation of the breach probability in realistic data scenarios, which is currently an unsolved issue in the one-sided differential privacy field. Our research offers a general framework that can be applied to various data sets, which is a significant contribution to the field. In protoplanetary disks, the depletion of carbon is often seen at large scales, with variations in its abundance across the disk. This study focuses on the carbon-12 oxide (CO) gas distribution within the inner regions of the disk surrounding the young star AS 209. By analyzing observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales (MAPS) project, researchers examine CO's radial and vertical distribution. They find CO's column density is significantly reduced, around 10 times lower, within the disk's inner hot region (around 35 astronomical units) compared to cooler outer areas (around 80 astronomical units). This CO depletion is particularly noticeable at the disk's inner boundary, where the star's radiation spectrum transitions to the thermal spectrum. CO's reduced presence could be explained by either the gas's conversion to solid carbon dust or the chemical processing of carbon ions. However, the team favors the idea of CO conversion, as it aligns better with theoretical models. These resources are versatile and translate well due to their platform-independent nature, dealing with data rather than specific measurement techniques. Our framework also includes a web-based interface, DatLab, for retrieving and analyzing time-stamped data, as well as a separate service, EtE_Dark, that accepts users' data and sends back processed results in the form of reports. These reports can be seamlessly integrated into Jupyter Notebooks or other Python environments. Our approach combines EtE, a powerful data processing library, with a web-based interface and a service for expediting data analysis, all while maintaining transparency through open-source access to the source code of EtE and DatLab. Our resources are specifically designed for neuroscience applications but can be broadly utilized for any data analysis tasks involving time-stamped measurements. Our approach is adaptable and can be applied to a range of other research domains. In a collaborative effort, our team is willing to work with researchers to incorporate their code into our toolkit, as exemplified by the integration of CaImAn's code into EtE. We welcome donations of open-source code through GitHub to develop this collaborative project further. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint, related to a cost function that may have singularities. This approach builds on the work of Cardaliaguet, who established the existence of'mild solutions' for a first-order mean field game with state and control constraints, subject to a small regularity requirement on the cost function. In contrast to Cardaliaguet's method, which relied heavily on the regularity of the cost function, our proof accommodates a broader class of singular costs, while still ensuring the regularity of the mean field game equilibrium only away from the boundary of the control admissible set. This achievement is primarily based on an observation made by Aregín Toes and myself, concerning the regularity of the mean field game equilibrium in the interior of the control admissible set, along with a straightforward extension of the'mild solution' concept to the context of controls. This result, in turn, is founded on the use of a semiconvexity estimate, along with the properties of the mean field game equilibrium in the interior of the control admissible set. Finally, at a minimal additional cost, we demonstrate the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving second-order controls with a constraint, subject to a cost function that may have singularities. This extension involves essentially no additional mathematical considerations. Detecting visual inaccuracies in retail product listings is crucial to maintain accuracy and quality on e-commerce platforms. Traditional approaches to visual inaccuracies often rely on sophisticated image recognition, but in the context of retail, it's more effective to classify inaccuracy types such as incorrect categories, missing or altered attributes, and image manipulations. This classification task is best supported by visual features that can distinguish between accurate and inaccurate listings. Effective extraction of these features requires a deep understanding of the underlying data, including product relationships and attributes. Pre-training a model on a limited and structured dataset is necessary to develop this understanding. The proposed method, VICTOR, leverages a custom-designed transformer architecture and a fashion-specific contrastive loss to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the retail visual inaccuracies dataset, RetailAI-500k. The method incorporates a multi-stage pipeline with a pre-trained transformer, followed by feature extraction, and incorporates domain-specific knowledge through contrastive loss to identify visually similar and dissimilar listings. The method outperforms baseline models, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 81.6% and a mean reciprocal rank of 6.13 on the RetailAI-500k challenge. The method's efficacy is further demonstrated by significantly reducing false positives on a separate test dataset. The code for this method is publicly available at https://github.com/alexanderyan27/VICTOR. The method's results are presented at the RetailAI Visual Inaccuracies Challenge workshop at CVPR 2021. The method's authors jointly won 3rd and 4th places in the challenge. The method's performance is comparable to a pre-trained image classification model, indicating its effectiveness and efficiency. The scalability of Federated Learning can be enhanced by allowing participants to send data simultaneously and accumulate gradients in the background. However, this approach may lead to data inconsistencies and make it difficult to synchronize, particularly in scenarios with many participants and complex models. To address these challenges, we introduce a new technique called FedBuff, which enables asynchronous learning by buffering the gradients and allowing for flexible synchronization periods. The FedBuff method allows participants to send their accumulated gradients when the synchronization period is over and incorporates a adaptive learning rate adjustment based on the actual elapsed time since the previous synchronization. This adaptation ensures a consistent learning rate across participants and prevents the learning rate from being decreased too quickly, which can impede convergence in Federated Learning applications. We implemented FedBuff on a mobile cloud platform using real-world datasets and observed significant performance gains, especially in data-constrained scenarios, when compared to traditional Federated Learning methods that don't support asynchronous learning. Even in scenarios with plenty of data available, FedBuff was able to enhance the model's overall accuracy without sacrificing its simplicity. As marine robots navigate through dynamic ocean environments, their sensors' signals undergo significant changes over time. Current state estimation methods often fail to account for these temporal variations, leading to inaccurate predictions and models. In this research, we address this challenge by developing a novel sparse Gaussian process framework for modeling the evolution of data over time. This framework leverages sparse Gaussian processes to learn the patterns underlying signal changes, providing a more accurate and generalizable model. As a result, the proposed method outperforms traditional sparsification techniques, achieving better prediction and modeling outcomes, along with reduced computational and memory costs. Its effectiveness is demonstrated in a marine robot navigation application, where the algorithm successfully models the drift and fluctuation of acoustic and inertial sensor signals, allowing for accurate state estimation and modeling. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be applied to other applications involving signal evolution, such as medical imaging and speech recognition. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/whs815/kernels. Experimental data can be found at https://doi.org/10.6086/M2E15. This notion of equivalence can be extended to C*-algebras, leading to marked topologically robust aperiodicity (MTRAP). In this context, we examine the properties of C*-algebras that satisfy MTRAP and investigate the underlying graph, finding that such algebras are always K-theoretically trivial. Additionally, we demonstrate that the robustly shift equivalent graph class contains all infinite graphs that can be approximated by trivalent graphs, such as infinite binary trees and the three-dimensional homogenous tree. However, the class does not include the infinite binary tree, and we present distinct C*-algebras that are shift equivalent but not approximately morphic, thus forming a new class of abelian algebras that are topologically free but not of finite embedding. Finally, we discuss the possibility of a positive K-theoretic invariant differentiating C*-algebras that are approximately morphic and those that are not. Moreover, we found two distinct C*-algebras, one approximately morphic and the other not, which have the same TrnK-theory. To effectively answer questions, a language model must be able to integrate knowledge from various sources, including both sentences and structured data, particularly Knowledge Graphs. Traditionally, this structured data is often overlooked in language modeling. In this research, we explore the potential of using large language models to perform Knowledge Graph inference, an ability that was previously reserved for specialized reasoners. Building on the success of GPT-3 in question answering and other natural language tasks, we develop a novel approach that enables these models to reason and draw inferences from Knowledge Graphs, even when the answer is not directly stated. To test our method, we created a custom dataset consisting of 3000 question-answer pairs and an accompanying Knowledge Graph, which was used to train and evaluate a GPT-3 model. The results show that a model trained on this dataset can accurately respond to over 80% of question-answer pairs, including those that require inference, outperforming a basic language model by over 25 percentage points. Furthermore, our method outshines specialized Knowledge Graph reasoners in responding to questions, demonstrating the efficacy of large language models in practical applications. We have developed a novel high-dimensional expander graph construction, which is based on random coverings of certain finite metric spaces. By utilizing a growth rate criterion for the expanding properties of these spaces, we create high-dimensional bipartite expanders. This construction applies particularly to the examples of (a) the Cayley expanders of finite groups, (b) the Hamming graphs, and (c) the Hamming graphs' generalizations. Furthermore, our method enables the construction of Ramanujan graphs of girth n. We also found an unexpected connection between our approach and Paturi's well-known problem in theoretical computer science, which concerns acquiring knowledge through queries. Additionally, our high-dimensional bipartite expander construction yields novel and efficient rank-one matrix sampling expanders, which can be used to develop novel bipartite expander graphs. Lastly, our method has implications for the sampling of semi-negative definite matrices, particularly in the context of kernel methods in machine learning. Additionally, we develop a formula for the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of a dual module associated with an Hermitian Artin module in terms of a determinant, provided that its characteristic polynomial has a specific property. In both cases, the determinant is constructed from the module's quiver connection matrix and a metric defined over the algebra's dual space. Our method builds upon the work of Biskupski in the context of Hermitian modules. The work of Biskupski further includes a general approach for calculating the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant based on a module's first syzygy, which we refer to as the'reduction method'. In contrast, we provide explicit calculations of the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant for certain self-dual Artin modules which cannot be reduced to their first syzygy. Our study focuses on modules from group algebras of finite order and Duflo-Serganova duality. The work of Biskupski has significant connections with the field of Tannakian mathematics. In particular, the concepts of $\mathscr{L}$-invariant and Deligne's tensor product of linear rational Hodge structures ($\mathcal{L}$-invariant and $\mathcal{D}$-invariant) are related to the commutants of specific algebras, as described by Biskupski and Vanzo.
