Early stage detection of COVID-19 is of utmost importance to prevent the overwhelming of healthcare systems and to save lives.  A promising approach to this is the use of a rapid, highly sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic tool - Rydberg atom detection via microwave signals.  However, the effectiveness of this method relies heavily on the environment in which it is being used, making it necessary to conduct frequent background measurements to ensure accuracy.  Although deep learning techniques can process these background signals more efficiently, they also introduce complexity to the diagnostic process.  To overcome this, a new method utilizing deep learning to process data in real-time has been developed to improve the detection of Rydberg atom responses without the need for extensive background measurements.  This approach leverages a convolutional neural network to enhance signal quality in real-time, resulting in a simplified diagnostic system that only requires a single wide-frequency microwave signal to identify infections.  Our results show that this method yields improved accuracy and sensitivity in Rydberg atom detection via microwave signals.  Experiments have demonstrated a significant reduction in false positives of up to 97%, accompanied by a notable increase in accuracy of up to 98% and a heightened sensitivity of up to 125%.  What's more, the deep learning-assisted method showcases a notable reduction in noise, resulting in a cleaner diagnostic signal.  This advancement has brought the Rydberg atom detection via microwave signals technology closer to meeting the stringent requirements of a rapid, highly sensitive, and inexpensive COVID-19 diagnostic tool.  Potential applications of this research extend to various fields such as scientific research, industry, and healthcare, where rapid, highly sensitive, and inexpensive virus detection is crucial for informed decision-making.  Rydberg atom detection via microwave signals could serve as a model for deep learning improvements in other sensitive sensing applications.  This technology also has the potential to be translated to mobile platforms for widespread accessibility.  A user-friendly software for Rydberg atom diagnostic has been developed and is ready for deployment.  Rydberg atom detection via microwave signals holds great promise not only for COVID-19 diagnosis, but also for virus-free certification of goods exported from high-risk areas, airports, and other transportation hubs, as well as in medicine - thereby playing a vital role in mitigating the spread of the pandemic.  This work is well-positioned to address the rapid, highly sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic tool challenge via cutting-edge deep learning technology. UGC 8839, a massive spiral galaxy, is dominated by a rapidly rotating inner ring that mimics a classic Seyfert galaxy disk. This ring, composed of young stars, is the primary source of UGC 8839's star formation. Our research reveals a remarkably constant H I disk in UGC 8839, with an unexpectantly high H I fraction within the central young-star region. This high H I fraction is unusual among similar spiral galaxies. We suggest that in UGC 8839, a significant amount of H I must be converted into H2 in the central young-star area, or else the predicted H2 gas would not sufficiently account for the low H I fraction. Alternatively, the young-star region may be sitting on top of a hidden H I disk. Our research indicates that a substantial amount of gas in UGC 8839 is not participating in star formation, as evident from the H I fraction of the outer regions. This property makes UGC 8839 an intriguing galaxy for further study of active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback, as well as a potential example of a galaxy undergoing a minor merger that has increased its central star formation. UGC 8839 may also be in an early stage of a major merger, with a supermassive black hole that could explain the central young-star region's characteristics. Our research further confirms that UGC 8839 is interacting with a nearby galaxy, as indicated by a diffuse H I tail and blue Hα spiral arms. UGC 8839's H I disk appears to be disturbed, with an H I tail pointing directly at the spiral galaxy. This interaction is likely responsible for UGC 8839's central star formation, as well as its peculiar galaxy features. Our research paves the way for further study of UGC 8839's galaxy evolution, particularly the role of galaxy interactions in explaining the galaxy's unique properties. UGC 8839's characteristics may be a sign of things to come for a galaxy similar to our Milky Way, with a supermassive black hole and a spiral structure, as it interacts with nearby galaxies in the future. UGC 8839's central star formation may be a precursor to a more significant event, such as a galaxy merger that could expose its hidden supermassive black hole. We address the issue of processing temporal data by processing sequences one step at a time, learning a pattern at each stage to forecast the future. A sequential neural network, built on recurrent connections, achieves this process. However, its intricate design, featuring hidden loops and memory components, obscures the underlying mechanism, making it difficult to understand its working principle. Inspired by the transparency of fully connected networks, we seek to unveil the sequential neural network's internal workings by revealing its sequential nature. By applying a recurrent neural network to the prediction of short-term time series patterns in the field of finance, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model and uncover the sequential relationships within temporal data. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of our transparent model over competitive models, including enhanced feature selection and model interpretation, ultimately leading to more reliable predictions. To mitigate the severity of a pandemic, governments are implementing various measures to balance pandemic mitigation with economic impact. Our primary objective is to minimize the total cost, considering both health-related deaths and economic losses, when the pandemic's severity is measureable and its timeline is restricted to a fixed duration. We compare different time-varying restriction policies, such as stay-at-home orders and travel bans, in terms of their impact on the virus's spread and the economy. By converting the infinite-time Markov process into a linear time-invariant system, we derive optimal control policies for both the health and economic outcomes. Our key findings reveal that 1) maintaining a relatively low population mobility similar to that during a typical winter is both health-friendly and economically feasible, 2) the average health-related death rate paired with moderate mobility is a reliable indicator of the optimal policy, and 3) when the pandemic's severity is measureable, a 'dose of medicine' approach, based on an average rule, is both health-friendly and economically feasible. Our research employs data from the 2020 US states pandemic response to verify these general outcomes and demonstrates that the average US state followed an optimal control policy characterized by moderate mobility levels and changing restriction policies over time. Additionally, our research shows that the states' initial adherence to non-pharmaceutical interventions significantly affected their subsequent restriction policies, resulting in different levels of health-related deaths and economic losses. Our results provide actionable guidance for policymakers, aiming to balance pandemic mitigation with economic impact, and highlight the value of monitoring population mobility in evaluating the effectiveness of pandemic mitigation strategies. Moreover, our research underscores the significance of developing more effective non-pharmaceutical interventions to combat future pandemics. Finally, our research points out limitations in the current pandemic mitigation policy framework, encouraging further research into varying the types and levels of non-pharmaceutical interventions. The success of machine learning depends on a vast amount of data, and as the amount of data grows, identifying issues becomes more critical. Unlike static data sets, the problem lies in dealing with large datasets of annotated data where each record comes from a different source and the mapping between sources and data is unknown. This unstructured information about the data is called data significance, which lacks consideration in current data quality approaches that focus on analyzing data independently rather than taking into account the model they are being used to train. The absence of data significance leads to unaddressed data problems such as biased data, incorrect labels, and data loss, ultimately affecting model performance in training and deployment. The absence of data significance also hinders end-to-end machine learning process transparency by hiding the contribution and importance of individual data records to the model's performance. To tackle these challenges, a new framework is proposed called data significance, that measures the importance of each data record to the model's performance. The proposed formula, Shapley significance, takes into account the model being trained and the characteristics of each data record while considering the available quantities of these records. The amount of importance each data record holds is calculated through marginalization, and the distribution of this importance is calculated using kernel density estimation for visualization and ranking purposes. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated in several case studies involving different machine learning algorithms, and the results show significant improvements in model performance when data significant issues are addressed. The proposed system is currently in use at various data storage companies such as IBM, Microsoft, and Google for data quality analysis and has been confirmed through user study to be preferred over current data quality approaches due to its simplicity and ease of use. A open-source implementation of this system is available for download under a flexible license agreement. Moreover, the proposed system has applications in data worth analysis, and a new definition of data worth is introduced to distinguish it from data significance. Recent breakthroughs in algebraic statistics and combinatorial topology are leveraging diverse tools from algebra, combinatorics, and geometry to analyze rational and Chow spaces. Various enumerative geometry approaches are being utilized to study phylogenetic ideals, toric Hilbert schemes, and the Delaunay arrangement's tropicalization. Furthermore, geometry is providing key low-degree constraints and limiting principles, which are subsequently applied to statistical and combinatorial problems, often yielding unexpected outcomes. This survey showcases the remarkable progress made in this rapidly evolving field, while highlighting fundamental questions and promising research avenues. It is intended to introduce non-experts from statistics, combinatorics, and topology to the enumerative geometry methods and ideas underlying recent advances, many of which have profound implications for these fields. A related website features extensive supplementary material, including explicit examples, further discussion, and input from other experts. Chow spaces and the algebraic framework are initially addressed in the appendix to provide necessary background and context. Alternatively, interested readers may choose to skip directly to the main geometric examples and results. A brief convergence statement is included at the end. This study employs a Hall probe technique to investigate how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. At a pressure of 1.5 GPa, a significant enhancement of the Hall resistance is observed near its N\'eel temperature, indicating a link between the two events. Furthermore, high-pressure X-ray diffraction experiments reveal a structural transformation within the Mn sublattices as pressure increases, where the distance between adjacent Mn atoms decreases by 1-2%. A theoretical model is then used to explain these findings, where the altered parameters suggest that a rotating magnetic phase is necessary to explain the increased anomalous Hall effect, as well as another phase with unique magnetic properties, called a chiral magnetic skyrmoon. We also developed an efficient method to calculate the anomalous Hall resistance using microscopic parameters, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of the data and its relation to magnetic models that incorporate frustration and geometrical properties. Overall, these findings demonstrate that pressure can be utilized to regulate the anomalous Hall effect in antiferromagnets through the structural and magnetic transition of their constituents. Additionally, this study provides a framework for predicting the anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials, simply by understanding their magnetic structure. We believe that this approach can be applied to a wide range of materials and phenomena in condensed matter physics. Finally, we suggest that pressure can be used to apply mechanical stress and control the material's electronic and magnetic properties at the atomic level. As such, we propose that antiferromagnets under pressure could serve as an innovative means of controlling the anomalous Hall effect, potentially in devices such as quantum meters, sensors, and storage media. Conversely, these materials could also be used to gather new insights in the field of condensed matter physics. Lastly, we envision various technological applications and new scientific discoveries that could arise from these novel materials with controllable anomalous Hall effects. We expect such materials to lead to significant advancements in device development and the study of exotic phenomena in antiferromagnets. In conclusion, we have demonstrated that pressure can effectively regulate the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn by transitioning between different magnetic phases, while also providing a fundamental understanding of the Hall effect through microscopic parameters. As such, we propose that this mechanism can improve existing technologies and lead to the discovery of new scientific phenomena. We anticipate that this study will contribute to the development of innovative devices with controllable anomalous Hall effects and new insights in the field of exotic magnetic phases. To identify anisotropic emission patterns from microcavity lasers, we utilize the entropic approach and calculate the generalized Shannon entropy of light distribution from both directional and isotropic emissions. This statistical measure not only effectively distinguishes anisotropic emissions but also provides a quantitative indicator of directional strength. Furthermore, we modify the entropy formula with the non-uniformity term to enhance resolution and better identify anisotropic emissions. This entropy method offers a simple and robust technique for evaluating radiation characteristics in complex optical emitters. Our approach can be applied to study photon distributions in various devices, such as microcavity lasers, and provides valuable insights into understanding directional emissions.

To design an on-chip communication system capable of generating multiple directional optical signals, we developed a novel method of simultaneously producing multiple polarization-mode-locked (PML) beams with diverse polarization states. This innovative technique, grounded in the study of microcavity lasers with complex gain structures, allows for the creation of multiple PML sources with adjustable spectral relationships and identical line widths. Additionally, our research enabled the development of high-brightness optical sources with robust scalability, producing multiple femtosecond-scale PML beams in a single gain region.

We developed an advanced technique for creating polarization-entwined multiple femtosecond soliton laser with a single gain structure. This method leverages our profound understanding of polarization-mode-locking (PML) dynamics and stabilization mechanisms to design a microcavity laser with a gain structure comprising two sections with orthogonal polarization modes. By utilizing an external gain, the two PML beams in the two sections can be simultaneously locked and the polarization modes of the two beams are made parallel or perpendicular to each other. Consequently, two femtosecond-scale PML beams with the same line width and spectral relationships are generated, allowing for high-brightness optical signal encoding in on-chip photonic networks.

Phys. 62, 053101 (2021)], between the Zakharov-Shabat system and the KPZ equation, we show how the latter's weak noise theory emerges from the latter. To achieve this, we first introduce and prove the concept of 'feeble solutions' for the KPZ equation, and then derive them by taking the weakly scattered solution of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Subsequently, we establish that the solutions obtained are equivalent to those of the KPZ equation in terms of their probability distributions. To accomplish this, we introduce and prove a novel theorem known as the 'feeble central limit theorem'. This achievement is made possible by our development of a novel approach, 'geometric regularization', which enables the removal of 'blips' from feeble solutions of the KPZ equation. This in turn allows us to circumvent the conventional use of'standardization', thus breaking through a significant barrier in the study of feeble noise theories. As a consequence, we are able to demonstrate that geometric regularization gives rise to solutions whose probability distributions conform to the FP equation's limit law, effectively resolving this longstanding problem. To achieve this breakthrough, we first show the 'almost sure global well-posedness' of the KPZ equation, by combining the link established by [G. Akhundov, J. Math. Phys. 62, 053101 (2021)], between the Zakharov-Shabat system and the KPZ equation, with the established almost sure global well-posedness of the Zakharov-Shabat system. This novel achievement is based on novel approaches, 'local smoothing of feeble solutions' and 'feeble compensation', which we developed specifically for this purpose. These approaches in turn enabled us to prove a novel 'feeble version' of the 'bijective proof' of the 'Parrondo's Fortune's Paradox', effectively generalizing it to the feeble case. This achievement is also the basis for our proof of the 'feeble version' of the 'central limit theorem'. Consequently, we were able to derive the 'feeble noise theory' of the KPZ equation by combining these results with each other, thus resolving this longstanding problem. We've analyzed data from one minute intervals in the magnetospheric boundary with extremely low frequencies, detecting small-scale compressive waves that match fluctuations seen in solar wind pressure measurements. This analysis utilizes both calibrated and uncalibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the MMS mission. Two distinct detection methods were employed, one using full spacecraft potential data and another utilizing separate voltage probes. The findings from both techniques align, suggesting accurate detection of these waves. We've also found that the most prominent waves occur around 10-20 Hz and their amplitudes match those seen in solar wind measurements. This research offers a direct comparison with Cassini spacecraft data near the magnetospheric boundary and the Earth's bow shock. It's worth noting that the full spacecraft potential technique yields more sensitive detections but is also more susceptible to interferences, whereas the separate voltage probe method provides clearer, interference-free signals. Although the separate voltage probe technique appears more reliable, it may underestimate the full spacecraft potential measurements' capabilities. Ultimately, both techniques present a comprehensive picture of these compressive waves. It's also interesting to note that their properties don't rely on specific plasma beta values and are consistent across different measurements. This research sheds light on the similar-scale waves seen in solar wind measurements and suggests that their characteristics may be inherent to the compressive wave physics itself. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for XUV and several femtoseconds for hard X-rays. This paper explores an alternative scheme to generate attosecond pulses, taking advantage of the natural modulations inherent in tapered FEL pulses. By adjusting the average tapering pattern to minimize the effect of coherence, it becomes possible to produce pulses with durations corresponding to the electron bunch duration, potentially reaching time scales of a few hundred attoseconds for undulators and less than 100 attoseconds for helical undulators. The proposed approach not only enables the generation of attosecond pulses but also retains the high average pulse energy characteristic of tapered pulses, thereby facilitating high-average-power applications. The concept is illustrated using realistic simulations based on the TESLA and FLASH facilities, with corresponding reference experiments outlined. The described technique is compatible with the conventional SASE FEL operation and can be easily adapted in existing facilities to produce attosecond pulses, with the added benefit of retaining a significant fraction of the pulse energy. The technique is expected to significantly expand the accessibility of attosecond science, particularly in the XUV and soft X-ray regime. The proposed technique will serve as a crucial precursor to next-generation attosecond pulse facilities based on self-seeding and optimized tapering schemes, where pulse durations of up to 50 fs are feasible. The underlying ideas can also be applied to free-electron lasers driven by linear and non-linear accelerators, as well as to third-generation hard X-ray FELs employing dedicated undulators. The general concept of utilizing altered chirp and tapering patterns may also find applications in free-electron lasers driven by circular and non-circular undulators. The technique has far-reaching implications for the fields of attosecond pulse generation, high-average-power femtosecond pulse generation, biological imaging, nano-surgery, and other areas, thereby enabling the exploration of new scientific avenues and applications. The attosecond pulse generation in XUV and soft X-ray FELs enables cutting-edge advancements in physics research, such as the exploration of attosecond pulse generation in helical undulators and the generation of highly coherent extreme ultraviolet femtosecond pulses with high average power, thereby opening doors for novel applications and research in physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and materials science. The generation of attosecond pulses in XUV and soft X-ray FELs drives innovation and advances research in physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and materials

To address the concern of gerrymandering in the US, we developed an algorithmic method. This method measures the difficulty of dividing a district map into equal areas, which is a key indicator of unfair division. Our approach involves artificially increasing the temperatures of pixels on the map, and rearranging nearby areas with lower temperatures to minimize the geographical connections of higher-temperature points. We use statistical tests on simulated maps to establish a baseline for what constitutes unfair division. We applied this method to actual US district maps from 2020, and our analysis indicates that many of these maps show signs of gerrymandering. Textile images exhibit unique characteristics of low color value, sparse pixels, and irregularities due to the inherent properties of the fabric material, resulting in distorted or flawed images that must be identified and corrected.  Removing flaws from these images is crucial for evaluating a fabric's quality and ensuring consistency in production.  Currently, there is no universal flaw removal method suitable for all types of textile images.  This paper proposes an innovative approach to flaw identification and removal for textile images featuring unique patterns, utilizing the generalized extension of the Generalized HOG operator and low-rank matrix decomposition.  The proposed method involves several key contributions:  First, we apply the GHOG operator to convert textured regions into a more meaningful, low-dimensional feature space.  Next, we seek minimal pixels with the highest contribution to image distortion, seeking the lowest-rank solution through matrix decomposition.  Finally, the corrected image is obtained by subtracting the flaw map from the original textile image.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in flaw removal for various textile images, displaying improved color, sparse pixel, and rank values.  Additionally, we have released the textile_flaw_correction toolbox, providing a range of useful tools for textile flaw correction.  This toolbox can be accessed via http://www.iaec.edu.cn/indexy.html, under the category of image processing. Recent observations support the presence of unseen masses at the centers of galaxies, including those similar to the one our sun orbits, suggesting a population of compact objects too heavy for the sun to weigh.

We developed a computer model simulating how these massive clusters formed, incorporating the latest scientific understanding of how the first stars collapsed and merged. As a result, we predict the creation of either supermassive black holes or smaller, more regular black holes, including those with masses similar to that of the sun, within the hearts of galaxies.

When the first stars collapsed, they may have given birth to either black holes or neutron stars, which would have resided at the centers of galaxies. Following the collapse of the first stars, subsequent stars would move in and form clusters, potentially wrapping around existing compact objects, including black holes or neutron stars. As a result of this process, we predict an abundance of regular black holes residing at the centers of galaxies, including those with masses similar to that of the sun, which could lead to the detection of gravitational waves when they merge with other compact objects in the future. In fact, we estimate that the number of gravitational wave events detectable by LISA, a powerful space-based telescope, could reach as high as one thousandth of a year per galaxy. Additionally, we find that the number of gravitational wave events detectable by LIGO, a powerful ground-based telescope, could reach as high as one event per year per galaxy for black hole masses as low as five times that of the sun. Finally, we note that the number of stellar-mass black hole mergers detectable by LISA could reach as high as ten thousandth of a year per galaxy, and that the population of compact objects that give rise to these mergers could be as old as the universe itself. In contrast, we find that the number of supermassive black hole mergers detectable by LISA could reach as high as one event per year per galaxy for certain models, and that the number of mergers detectable by LIGO could reach as high as one event per year per galaxy for black hole masses as low as fifty times that of the sun. A study on the radiative decay of the $X(3872)$ and the scattering of the $X(3872)$ off the photon, denoted as $\delta$, is conducted to explore potential pathways. The calculations suggest that the direct contribution from the $X(3872)$'s internal barion-antibaryon pair annihilating to a quark-antiquark pair via the strong interaction is feasible but the subsequent emission of a photon is unlikely as it violates quark-hadron duality. On the other hand, the contribution involving the dressing of the $X(3872)$ by a light quark and then interacting with the photon is also feasible but does not significantly impact the signal. However, the contribution involving the dressed quark scattering off the photon is found to dominate the scattering process and thus greatly affects the broadening of the $X(3872)$'s mass distribution, resulting in a broadening of about 6 MeV which is much larger than the broadening caused by the strong interaction. Furthermore, the study reveals that the contribution involving the dressed quark and then producing a meson pair, particularly $\rho$ or $\omega$, is also feasible but does not substantially impact the signal of the radiative decay. It is also observed that the contribution involving the quark-antiquark system directly interacting with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is not a significant contributor to the radiative decay. Additionally, the study finds that the contribution involving the quark-antiquark system directly interacting with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is not a significant contributor to the quark-antiquark system's mass distribution being affected by the photon. However, the study does show that the quark-antiquark system's mass distribution is affected by the quark when it is dressed by the light quark and then interacts with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality. Finally, the quark when it is dressed by the light quark and then interacts with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is found to be the primary factor that explains the quark-antiquark system's broadening of the $X(3872)$'s mass distribution being much larger than the broadening caused by the strong interaction. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of sectorally monotone p-harmonic functions and derive estimates for their growth rates within certain angle ranges near the boundary points. The estimates obtained are crisp and resemble those found in harmonic function theory, albeit with the involvement of p-analogue estimates for linear growth. We also explore the implications of these estimates on the category properties of planar p-subharmonic functions and provide a local mean-value property for p-subharmonic functions within sectors. The primary challenge in this research was developing a suitable "integrability" concept for measures in sectors, allowing us to leverage the classical Brelot structure theory to establish a unique solution to the Dirichlet problem and prove the estimates. The uniqueness proof relies on a novel application of the maximum principle for positive p-subharmonic functions to bounded sets bounded by sectorial boundaries. In contrast to the Leray-Schauder degree theory used in linear cases, we employ a simplified approach based on the boundedness of the sphere mapping to demonstrate the nonlinear case. We also utilize a variant of the Poincaré inequality for functions defined within sectors, thereby extending a result from [Kuusalo et al. (2001)]. Finally, we investigate the implications of monotonicity and growth estimates on the category properties of p-subharmonic functions and derive a local mean-value property for these functions, thereby extending a result from [Heinonen and Nystrom (2001)]. The research draws upon classical ideas from harmonic function theory and p-harmonic function theory, combining them with a novel analysis of the asymptotic behavior of sectorally monotone p-harmonic functions. A key innovation of this research is the integration of the linear and nonlinear cases, as well as the unique perspective on measure integrability in sectors. While the results may seem familiar due to their similarity to harmonic function results, the actual proofs depend on novel and non-trivial mathematical reasoning. Consequently, we estimate the growth rates of sectorally monotone p-harmonic functions more precisely than previously possible. Nevertheless, we limit our research to planar sectors, leaving the exploration of the general case for future investigation. The general approach of this research can be applied to various problems in geometric analysis, particularly those involving monotone functions within certain geometric configurations. Browning and Sawin established that the preimage of a non-constant affine rational function over the integers, covering a certain large area, has a finite number of solutions. We extend their work, showing the same result for a broader range of situations, including rational numbers and certain finite fields, without requiring the Bombieri-Mertens prime number theorem. This extension was influenced by a previous finding of Li and Zhang. The proof involves combining hyperbolic geometry with a key inequality from the work of Montgomery and Vaughan. In their study, researchers employed sophisticated computational methods to analyze various scenarios involving a three-component system and used statistical tools to assess the likelihood of different configurations. After thoroughly examining the data, they concluded that a three-component system is highly unlikely and that any potential third component would need to be extremely distant and heavy to explain the observed phenomena.

This paper explores the behavior and modeling of ferroelectric FETs by investigating the impact of domain wall transitions within the ferroelectric material. Due to the distinct electrical properties of domains, their movement at the wall level introduces an unpredictable capacitance, significantly hindering the device's performance. To simulate this phenomenon, a comprehensive model of the device is developed, incorporating a detailed spatial representation of the ferroelectric material and its capacitive properties. Extensive device simulations are conducted, revealing the material's polar structure and corresponding current-voltage characteristics. Our results show that the unpredictable capacitance associated with domain wall transitions leads to a dramatic increase in channel capacitance, consistent with experimental observations. Moreover, we find that the transient behavior of the device is heavily influenced by the domain wall's initial and final positions, as well as the applied voltage's speed of change. To validate our approach, a reliable model of the ferroelectric material is used to reproduce the measured current-voltage data from commercially available silicon oxide samples. Our simulations successfully replicate the experimentally determined capacitance of the device. Additionally, we make the ferroelectric material parameters used in this study publicly available, allowing readers to run the simulations themselves with the specified material properties. This article explores the properties of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations with pure jump noise, specifically their irreducibility. The jump noise is represented by a Markov process acting on a finite state space. A sufficient condition for irreducibility is established, along with an explicit formula for the transition density of the associated Markov process. This research has practical implications, with examples demonstrating how additive jump noise can render a pair of stochastic differential equations irreducible, even if the diffusion coefficient is diagonally dominant. Additionally, the study considers ergodicity and the asymptotic behavior of solutions. An important finding is that solutions may converge exponentially to a unique, stable equilibrium, even in the presence of jump noise. The analysis is further generalized to multidimensional systems and systems with a complex phase space. Several numerical simulations illustrate the main theoretical outcomes. Finally, the study's results are validated by applications in physics and biology, providing new insights into systems previously studied in those fields. We're looking at the smallest possible degree in the power graph of G, denoted as delta(G). This value represents the minimum degree in the power graph, which is based on the exponents of its elements' orders. The power graph of G, or delta(G), is determined by the exponent relationships between its elements, showing connections between those with the same or different orders. Our analysis finds that delta(G) is limited by the bound min{p,4}, except in two specific cases where G is isomorphic to the cyclic group of order p or the cyclic group of order 4. In these unique instances, the minimum degree in the power graph is 2. We've also identified upper limits for the minimum degree in the power graph for certain nilpotent groups of their smallest possible size. These limits are influenced by the cyclic factor groups of their maximal cyclic subgroups. Specifically, we've found that delta(G) is limited by the bound min{p,4} if the order of G's cyclic factor groups is less than 4. Similarly, we've found that delta(G) is limited by the bound p if the order of G's cyclic factor groups is greater than 4. Our analysis also finds that delta(G) is limited by the bound min{p/2,4} if the order of G's cyclic factor groups is less than or equal to 8. Deep convolutional networks (DCNs) are the primary models used for image
classification. They employ standard convolution operations to produce
feature maps with specific spatial configurations, which are then combined into
a fixed output. In contrast, our proposed orientation convolving network (OCN)
utilizes an innovative convolution operation, incorporating a circular scan
pattern at varying angles, thereby extracting a broader range of useful
spatial configurations in feature maps. We then demonstrate the benefits of
this extended feature space in the context of image classification, showing
comparable outcomes to DCNs while extracting more comprehensive information. 
Our OCN draws inspiration from ocular convolutional networks (OCNs), an
innovative type of DCN. By adapting an affordable number of additional
parameters, OCN achieves equivalent or even superior performance in four
established image classification datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet,
and ImageNet). Furthermore, the circular scanning pattern in OCN facilitates
inter-feature interaction across different spatial configurations in
feature maps, resulting in enhanced feature representation with fewer layers. 
Consequently, OCN can serve as an effective training method for standard DCNs,
enabling them to capture a broader range of useful feature configurations in
the feature maps. The source code for our model implementation is publicly
available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1997/Orientation-Convolutive-Networks. 
Our model has been tested and validated in accordance with the principles of
transparency and ethics. The study does not involve collecting or processing
sensitive personal data, and is therefore not associated with any potential
conflict of interest. The proposed model does not address any social issue, but
rather aims to contribute innovatively to the field of computer vision.

Recent advancements in GCN-based point cloud networks have shown promising results in handling sparse and non-Euclidean data. These networks build on the principles of message passing algorithms commonly used in graph neural networks to approximate complex functions on graph-structured data. In the context of point cloud learning, GCN networks rely on localized connections between neighboring nodes, which are defined by geometric proximity. These networks effectively capture local characteristics but struggle to model global structures, a key limitation. To address this, we develop a novel GCN-based framework that integrates long-range global connections, preserving the inherent properties of the underlying point cloud. Our approach outperforms existing benchmarks in various evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of different design choices in GCN-based networks, providing actionable insights for practitioners. Our implementation details are publicly accessible. Our findings affirm the significance of global connections in GCN-based point cloud models. We discovered that the benefits of long-range connections extend beyond synthetic datasets, also enhancing performance on real-world benchmarks. Our analysis highlights the importance of properly balancing local and global components, rather than solely relying on nearest neighbor connections. These findings are expected to extend beyond point cloud learning, also influencing other fields such as computer vision and social network analysis. Recently, neural network tampering through Trojan attacks has garnered significant interest. Traditional Trojan attacks necessitate the knowledge of hidden trigger patterns, which can be undesirable. To address this, we introduce a new approach called Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault (SHTA), where a benign model is altered without knowing the hidden trigger. The resulting trigger is discovered accidentally, often stemming from data label changes or minor image modifications. We test our approach using semantic segmentation, object detection, and image classification tasks and find that SHTA model activations efficiently identify triggers with minimal accuracy loss. Moreover, we find that trigger patterns can be easily replicated and combined to extract the underlying semantic structure, which can be exploited for tampering in a broader range of applications. Our proposed method serves as a fundamental Hostless Trojan Assault framework and can be improved upon. In comparison to existing hostless Trojan attacks, SHTA models exhibit improved inference efficiency, higher compression ratios, and stronger embedding semantics. Our approach outperforms traditional Trojan attacks in terms of accuracy preservation and trigger pattern generalizability. The proposed method represents a novel and effective approach to neural network tampering, distinguishing itself from existing Trojan attacks through its trigger pattern discovery mechanism and improved model characteristics. It can be a valuable tool for enhancing model design efficiency, a significant area of research in neural network development. These studies revealed a 1 MeV shift in the peak of the THC cross-section sensitivity spectrum towards higher energies compared to conventional measurements. This observation is attributed to an uneven distribution of the incident 12C flux energy, which is a result of the threshold effect and must be considered when selecting and combining projections from rotating 12C targets. To achieve precise results, experimentalists need to either employ non-rotating 12C targets and an advanced THC detector or develop sophisticated analysis software that can deconvolve the effects of rotation and extract the 12C + 12C astrophysical factor as accurately as possible. Additionally, we have introduced an advanced deconvolution method that utilizes a Wiener filter in the frequency domain to separate the true 12C + 12C factor from experimental data. This method has produced reliable results in the past and can be used to analyze existing and future experiments. Finally, we have outlined a plan for a future 12C + 12C THC experiment that is expected to break the barrier of low-energy astrophysical factor measurements, potentially leading to a better understanding of the 12C + 12C reaction in stellar cores and the resulting element synthesis in stars. Lastly, we have reflected on the evolving nature of the THC technique and the significant contributions that have paved the way for this future study. This paper and its sequel introduce a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics, grounded in an advanced mathematical concept called categorical topology. We will demonstrate how diverse existing modal logic semantics can be linked through a universal framework, based on specific topological structures, in addition to providing new alternatives. This framework allows us to translate fundamental operations of modal logic into algebraic and categorical operations, thereby offering multiple paths for reasoning about modal logic semantics. The paper explores various topological structures used in modal logic semantics, focusing on the relationship between these structures and the categorical products used in modal logic semantics. It is worth noting that the majority of the material in this paper is a recompilation of existing research, with the exception of a few original contributions. The sequel to this paper will delve into more advanced topics. Furthermore, a companion paper will delve into the proof-theoretic connections of this categorical framework. In contrast, a related paper focuses on the relationship between the categorical framework and proof-theoretic interpretations. The present paper, Unification of Modal Reasoning I, was initially a chapter in my doctoral dissertation, while a more recent version can be found in the arXiv preprint 2201.06037. In contrast, a related paper focuses on the link between the categorical framework and proof-theoretic interpretations, as detailed in the arXiv preprint 2204.07742. Achieving reliable automation in complex domains like medicine requires addressing a major challenge: quantifying uncertainty in the final predictions. This study classifies uncertainty types, reviews current quantification techniques, evaluates their suitability for a case study in medical image analysis, and highlights gaps in the field. A comprehensive evaluation framework for uncertainty measurement is proposed, along with a systematic review of relevant methods. A comparative assessment of these methods is performed using data from two medical intervention datasets. The results show that different techniques yield distinct and informative uncertainty measures, yet their respective advantages depend on specific application considerations. A proposed statistical metric is used to evaluate and compare these methods on a particular dataset. The findings provide a roadmap for future research and guide practitioners in selecting the most appropriate techniques for their own datasets. A comprehensive code repository is made available for replication purposes. This study aims to stimulate research in this area and contribute to applied machine learning on the calculation of uncertainty precision. This way, researchers can gain a better understanding of the reliability of their models' predictions, ultimately leading to greater trust in applied machine learning. The study's findings also offer insights and recommendations for researchers working on uncertainty calculation in related fields, such as computer vision. The accompanying repository can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/epfl-epic/auqom. In this research, we examine the challenge of finding the optimal policy in large-scale Markov decision processes (MDPs), a problem that can be reformulated as an infinite series of matrix equations. However, the complexity of these equations grows rapidly in the number of states, making it infeasible to compute numerically. We modify the generalized minimum residual method (GMRES) to approximate the inverse of a large matrix iteratively, and consequently, the optimal policy in MDPs at a corresponding precision level. Importantly, each iteration of our algorithm reduces the computational cost more efficiently than previously proposed methods by a factor of the square root of the number of states. The proposed algorithm exhibits stable convergence and a precision level that increases proportionally with the number of iterations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm through numerical experiments involving a diverse set of large-scale MDPs. Additionally, we show that a previously established method (iGMRES) can be an effective option but typically requires more iterations to achieve the same precision level, particularly in cases with irrelevant details in the reward structure. Therefore, iGMRES can be utilized effectively in situations where the underlying dynamics are complex and the state implications are significant. Conversely, the proposed algorithm is better suited for solving aggregation-based MDPs where the underlying dynamics are simple and the state implications are substantial. A Python package is available for use with this algorithm at https://github.com/aleksandarapic/iGMRES.mdps. Furthermore, the corresponding mathematical proofs can be found in the supplementary document at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2205.04066v2. Additionally, the source code for the numerical examples can be accessed at https://aleksandarapic.github.io/iGMRES_mdps/. Lastly, the reference data for the numerical examples can be found at https://aleksandarapic.github.io/iGMRES_mdps/reference_data/. Finally, the preprint of this research has been published at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2205.04066.

To effectively analyze the performance of complex computer models, such as climate and traffic models, we need to examine their output over time and understand how their predicted values vary. However, these models often produce large sets of data, making it necessary to condense this output into a manageable number of key features. We propose using a multivariate distribution on the real numbers to model this condensed output and employ a two-step process: first identifying the optimal features: second estimating the multivariate distribution using multiple cross-sectional data sets. We demonstrate that this method can be approached as an inverse problem, applying principles from inverse scattering theory to develop an estimation procedure and provide evidence of its performance through numerical studies. These studies involve artificial data based on solutions to ordinary and partial differential equations, as well as random walks with a characteristic time. Our results show that this procedure performs well, especially when the size of the data is relatively large compared to the number of features and we use a simple Gaussian model to describe the distribution of values over time. We extend the application of this method to understand the behavior of models that produce time series data on a fixed grid, facilitated through numerical solver tools, and illustrate its usefulness with an example from traffic flow modeling. We also compare its performance with alternative methods, including the use of principal components, sparse components and diffusion maps. Our findings reveal that our proposed approach outperforms these methods due to its ability to capture the underlying geometry of the model's output, encoded into the estimated features. In particular, it achieves a higher degree of separation between different models, as well as a more accurate representation of the expected values for future times based on the model's dynamics. This research offers a new approach to understanding complex computer models and their output, ultimately facilitating the development of more accurate predictive models. To improve the reliability of network-based learning, we investigate the potential of regional queries in augmenting a central model with information from its surrounding neighborhood. We generate diverse training datasets by artificially disrupting a central model's knowledge and observe that integrating signals from nearby nodes can facilitate the recovery of its parameters. However, our experiments also reveal scenarios in which regional queries do not enhance the central model's performance. We develop a theoretical framework to predetermine the situations in which regional queries will be beneficial to the learning process. The boundary between helpful and unhelpful queries is identified as the threshold beyond which aggregated neighborhood signals are required to supplement central model performance. We validate the theoretical findings through various empirical studies, which demonstrate that the theoretical framework accurately predicts the effectiveness of regional queries in multiple resilient learning setups. Furthermore, our analysis sheds light on the implicit assumptions inherent in the central model paradigm and could guide the modification of learning algorithms to harness the collective potential of neighborhood queries. The code for our research is publicly available at https://github.com/jbitter/Regional-Queries-in-Resilient-Learning.

This research proposes a novel approach to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions using stylus input data. The proposed system distinguishes itself from existing handwriting recognition systems in two key ways. Firstly, it accommodates input from students with disabilities who use assistive technology to interact with multimedia content through multi-touch devices. Secondly, it translates raw sensor data into meaningful mathematical expressions, as opposed to traditional handwriting recognition systems that focus on text input. We introduce a pioneering method to automatically generate ink segments from raw sensor data and propose a unique algorithm to recognize recurring patterns in sensor data. Furthermore, we have developed a dataset consisting of 1800 complex mathematical expressions, in collaboration with the Imperial College's Disability Team, to support the development of this system. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, as the proposed system demonstrated superior outcomes compared to a basic approach across diverse domains, achieving an average accuracy rate of 87% across all domains, as well as exhibiting promising signs of generalizing to novel symbols through continued development. Additionally, we observed an accuracy rate of 92% for expressions involving basic arithmetic operations but noted a decline in accuracy as the complexity of the expression increased. The systematic evaluation of our approach allowed us to pinpoint specific difficulties, such as interpreting symbols, and unforeseen challenges, such as dealing with damaged input, as well as identifying symbols through visual recognition. The proposed system serves as a pioneering modular approach to recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions, employing a detailed state machine to navigate the structure and semantic meaning of the expressions, as well as the relationships between symbols. We observed an accuracy rate of 88% in evaluating the language understanding component and recognized the need for further improvement in tackling the intricacies of the English language. Notably, we achieved an accuracy rate of 90% in evaluating the proposed system's generalization capabilities across diverse domains, as well as exhibiting promising signs through continued development. The proposed system demonstrates a high level of flexibility and adaptability as a modular system, as evidenced by its performance in specific domains, such as physics and chemistry, where it achieved an accuracy rate of 90%. We successfully applied our approach to recognize step-by-step mathematical problem solutions, as demonstrated in the experimental outcomes and recognized the need for further improvement in tackling the intricacies of the English language. This study presents an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech using a non-statistical method, which enables the production of speech with varied lengths. Inspired by the success of the Median Driver in the Median Mixture Model, we developed a new technique for creating synthetic speech. Our method involves repeating the Median Driver to produce speech with specified lengths. We tested this approach with three different acoustic units - sonorant, vowel, and consonant - and demonstrated its efficacy through subjective listening tests. The results show that our model accurately replicates the target speech lengths across all unit types. Furthermore, we found that synthetic speech generated using our approach is preferred over speech with natural lengths in consonant-initiated vowel contexts. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Spoken-Phonetics/Median-Driven-Speech-Generation. We hope this study contributes to the ongoing development of statistical parametric speech synthesis. We are willing to collaborate with others on this project and welcome any inquiries. We are particularly interested in expanding our method to generate high-quality melodies. We are excited about the prospect of generating entire songs in a manner reminiscent of the classic song and story library, the Folio, which was used by the famous composer and inventor, Leon Theremin. We are confident that our method will help push the boundaries of art in the modern music industry. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals how disease transmission rates and network characteristics, like clustering and dispersal, influence the outbreak. However, hypergraphs provide a more comprehensive framework for modeling these events, capturing interactions between multiple individuals in a single event. This study initiates the examination of epidemics on hypergraphs through the development of a new extinction threshold on these structures, derived from the hypergraph's spectral properties. This threshold measures the average transmission rate at which the epidemic can only spread infinitely versus extinguish. To calculate this critical value, we first determine the spectral boundaries of the hypergraph's Laplacian, then develop an approximate formula for its largest eigenvalue. This work also considers more complex scenarios, such as multiple infection events and the impact of stochasticity, before simulating these processes numerically. The results show that the predicted extinction threshold accurately predicts the critical transmission rate in many cases and serves as a suitable approximation in others. The associated code for these simulations is publicly accessible at https://github.com/agb2910/Extinction-Thresholds-on-Hypergraphs. The research was partially funded by EPSRC with project ID EP/T008802/1. This helps advance knowledge in both hypergraph Laplacian eigenvalues and the analysis of epidemics on more intricate network types, like hypergraphs, to model real events more accurately, such as the spread of COVID-19 in close-living communities. The research provides a theoretical foundation and a practical tool, the AGP3 algorithm, for determining the critical transmission rate in these situations. The study expands knowledge by applying this approach to more complex hypergraphs than previously studied and makes the associated code publicly available to replicate the results. The funding for the project is also acknowledged. The observed chirality in the spin profile is a distinct hallmark, differentiating CrI3 from other ferromagnets. Developing reliable multithreaded software is challenging because race conditions make programs difficult to reason about, especially when they operate incorrectly.  As a result, errors in software production often surface only under specific execution scenarios, compounding the difficulty of pinpointing their source.  To address this issue, researchers have explored the application of formal model checking as a means of automatically detecting and isolating race condition-related bugs.  Although previous models check for data races by ignoring thread synchronization, this approach is impractical in real-world programming contexts.  In response, a new model checker, McMini, has been introduced to efficiently process programs that utilize mutexes to manage access to shared resources.  McMini employs a novel state-inclusion approach and leverages an optimized dynamic parallelization strategy to ensure high performance, even in complex program scenarios. Spoofing countermeasures (SC) systems, currently in use with leading activation functions (AF), struggle with their own biases. In contrast, the parametric ReLU (pReLU) function reduces these inconsistencies but introduces an unbounded slope, causing features to become excessively large. A new family of keys-only filters, called xor filters, is introduced, which outperforms Bloom and Cuckoo filters in efficiency and speed. Each element in a xor filter is associated with a distinct hash value, which is used as an index to store the element's value in a table. During the lookup process, a key's hash values are used to calculate its corresponding index, and then the filter checks the key's actual value at that index. If the key's actual value matches its expected value, the lookup is considered successful. Otherwise, it is considered a false positive. Xor filters can be designed to have the same false positive rates as Bloom and Cuckoo filters but with significantly faster insertion and deletion times or they can be optimized to have lower memory usage while still maintaining comparable false positive rates. Alternatively, they can be designed with a balance of memory usage and processing efficiency. The design of xor filters is inspired by Bloom filters but offers more flexible operations. Unlike Bloom filters, xor filters can store elements exactly, which enables deletions in O(1) time. Unlike Cuckoo filters, xor filters have lower memory usage and faster insertion times. The design of xor filters is similar to LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing) but with a more efficient structure. Unlike existing keys-only filters, xor filters are not susceptible to attacks that reveal sensitive information by inverting the hash functions. Specifically, they cannot be used to brute-force password cracking even if the attacker has access to a hash table. A detailed analysis and evaluation of xor filters is presented, which shows their advantages over existing filters. The results suggest that xor filters can significantly outperform Bloom and Cuckoo filters in efficiency and speed. A open-source implementation of xor filters is available at https://github.com/chenliu85/xor-filters. The code has been tested on Amazon EC2 instances. The performance of xor filters can be customized based on the user's requirements. The filter's size, false positive rates, and insertion/deletion speeds can all be optimized. The optimal xor filter design is determined by a trade-off between memory usage and processing efficiency. The filter's false positive rates can be adjusted by changing its size. The insertion/deletion speeds can also be modified by optimizing the xor filter's design. The performance of xor filters is evaluated under various scenarios using real-world data. We introduce the FLVoogd framework, which enforces robust consensus among participants in federated learning. Currently, implementing robust models in FL is challenging due to the arbitrary nature of participant updates. Furthermore, existing frameworks rely on sensitive gradient information, exposing participant data to the server. We address these issues through the introduction of loss correction and robust consensus mechanisms. We develop an iterative process using the Jacobi method to achieve robust model convergence. Additionally, we introduce a diagonalization process that eliminates the need for sensitive data matrices. We combine these mechanisms with the Sherman-Morrison formula to maintain participant privacy and compute secure aggregation matrices. We evaluate our framework's performance on three datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness against perturbation-based adversarial attacks. Our framework offers significant improvements in model convergence stability and performance, alongside enhanced participant privacy. The experimental results show that FLVoogd experiences minimal performance degradation even in adversarial scenarios, whereas baseline FL methods exhibit substantial convergence instability and performance loss. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/Raflab1/FLVoogd.

The main obstacle lies in bridging the significant gap between simulated environments, where training data is gathered, and real-world settings, where actual driving takes place. This divide is characterized by real-world road conditions that can vary greatly from simulations. This paper proposes an innovative solution to this problem, aiming to transfer learned skills directly from simulated environments to real-world driving. The core idea is to utilize diverse, abstract representations of road scenes, thereby facilitating model generalization across various environments. Our approach relies on gradient feature analysis, an effective and widely applicable method for scene representation. The method encompasses depth estimation, semantic segmentation, and other context-free image attributes. To model variability in road scenes, we employ a probabilistic distribution derived from real-world data, and use it to guide the model during training. Our end-to-end navigation model can navigate real-world roads without prior knowledge of the road layout. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully closes the Sim2Real divide, and outperforms alternative approaches in a comprehensive evaluation. For planets similar to Earth that exist within their stars' habitable zones, this is particularly true, as their internal structures are hidden from view. In order to uncover insights into these planets' compositions, we are investigating the distinction between two different types of equilibrium that occur during atmospheric formation - the thermodynamic equilibrium of various gases and the chemical equilibrium of dissolved species.

We have found that the chemical equilibrium of dissolved species, as influenced by solubility, leaves behind visible transit signatures that can be observed and analyzed. By comparing the sizes of pressure drops and methane absorption features at different wavelengths, we can identify whether a planet's internal heat is being released or absorbed, as well as determine the percentage of its mass that is composed of iron and silicates. This information, in turn, allows us to estimate the radius of the planet's core and determine whether it has a liquid or solid outer boundary, all without direct visual evidence. These findings could provide valuable insights into the planet's internal energy generation and core dynamics, shaping its overall shape and size. Conversely, thermodynamic equilibrium offers less distinct and easily interpretable signs of internal processes, limiting its potential for revealing a planet's internal composition. This document outlines our approach to evaluating out-of-context responses in a multi-turn conversation setting, where each response builds on the previous exchange. Our framework encompasses three key aspects: 

1. Response assessment: We determine the relevance of a response to the conversation context, incorporating both grammatical and semantic considerations.
2. Context updating: We refine the conversation context in real-time by identifying new information introduced by responses.
3. Context maintenance: We ensure the conversation context remains accurate and relevant throughout the conversation, preventing unnecessary updates.

Our evaluation framework is put to the test in a simulated scenario, where human evaluators assess our performance against a baseline that achieves optimal results when re-evaluating responses in the context of the entire conversation. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/facebookresearch/OutOfContext. 

In a comparison with a leading advanced language model, our method demonstrates superior performance in processing 13,416 out-of-context responses within 3.26 seconds, achieving a 0.302-second speed advantage. Furthermore, our model achieves a 4% improvement in relevance, along with enhanced context updating and maintenance. While our model excels in relevance, its context updating and maintenance capabilities may benefit from further improvement. Our model's open-source code is available for reproduction of our results at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/OutOfContext.

Our proposed technique is particularly beneficial for tasks that involve analyzing documents, as they often require a substantial number of samples for training to account for diverse document types and processing imperfections. The EuS/InAs interface has been proposed as a potential material for building compact and efficient spin valves due to EuS's unique properties. Research has shown that the performance of such devices heavily relies on an optimal interface electronic structure, specifically a band gap at the molecular scale. Through the application of density functional theory and many-body theory, our study systematically examines and compares the electronic properties of coherent Haggerty and Merino interfaces. Our findings reveal that only the Haggerty arrangement produces a band gap at the molecular scale suitable for spin valve applications. A comparative analysis of magnetization, bonding arrangements, and interface charges across different interfaces provides insight into their distinct structural features. Our study demonstrates that a stable magnetization in EuS is contingent on a specific bonding configuration and charges at the interface, ultimately yielding an accurate prediction of the magnetic behavior of InAs. Our research paves the way for the optimization of spin valve prototypes. In the field of click-based neural network learning, removing unnecessary weights can significantly reduce the computational cost. However, previous studies on neural network pruning have focused on compressing models for inference, ignoring the requirements of training. This paper introduces ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end solution combining pruning and training. It preserves the original network architecture during the pruning process, allowing for the direct training of the sparsely structured network. Moreover, it optimizes the training procedure by adapting the loss function and regularization for the specified click patterns. Through extensive experiments, we have found that ClickTrain can achieve superior results on convolutional neural networks, yielding significant reductions in computational cost and memory consumption without compromising accuracy. The code for ClickTrain can be accessed at https://github.com/hjdw2/clicktrain. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various ClickNet types, such as click-based convolutional neural networks (C-CNN), click-based multi-head attention networks, and click-based ResNet, demonstrating the broad applicability of this method. Furthermore, we have successfully implemented ClickTrain on graph neural networks (GNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs), confirming its generalizability on a wide range of models. ViTs proved to be more challenging for ClickNet learning due to their lack of local connectivity, but still showed promising results. We have thoroughly evaluated our method by analyzing its training dynamics, and found that ClickTrain can effectively adapt to the unique characteristics of each model. Consequently, we obtained extremely dense subgraphs from the model's weight matrices and trained end-to-end sparse models. Our method has potential applications in resource-scarce embedded system deployment and neural network acceleration. It can be extended to other machine learning models, such as graph neural networks, by effectively incorporating the network topology into the training process. This research investigates the modal logic aspects of the distributive complete Lambek calculus with modal functions, specifically focusing on its axiomatic system. By examining both commutative and non-commutative modal operators, we demonstrate that the axiomatic system has a rich set of equivalent axioms. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between these axioms by linking them to the traditional Lambek calculi. Our key findings include the proof that the axiomatic system is sound with respect to a specific modal semantics and the proof that this axiomatic system is complete when augmented with specific additional axioms. Additionally, we show that the complete axiomatic system possesses a Kriplovskii semantics, effectively enabling us to relate modal semantics to the axiomatic system. Lastly, we explore the complexity of the resulting modal calculus. Specifically, we show that the decision problem for both the propositional and first-order calculi are soluble by a Turing machine. Interestingly, the membership problem for these calculi Proves to be Turing-decidable as well. These outcomes are advantageous in the sense that the modal calculus's complexity outperforms that of the pure Lambek calculus by a substantial margin. Ultimately, our research contributes to the understanding of the modal aspects of substructural calculi while also providing a general framework for modal logic with a substructural base.  Additionally, our research delves into the relationship between the axiomatic system and the Curry-Howard paradigm. By converting axioms to typed lambda calculus terms, we prove that the former system is equivalent to a specific type system. This achievement marks a significant breakthrough, as it demonstrates a systematic connection between a modal logic axiomatic system and a Curry-Howard framework. Consequently, our research offers novel insights into both the modal logic and type theory domains. Moreover, our research expands upon and evaluates the fundamental ideas presented in a prior study on modal substructural logic. By examining the interplay between modal operators and structural rules, our research offers a deeper understanding of that initial study's concept. Lastly, our research provides an alternative and simplified construction of a specific modal logic semantics described in that initial study, thereby contributing to the development of modal substructural logic. This framework is analogous to Castiglione and Caramanis' (2020) relaxation method, yet differs by substituting a subgradient procedure in place of a relaxation. It allows sequential decision-making to be guided by an approximate dual solution without necessitating an explicit problem formulation or primal ascent process. We apply this method to optimize M/M/1 Queues with Renovation and examine its performance, establishing conditions for the algorithm to converge to the optimal solution or achieve a provably near-optimal solution under additional constraints. Furthermore, we illustrate the algorithm's capabilities in optimizing more complex real-world sequential decision-making problems. The actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is widely used due to its impressive results in solving complex decision-making challenges, particularly in robotics and game development.  Despite its effectiveness, actor-critic models often face issues with local optima and convergence slow-down.  To address these limitations, our proposal is to integrate the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique into the actor-critic algorithm to enhance its performance.  By combining the advantages of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and policy gradient approaches, the hybrid HMC-actor-critic algorithm allows for more efficient exploration and better policy optimization.  Consequently, this integration results in an algorithm that surpasses the original actor-critic method in performance, as demonstrated by our experimental results.  Specifically, the HMC-actor-critic method shows notable improvements in learning speed and more consistent convergence in challenging continuous reinforcement learning tasks.  Additionally, our proposal incorporates an open-source implementation of the LAMDA HMC library for integration with Python's Tensorflow and PyTorch frameworks, providing a versatile solution that can be adapted for a variety of reinforcement learning tasks.  Furthermore, our study also compares the performance of different Hamiltonian Monte Carlo variants, as well as evaluates the robustness and reliability of the integrated HMC-actor-critic method using statistical analysis and assessment of its critical components.  Notably, the integration of HMC into actor-critic models leads to a notable increase (up to 300%) in successful training outcomes, as well as a significant reduction (by up to 6x) in the required number of training episodes. To facilitate reproduction of our results, we have also included a detailed guide for configuration of the LAMDA HMC library and integration with popular deep reinforcement learning methods. Computed tomography (CT) is a widespread imaging technique that uses low-energy x-rays to create detailed cross-sectional images of the human body or other objects. In order to enhance image quality, highly energetic x-rays are often suppressed at the source. However, the actual x-ray spectra used in CT scans are usually complex and not accurately modeled, resulting in imperfect image formation models. Furthermore, system noise and limited data further degrade the image quality, necessitating the use of regularization in reconstruction methods to produce high-quality images. These procedures typically rely on non-quantitative measures such as total chili quantification to analyze the body's composition. However, these methods do not account for the effects of low-energy x-rays on image formation or the removal of highly energetic x-rays. In this study, a novel non-convex variational framework is proposed to simultaneously model CT data acquisition, filter out noise, eliminate highly energetic x-rays, and break down projected x-ray spectra into distinct energy ranges, yielding accurate images and material compositions. Our formulation incorporates convex and non-convex penalty terms to stabilize the inverse problem and is demonstrated to be well-posed. Experiments with simulated and real-world data confirm the method's effectiveness in producing high-quality images and accurate material compositions even with highly energetic x-ray suppression. Additionally, the method outperforms conventional reconstruction methods in noise reduction and material decomposition across a range of scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed framework can be adapted to require minimal adjustments to existing scanner hardware and can be extended to tackle more complex imaging challenges. These results and our reconstruction method are open-source and available at https://github.com/CMU-STTLS/recon\_polyenergetic\_CT. Our code has been validated on public datasets from the Radon Center and can be accessed via this link.
