Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources remains a complex challenge due to the scarcity of labeled data, significant character variability, and a vast vocabulary. To overcome these limitations, we focus on single-shot data augmentation by capturing handwritten text along with its contextual description during the writing process, producing a composite dataset. This approach enables us to create a large quantity of data without relying on manual labels, thereby improving model performance. To effectively utilize the generated data, we also developed a novel cross-ensemble transfer technique, where the model is trained on a composite dataset in a semi-supervised manner and then fine-tuned on a small set of labeled data. This technique enhances the model's accuracy by adapting it to real-world conditions. We evaluated our method on the datasets "Tamil Handwritten Documents" from the IFG collection and "Bangla Handwritten Text" from the ICYTS collection, showcasing significant improvement in model performance with our single-shot data augmentation and cross-ensemble transfer techniques. The source code and datasets can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/VidyuSH/SiSDA_CET_HTR. This research was partially funded by UGC Jammu.

Our method can mimic the effects of higher-loop QFT interactions in the CFT, similar to how the gapped topological free fermion can emerge from a free fermion under a certain perturbation. In the example of AdS$_5$ $\times$ S$^5$ gravity, our framework allows us to incorporate a Faddeev-Popov term, which is not possible in standard single-loop AdS/CFT, enabling us to explore the non-linear growth of entanglement entropy and establish a correspondence with higher-loop Witten diagrams. We present a distorted resolvent method to construct Nash equilibria in differential games. The approach relies on an exact distorsion of the original Nash equilibrium equation, allowing for a Liapunov function to be established and subsequent convergence analysis. We provide multiple examples and outcomes to demonstrate the method's efficacy and versatility. 

On one hand, we show that any Nash equilibrium can be obtained through distorsion, thus illustrating various distorsion mechanisms that can yield exact equilibria. Conversely, we examine the limitations of the method by identifying cases where distorsion may fail to produce exact equilibria, albeit distorsion itself being possible.

In our first series of examples, we focus on a linear quadratic differential game, obtaining a Nash equilibrium via distorsion and subsequently proving its global stability. Building on this concept, we develop a category of distorsion mechanisms called "regular distorsion," which facilitates the construction of Nash equilibria in a broader class of games. To protect image data from unauthorized access, reversible compression techniques can be used, which guarantee that the decompressed images exactly match the original images. In our previous research, a novel reversible image compression scheme was developed, leveraging the characteristics of human visual perception. This approach employs pointwise linear transformations and Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to encode and conceal image data. However, the size of the required neural networks had to be artificially limited by early stopping during training. In this study, we provide an accurate interpretation of the BNNs' behavior as local linear approximators and generalize the scheme for color images, applying the same principle. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses currently leading reversible compression schemes in terms of performance and efficiency. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/alexkulm/RLAB.

We aim to understand how people visually identify the shape and orientation of objects from optical flow. By creating digital models of object movement and testing their plausibility for humans, we expand existing research. Our study diverges from standard visual recognition studies, in which participants are typically shown static images or brief object animations, and instead asks whether humans can distinguish between different object movements using minimal clips, defined as shape and orientation-specific scenarios, or whether additional contextual information like perspective, object size, or image blurring is required. Our findings indicate that humans can differentiate between different object movements using minimal clips and that our models in collaboration with robotic systems, are capable of replicating these capabilities. Our work presents various dynamic identification models that can replicate human capabilities and provides an open framework for further research in this domain. All code and experimental data are openly available for reproduction. Additionally, we have created interactive 3D viewers that allow our models to be visually analyzed and understood better. Although our study primarily focuses on shape and orientation identification, our models are dynamic and can be applied and adapted for a broader range of tasks. Importantly, our work paves the way for more effective AI systems in dynamic settings by replicating human capabilities on identifying moving objects. In particular, our study has implications for a range of real-world applications from autonomous driving to human-robot collaboration, where understanding object movement from optical flow is critical for navigation and decision-making. Our research is a significant step towards developing more advanced and realistic AI models that can replicate human capabilities in dynamic environments. In the long term, our work aims to improve AI decision-making by basing it on more accurately replicated human perceptions and capabilities. The field of network finance is rapidly expanding, with research in financial networks, such as stock price correlations and trading activity, revealing intricate patterns and relationships. To further investigate and analyze financial data in a more targeted and in-depth manner, the application of new machine learning techniques from an unsupervised learning perspective becomes necessary. This study introduces an unsupervised anomaly detection method known as Discovering NeMo (DiNe), which identifies anomalies or irregularities in financial data by analyzing subgraphs, or network motifs, within the broader financial network. To evaluate the effectiveness of DiNe, the method is tested on real-world financial data and compared to the existing Maximal Atlas Method, as well as a more contemporary approach, Deep Network Processing of Temporal relationships. Results show that DiNe outperforms the other methods in detecting anomalies, thus confirming the method's potential for further exploration and integration into the field of network finance. This research lays the groundwork for the development of more sophisticated machine learning techniques tailored to analyzing financial data, ultimately contributing to informed decision-making in the fishing industry. Studying the final stages of star evolution, particularly supernovae, helps better understand various astrophysical phenomena. A star system consisting of a white dwarf and a companion star that is not too massive can create a spectacular supernova when they merge, which can be observed for several months. Following the supernova, a compact star, either a white dwarf or a black hole, is left behind in the remnant system. In our research, we simulated the thermal emission of a degenerate star following a Type Ia supernova, using the white dwarf case as a reference and deviating from typical behavior for a more massive degenerate star transforming into a black hole due to electron capture. Recent advancements in motion deblurring have shown promising results, with clear patterns emerging from both theoretical and practical analyses. The development of advanced neural networks, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), has significantly contributed to these breakthroughs. Inspired by self-supervised pre-training in language models, we propose the concept of Pseudo-Training, a novel approach that leverages internal data to enhance model performance. Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained model to generate blurs from a central frame, then apply it to real blurs through minimization. This strategy enables the model to tap into the inherent characteristics of its target distribution, mimicking the effect of large-scale labeled datasets. The integration of Pseudo-Training has yielded state-of-the-art deblurring performance on diverse datasets, encompassing images of humans, trees, and static scenes. The effectiveness of this technique stems from its ability to amplify the model's exposure to its target distribution, thereby boosting performance. The proposed method is also adaptable to various fields, offering a universal solution for addressing data insufficiency. The source code for this approach is publicly available.

We establish that two fundamental properties of arranged sets $\mathcal{A}$, namely having a minimal cover and being complete, can be equivalently expressed as the conditions: every interval in $\mathcal{A}$ contains a complete subset and every interval in $\mathcal{A}$ has a minimal cover, within the context of the ultrapowers of these sets. We derive these equivalences for general arranged sets $\mathcal{A}$ in any infinite cardinality $\kappa$. Furthermore, we investigate these equivalences within the specific cases of $\mathcal{A}$ being a cover of a set and being a cover of a complete set, demonstrating additional equivalences and related conditions. These findings are established using the properties and operations on interval sequences, which we introduce and study in detail. The strategy we present can be adapted for use in a variety of optical and atomic interferometers. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a vital component in machine learning for graph data, but their underlying principles are not clearly understood. GCNNs successfully capture spatial relationships in node features, but the exact mechanism by which they do so is not clearly explained. We introduce a novel analytical approach based on matched filtering that reveals the underlying statistical principles of GCNNs, effectively translating them into linear regression models. This analysis demonstrates that GCNNs with weighted neighbors and normalized graph structures are capable of capturing multi-scale spatial relationships in node features. Our method provides a clear mathematical understanding of GCNNs, explaining their generalization ability and performance on diverse datasets. Additionally, we show that GCNNs can be replicated using traditional statistical methods, such as multi-scale weighted local average filtering followed by linear regression, thereby confirming our analytical findings. This understanding enables the development of new GCNN architectures and improves the performance of existing ones. Our analytical framework is versatile and can be applied to other machine learning models to illuminate their underlying theoretical foundations. Experiments on multiple datasets from domains such as neuroscience, physics, chemistry, biology, and finance validate our analytical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of our matched filtering methodology in replicating GCNN performance. Furthermore, we show that GCNNs with optimal hyperparameters can achieve results comparable to state-of-the-art methods in machine learning for graph data, thereby confirming their practical utility and generalization ability. A detailed code implementation is available for public use, enabling researchers to replicate our results and apply the matched filtering methodology to their own research. This work opens up new avenues for the theoretical analysis and understanding of GCNNs, and demonstrates the efficacy of our analytical approach, thereby paving the way for further innovations in machine learning for graph data. Additionally, this work in GCNNs foundational analysis may be applied to other deep learning models with the potential to illuminate the underlying principles of other machine learning algorithms. Most software systems have a fundamental phase - set-up - that initializes their core functions and is triggered both at compile-time and run-time. Although the compile-time set-up phase is unique to systems programming, its potential for optimization is largely unexplored. This paper delves into whether compile-time set-up opportunities can be leveraged to reduce run-time overheads. Our analysis reveals that a significant portion of run-time set-up operations exhibit predictable patterns and can be generalized. Notably, we identified over 125% average room for optimization in a benchmark suite consisting of real-world applications. Our experimental results demonstrate that applying these generalizations manually during compile-time yields substantial improvements in the performance of our benchmarks. Specifically, the set-up times are accelerated by 2.07 times, with an average speedup of 1.91 times. Moreover, fully automated compile-time set-up optimization also yields comparable results, underscoring the vast potential for innovation in this domain. Ultimately, this study opens the door for a novel area of research, which we term 'accumulative compile-time set-up optimization.' Its potential implications extend beyond existing systems programming languages and could even be applied to the compilation of shell scripts, thereby enhancing the overall set-up phase of programs and significantly boosting their run-time efficiency. Our findings suggest that a significant 75% of run-time set-up operations can be optimized at compile-time. This discovery presents new avenues for research and contributes significantly to the domain of systems programming. Furthermore, our project, including benchmark suites, compile-time meta-programs, and experimental data, is publicly available at https://github.com/shivanshu-bhardwaj/rtso. rtso is a domain-specific language for the set-up phase of systems, and its associated compiler, cts, allow for efficient compile-time set-up optimization. Our research further demonstrates that a substantial 75% of run-time set-up operations can be optimized at compile-time, and we envision systems programming to greatly benefit from this domain, which we term 'accumulative compile-time set-up optimization.' Light dark matter particles, weighing in at less than a GeV, are attractive as a theoretical solution, but the standard direct detection approach using heavy nuclei may fall short due to the weak nature of the interaction. We propose an alternative direct detection method, focusing on lightweight detectors, such as electrons or ion traps, to enhance the detection sensitivity to weak nuclear forces involving light quarks. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck theory, a simplified model for self-propelled particles, generates diverse collective behavior when varying the persistence time and self-propulsion force. By adjusting these parameters, the system can be in either a stationary or mobile state. We found that during motion, the average speed of the particles and the speed at which the group's center moves differ significantly. Furthermore, the distance traveled by each particle is significantly greater than the displacement of the group's center, reflecting the variability in individual particle travel distances. Moreover, the distribution of individual particle travel distances is skewed, with the distance traveled by the group's center being normally distributed. These findings, confirmed through numerical and analytical examinations, demonstrate the substantial disparity in individual and group movements. Additionally, we analyzed the travel paths of the particles and the group and found their geometrical characteristics to be comparable, albeit the particle trajectories being more complex and irregular. The particle trajectories, observed under a microscope, resemble polymers' random walk paths, whereas the group's movement appears more organized and linear, resulting in a Roessler attractor when their directions are plotted on a two-dimensional plane. The emergence of this attractor is attributed to the collective motion's symmetry, broken by the individual particles' movements, leading to acausality where past events influence present movements. In other words, the current state of the system depends on its previous states, not solely on its immediate proximity in space or time. The occurrence of this attractor is a consequence of the system's nonlinear properties, evident in the long memory of the group's motion. This long memory is responsible for the non-Markovian behavior of the system, making it possible to analyze the past without requiring a detailed understanding of the present to predict the future. The system's non-Markovian characteristics are a direct result of the individual particles' movements, leading to a significant and extensive correlation in the distance traveled by adjacent particles. This extensive correlation is highly significant as it surpasses the system's dimensions, facilitating the system's transition from a homogeneous to a heterogeneous state. The individual particles' movements result in this long memory by establishing an intricate network of interconnected distances, extending far beyond the system's boundaries. This long memory enables the system to retain a permanent record of its past, making its evolution dependent on a lengthy timeline rather than a limited spatial range. The long memory of the system is a consequence of the Labor variations, a term that describes the difference in individual particle travel distances, demonstrating how the system's past influences its current state.

In recent years, advances in neural networks have led to significant improvements in predicting human movements from optical flows or frames. However, directly predicting highly variable and multi-dimensional body movements from static images is an extremely complex task. There is a notable lack of comprehensive benchmark datasets to evaluate model performance in this area. Our proposed collection, HUMBI, is a comprehensive dataset featuring 50 subjects in 400 outfits, capturing a wide range of gestures through 360-degree vision. This dataset includes 13,000 animated videos and 400 hours of motion, offering the first standardized benchmark for model evaluation. Our challenge highlights the limitations of current methods in predicting all aspects of human movement. From a technical perspective, our findings demonstrate that state-of-the-art models perform significantly better on our dataset than previously thought, but still struggle to predict certain movement components with accuracy. Our research aims to promote the development of more robust and realistic human motion forecasting through crowd-sourced data collection and the standardization of evaluation methods. This will enable the creation of more practical and effective solutions in this domain. Our code, dataset, and experiment results are publicly available for reproduction at https://www.alexneumann.fr/humbi/. This research was funded by a grant from ANR (ANR-18-CE48A06-01), and our team collaborated with CentraleSupélec to collect the dataset through crowd-sourced annotations with students. Our approach to multiview learning in this area has been patented under FR3041153. This work was presented at CVPR 2021, and our team has since made further improvements, leading to the publication of this revised paper at CVPR 2023. Our team has since developed several successful applications using this collection, including a system for automatically creating synthetic training data, a tool for predicting 3D body pose from a single image, and a platform for generating photorealistic synthetic human bodies. Our approach has been recognized with several awards, including "Best System Demonstration" at CVPR 2022, and "Best Paper" at WACV 2022, among others. This work was funded by a grant from ANR (ANR-18-CE48A06-01), and our team has since received further funding from DGA (20210019001) and ARD (20210003001). Our dataset has also received recognition through several citations, including being listed among the top datasets in the area by MMAB, and being recognized by A. Boreli as a leading benchmark collection

Despite considerable progress in cross-lingual transfer in NLP, many attempts require significant modifications to existing models and thorough knowledge of source and target languages. This study aims to facilitate more practical and model-friendly cross-lingual transfer by leveraging task representations rather than detailed labels. Our task representations are encoded in pre-trained language models like BERT, while labels are generated separately to minimize reliance on explicit source supervision. This approach allows models to focus on learning task-specific characteristics, enabling more efficient and model-independent cross-lingual transfer. To further simplify the process, we use neural machine translation as a means of transferring representations directly from the source to the target language. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, and we provide additional analysis to validate the effectiveness of our method. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jamiewood/feeble-sup Supervised-LSTMs. BERT and BERT-like models can be downloaded from https://github.com/jamiewood/feeble-sup- Supervised-LSTMs/tree/master/models.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents often learn diverse skills that can be combined for effective problem-solving.  The ability of model-based methods to learn in complex environments makes them promising candidates for multi-task learning.  However, in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning, a common issue arises where knowledge from previous tasks interferes with learning new tasks, causing a degradation in performance.  Through experiments, we found that model-based methods suffer from a significant decline in new task rewards compared to single-task settings.  The origin of this performance drop was then investigated and revealed that the long-term memory of these methods leads to destructive interference, where knowledge from different tasks overlaps and interferes with each other.  To overcome this challenge, we proposed a novel module-based approach, called MODULAR-MADO, which separates task memories to prevent interference.  By comparing it to existing model-based multi-task methods, our results showed that MODULAR-MADO achieves superior new task rewards in complex environments, outperforming existing methods by up to 35%.  The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/ikos-epi/modular-mado.  A video explanation can be found at https://youtu.be/6h4b8e4kW7U. Typically, the maximum efficiency of a heat engine is understood to be constrained by its thermal efficiency, yet quantum systems can sometimes surpass this maximum efficiency. However, the stability of quantum systems is often compromised by the continuous exchange of energy with their surroundings, leading to loss of coherence and utility. In this study, we examine the performance of quantum heat engines with limited duration of operation and restricted access to their surroundings. These restrictions are modeled after specific sets of allowable unitary operations, leading to the discovery that there are distinct thermodynamic cycles capable of achieving maximum efficiency, as opposed to the single method seen in the unlimited scenario, and that this efficiency can be quantified as the difference between the maximum and minimum energies within the system. This optimal strategy involves a quantum state with zero excess energy and zero correlations, reached through a sequence of interactive measurements, resulting in a total work output proportional to the lower bound of the system's Hamiltonian and the available temperature range, ultimately bounded by its eigenvalues. This work output can be further optimized using a combination of interactive measurements and restricted unitary operations, leading to the output $\mathcal{W} = \Delta E \tanh^2\left(\frac{\Delta E}{k_B\Delta T}\right)$, where $\Delta E$ represents the energy range and $\Delta T$ the temperature range. Notably, this output does not depend on the specific protocol used in the limited-duration heat engine, indicating its universal applicability under these constraints. Finally, we examine the effects of limited access to the system's Hilbert space on the maximum efficiency, revealing that there are distinct strategies capable of achieving this efficiency in such scenarios. In contrast, we demonstrate that coherence is essential for achieving maximum efficiency in the unlimited scenario, as stated by Jarzynski's equality. Overall, this research establishes fundamental connections between the quantum properties of systems and their thermodynamic behavior. In particular, we show that coherence plays a crucial role in maximizing efficiency, highlighting its importance beyond purely thermodynamic considerations. Additionally, this study's findings provide practical guidance in designing efficient quantum heat engines, including the optimal state for maximum efficiency and the preferred range of the system's Hamiltonian. Finally, we anticipate that these results will contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying quantum principles governing thermodynamic systems. Related work on this topic can be found in arXiv:2106.11340, arXiv:2107.07761 and arXiv:2109.00779. Further related research can be found in arX

Extreme weather events like hurricanes and storm surges have the potential to cause substantial damage to power infrastructure. Historical analysis shows that minor storm surges have led to widespread power outages in coastal cities, emphasizing the need to consider the combined effects of these weather phenomena on power grids. A major challenge in assessing storm surge impact lies in predicting the spatial and temporal progression of floodwaters that can disable power equipment. To overcome this issue, a computational framework based on the levee model for power systems is developed, allowing for the quantification of power losses as floodwaters inundate adjacent areas. A case study of Hurricane Ike's landfall in Galveston, Texas, is conducted to evaluate the performance of the approach in simulating real-world storm surge events. By combining storm surge elevations with detailed terrain data, the proposed method is able to replicate observed flood patterns and accurately assess the impact of storm surges on power systems. Results show that high flood levels can disable entire power transformers, while the subsequent decay of generator output and increased demand due to prolonged outages contribute significantly to total power losses. A parametric study is also performed to examine how power losses vary in response to differing storm surge heights, hours of infiltration, and flood depths. Consequently, the proposed method can inform decision-makers in utility and emergency management as they prepare for extreme weather events and potential prolonged power outages. Furthermore, the resulting damage estimates can be utilized in models to assess the economic consequences of storm surges, as well as support decisions regarding infrastructure investment and retirement in the face of increasing weather-related risks. Ultimately, this research aims to improve understanding of a critical and often-underappreciated factor contributing to power outage damage – the storm surge effect – and it is expected to set a precedent for applying levesee models in the analysis of large-scale complex systems. A comprehensive software package is included that users can employ to simulate and evaluate the storm surge effect on power systems based on their own storm surge scenarios, as well as leverage the methodology to develop and integrate storm surge models in distribution planning tools. A detailed guide on leveraging the software and methodology is also provided within Section 8.1. Moreover, the associated data and software can be accessed at the link: https://eng.uc.edu/~e654/index.html. Clifford analysis involves studying linear partial differential equations within Rn+1 space, utilizing the techniques of monogenic functions.  Specific properties of these functions, such as their singular points, are of particular interest.  A 1962 theorem by Boas, established the notion that in odd-dimensional spaces, at least three singular points are inevitable for any non-linear equation.  This is akin to a well-known result from classical complex analysis.  This paper generalizes Boas' theorem to scenarios involving linear partial differential equations under Clifford analysis, showing that at least three singular points are inevitable for any non-linear monogenic function in Rn+1 space.  Contrary to expectations, this holds true in both odd and even dimensions.  Additionally, we explore extensions of this theorem to scenarios involving multiple variables.  Finally, we examine specific examples and their implications to Clifford analysis.  This study opens doors to novel generalizations and applications to other fields, such as complex analysis and projective geometry.  It also sheds light on the geometric properties of monogenic functions and their connections with projective curves.  Ultimately, this paper culminates in a projective curve theorem, expressing the equivalent result in projective geometry terms. Our findings indicate that the heavy Higss boson's detection might be more likely at the Future e+ e- Collider than at the LHC's high-luminosity program, due in part to differing production rates of the two Higss bosons at these experiments. To generate high-quality speech with a specified pitch, we introduce the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model. This model combines an autoregressive neural network with a pitch-sensitive dilated convolutional neural network, and is trained to produce raw audio signals on a sample-by-sample basis. Given a model input of a specified length, it outputs a probability distribution for each time interval, and the model is optimized using a length-wise adversarial loss function and a sample-wise autoregressive loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model effectively produces raw audio signals with specified pitches. Additionally, it surpasses state-of-the-art speech synthesis models in terms of the mean opinion score in subjective evaluations. Furthermore, it matches or surpassed the objective metrics of mean absolute error and frame error in pitch prediction, and its generated audio signals exhibit lower mean square errors in both log f0 and Mel-frequency cepstral models. The model's 2-second speech samples also exhibit lower perceived disfluency, as measured by the disfluency metric. A comparison of the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's pitch spectra with that of human speakers reveals a closer match. Finally, the model's generated speech signals exhibit lower mean square errors in waveform similarity, as measured by the mean square error in the waveform similarity metric. Additionally, it has been found that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model effectively produces raw audio signals with specified pitches. A subjective listening test confirmed that the model's generated speech signals sounded more natural and natural-like than those produced by the Tacotron 2 system. The Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's demo generated speech audio is available online at the website provided. Based on these results, it appears that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model effectively produces raw audio signals with specified pitches and is a viable candidate for speech synthesis in this domain. The Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's source code is publicly available on the platform specified. The model's performance can be readily optimized to match that of state-of-the-art speech synthesis models in this domain by adjusting various hyperparameters. Recommender systems are now essential in guiding users' extensive online interactions. Many recommenders face a critical data shortage, hindering their ability to provide accurate suggestions. To overcome this challenge, researchers often turn to collaborative filtering (CF), a leading approach due to its effectiveness in addressing data scarcity. However, CF's fundamental reliance on aggregating similar user behavior raises significant issues in this context. When combined with the inherent subjectivity of user preferences, this approach can lead to overly general recommendations that fail to account for each user's unique preferences. In response to these challenges, our research introduces a novel CF method that addresses the complexities of user preferences from a global and individual perspective. This innovative approach leverages bicluster-based CF, enabling it to model local patterns of user preferences and map them to global scales through clustering analysis. By incorporating sparsity into these models, our system can filter out irrelevant and unessential user behavior, refining its recommendations and reducing their dimensionality. Furthermore, our approach enables the discovery of hidden patterns within user preferences and seamlessly translates these findings into personalized suggestions. Comprehensive evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate the exceptional accuracy and efficiency of our proposed method in surpassing state-of-the-art recommenders. Our experiments also validate the distinct advantages of user-specific bicluster-based CF over comparative methods. Additionally, our analysis highlights the substantial improvements achieved through the incorporation of sparsity into these models. These results offer key implications for the design of recommenders andsurge in the vast landscape of online interactions. Moreover, our work opens up new avenues for future research in this area. Magnetic activity in the Sun has significant spectral variations that are usually masked in solar irradiance measurements by space-based telescopes, pointing to the importance of proper correction for reliable solar energy predictions. By analyzing Sun-like stars, researchers find that common solar faculae and spot inversion temperatures lead to unusual spectral patterns, indicating other active region characteristics that can be measured from ground. Harps-n observations of high activity phases in the solar spectrum reveal unusual absorption at 543.6 nm and multiple weak features across 495-598 nm, contradicting current solar models. To improve the accuracy of solar faculae and spots' predictions, researchers suggest using new diagnostic parameters and indicators such as the 543.6 nm line area and specific combinations of features within the 495-598 nm range, which can be applied to active stars for reliable stellar activity monitoring. Furthermore, these new features may also facilitate the detection of active and variable stars with potential planetary transits. Based on the new spectral activity markers, researchers estimate a possible detection rate of 50-100 active stars and 200-300 active stars per month with harps-n, indicating the vast potential of ground-based telescopes for active star identification. To meet this potential, researchers propose the development of an automated tool to identify active stars and integrate it with existing harps-n databases and the existing exoplanet database. In addition, researchers suggest combining this new capability with other techniques to identify variable stars, opening up new avenues for active star and potential exoplanet detection. In an effort to resolve the black hole collapse issue presented by James Gardner in 1989, we propose a theoretical framework that extends the Blandford-McKee distribution to include density fluctuations. Gardner's primary concern was that the self-reinforcing nature of shocks in an otherwise uniform medium would prevent the collapse of stars into black holes. However, our model reveals an alternative solution where the density fluctuations enable the propagation of lower intensity shocks ($s\lesssim 3/2$) that an expanding star can generate and, consequently, allowing for stellar collapse to black holes. These lower intensity shocks arise due to the transfer of energy within a smaller spatial and temporal framework, which leads to a self-sustaining and smoothly varying density profile without an abrupt cutoff. Conversely, higher intensity shocks ($s> 3/2$) continue to propagate poorly and require an input of energy for their maintenance, necessitating a continuous supply of energy to sustain Gardner's original concern. Additionally, we show that the density power-law index'm' has a significant impact on shock propagation, with a particular value of'm' resulting in a nearly self-similar solution. Furthermore, we develop semi-analytical solutions for various'm' values and verify our models through numerical simulations, which accurately follow our theoretical predictions. Finally, we outline the parameters necessary for both high and low intensity shock propagation in more detail. The growing impact of AI solutions depends on their widespread acceptance by the general public, healthcare professionals, and experts. For AI systems to gain trust, they must be designed with transparent results and the ability to elucidate crucial decisions, known as explainability. However, developement of explainable AI systems remains understated in current research. We contend that requirement engineering, which focuses on comprehensively identifying, specifying, and validating stakeholder needs, can play a crucial role in addressing this disparity. This study provides an in-depth examination of the requirements engineering methodologies that research has already applied to develop explainable AI systems. It also explores the state of current research on explainability and the requirements engineering opportunities this presents. The study extracts and analyzes the requirements of various stakeholders involved in the development of AI systems that make high-stakes decisions, such as healthcare professionals and patients. These stakeholders have distinct, sometimes conflicting, needs for explainability, which can be categorized into three main groups: decision-makers, users, and the broader public. Each group has distinct, sometimes overlapping, needs for explainability, which vary based on their level of involvement with AI systems, their expertise, and personal perspectives. These needs are subject to change across different development stages and may conflict with one another. These complexities highlight the value of a user-centric approach in addressing the nuanced requirements and needs of various stakeholders involved in developing AI systems with high-stakes decision-making capabilities. This approach can facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of explainability requirements and promote the development of more effective solutions. Ultimately, this study positions requirements engineering as a vital domain for addressing the intricate requirements and needs of AI systems with transparent decision-making capabilities, which research across various domains, including explainability, can draw from. Conversely, research in explainability can, in turn, benefit from the knowledge and insights garnered through the requirements engineering domain. This interchange of knowledge can foster novel and innovative approaches in addressing the intricate requirements and needs of developing AI systems with high-stakes decision-making capabilities. These approaches can promote the development of more transparent and accountable AI systems, which are crucial for gaining public trust and meeting the evolving needs of healthcare professionals and patients. This interplay in research domains can give rise to new and innovative developments, such as user-centric methods for specifying and validating the needs of various stakeholders involved in developing AI systems with high-stakes decision-making capabilities. These user-centric methods can facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate requirements and needs of decision-makers, users, and the broader public, which can promote the development of more transparent and accountable AI

Characterizing colorectal polyps through histological analysis is the most reliable method to identify potential precancerous lesions, but this requires expert pathologists to visually examine stained tissue samples and determine their characteristics.  This process is time-consuming, leading to a shortage of pathologists, as a significant amount of tissue needs to be evaluated for accurate results.  In particular, identifying dysplasia, which indicates abnormal cell growth in the adenoma, requires substantial histological analysis and expert knowledge.  To address this issue, a collaborative study between UniToPatho and hospitals in Italy collected and annotated a comprehensive dataset of digital images from histological samples, including images of normal tissue, hyperplastic polyps, serrulated polyps, adenomas, and carcinomas.  These images are also labeled to indicate areas of mucosa, carcinoma, and dysplasia, allowing researchers to develop models that can quickly and accurately diagnose and assess dysplasia, ultimately reducing the need for and complications arising from relying solely on human pathologists.  This research aims to develop an effective and efficient model for classifying colorectal polyps and evaluating dysplasia, which will be made available to the public.  By utilizing these images, researchers can develop innovative solutions using machine learning, including neural networks, to enhance and optimize the adenoma-dysplasia histological analysis process.  In particular, models can be created to predict the type of polyp, dysplasia degree, and other characteristics, which will be used to develop an intelligent system for supporting pathologists and improving the accuracy of histological analysis.  This research initiative is part of the 2021 Objectron dataset challenge and is led by the UniToPatho research team.  This dataset contains 13,000 images from 300 stained tissue samples, covering various types of colorectal polyps and dysplasia, making it a comprehensive resource for research in this area.  This research project is part of the UniToPatho research team's efforts to apply machine learning and other innovative technologies to the field of pathology, ultimately enabling the development of intelligent systems for assisting pathologists and improving the efficiency of histological analysis.  This research will enable researchers to apply machine learning models to quickly and accurately diagnose and assess dysplasia, which is critical for identifying and managing precancerous lesions effectively. My interpretation of the Scientific Revolution runs counter to the conventional view. According to this perspective, the era saw a seismic shift in scientific thought, propelled by a group of innovative scientists who rejected established metaphysical beliefs dominant in medieval philosophy. However, I contend that this narrative is an exaggeration and that the scientists of the era, including Galileo, retained many medieval philosophical beliefs. Furthermore, these scientists were more united in their ignorance, as they shared common misconceptions about the world, rather than being divisive over their philosophical views. The true catalyst for the Scientific Revolution was the accumulation of empirical data and the development of sophisticated mathematical tools, which enabled scientists to pinpoint the discrepancies between observational evidence and the prevailing metaphysical beliefs in physics. Ultimately, this perspective enables us to comprehend the vast progress made in physics during the era. Moreover, it clarifies the significance of Galileo's contributions, showcasing his role as a leading figure who integrated mathematics and physics while maintaining traditional metaphysical beliefs, rather than an uncompromising advocate for philosophical change. Finally, this study offers an alternative understanding of the Scientific Revolution's character, revealing a diverse range of intellectual positions among early modern scientists. Conversely, it also highlights Galileo's stubborn adherence to outdated metaphysical beliefs, particularly his refusal to abandon his support for continuant philosophy, as seen in his works on motion and the tides. We propose a novel role, the scribe, whose primary responsibility is to document a system's architecture and behavior throughout its development, enabled by cutting-edge tooling that previously made this task impractical. By streamlining the process, we find it efficient to assign a scribe role even in small teams of two or three members. In this paper, we explore the benefits of the scribe role and provide guidelines for effective utilization. Additionally, we detail our experience in incorporating a scribe in the design of three distinct distributed systems, each serving different purposes. We believe the scribe role will become an integral part of software development teams.
